paragraphs.text: THE BOOK OF GENESIS.
In the beginning the Lord set in place heaven and earth:
for the earth was formless, hidden beneath the flood,
and God, immeasurable, moved above the vast waters,
while chaos and black darkness dimmed all things;
and as he ordered these to be parted, he speaks from heaven's pole:
"Let there be light!" And all things shone brightly in the world.
When the Lord had completed the works of the first day,
he founded the sky, whitening with newborn clouds.
The boundless sea receives its wandering shores,
sweeping along many rivers in mighty currents.
The third dawn uncovered the tawny face of the lands;
soon the dry land is given its name and called "earth".
Flowering shoots spring up over the windy plains,
and fruit-bearing boughs at once bend down their arms.
On the fourth day he brings forth the moon with the sun's lamp,
and fixes the stars that shine with trembling light.
These elements he gave as signs to the world beneath,
to teach the seasons that must change through their varied risings.
On the fifth day the flowing rivers receive the fish,
and birds of every kind hang their wings upon the air.
On the sixth the Father makes the cold snakes slither into coils,
and spreads the herds of four-footed beasts over all the fields,
and commanded all things to grow everywhere with manifold
offspring, and to roam and graze across the boundless lands.
When divine power had established these things by its command,
seeing that the things of the world still lacked a ruler,
it speaks these words: "Let us make man, exactly
in the likeness of our countenance, to reign over the whole world."
And though he could have composed him by a word alone,
yet he deigned himself to shape him with his holy right hand,
and from his divine breast breathed into the senseless breast.
When he saw him formed as if in his own image,
he judges that alone he would brood over gnawing cares.
At once he floods his eyes with a drenching sleep,
so that from a rib drawn out a woman might be formed more softly,
and a shared substance might strengthen the twin bodies;
and she is given the name Eve, which means "of life".
Therefore sons by custom leave their parents
and cleave to their wives, settling their homes with them.
On the seventh day God rested at the end of his works,
establishing it as holy for the joys of the age to come.
Then, when the throngs of living creatures were shown in order,
Adam gave each of them, one by one, the name that endures,
skilled in the wisdom that had been given him.
God deigns to address him, and Eve joined with him:
"Increase by manifold birth into the times to come,
that the sky and the lands may be full of your offspring,
and, as my heirs, pluck the various fruits
which the groves and fields yield from their rich soil."
When he had spoken thus, paradise is furnished as a joyful court
and faces toward the light of the rising sun.
Among these grows a tree bearing deadly fruit,
producing the mingled taste of life and death.
In the midst of these dwellings a river flows in a pure stream,
which waters the glorious gardens with its clear waves,
and from its surging spring cuts four channels.
The Pishon, exceedingly rich, rolls with gold-bearing waters
and wears down shining gems in its hoarse eddies —
the one is called prase, the other the burning carbuncle —
and with clear shallows washes the land of Havilah.
After it the Gihon glides past and enriches the Ethiopians;
the third is the Tigris, joined to the lovely Euphrates,
furrowing Assyria apart with its swift stream.
Here Adam was placed as guardian with his faithful wife,
and as its tiller he is instructed by these words of the Thunderer:
"Do not fear to pluck together the permitted fruits
which the unshorn grove has brought forth on its leafy boughs,
but take care lest by chance you gather the harmful apple
that flourishes with a twofold juice for separate effects."
Meanwhile deep night still held them blind,
and no garment had covered their newly formed limbs.
Among these dwellings and gardens of mellow berries
the foaming serpent, surpassing all animals in cunning,
crept silently in chilly coils;
turning over livid lies in his biting mind,
he tests the soft heart within the woman's breast:
"Tell me, why do you fear the happy fruit of this tree?
Has God not hallowed all the fruits that have grown?
Indeed, if you are eager to pluck this honeyed food,
the golden world will smile on you from its star-bearing pole."
She refuses, and fears to touch the forbidden branches;
but still her heart is overcome by its weak judgment.
At once, as she bit the mellow fruit with snowy tooth,
a clear sky shone forth, stained by no cloud.
Then the taste, planting its allure in her honeyed throat,
drove her to bring the gift to her unsuspecting husband.
As soon as he took it, the night was wiped away, and his shining
eyes flashed out clear as the world grew bright.
So when each of them looked upon their naked body,
they shade with fig leaves what they see as shameful.
As it happened, as the sun's light was now setting, they recognize
the Lord's sound, and in fear they make for hidden places.
Then the Lord of heaven addresses sorrowful Adam:
"Tell me, where are you now?" He answered thus, as a suppliant:
"O Lord, I tremble with fearful heart at your words,
great one, and naked I am worn down by chilling fear."
Then the Lord: "Who gave you the harmful fruit?"
"The woman handed it to me, saying that at once her eyes
were flooded with gleaming daylight, and that the clear bright sky
had shone on her, and the sun and the stars of heaven."
At once God's anger terrifies the troubled Eve,
as the Most High seeks the author of the forbidden deed.
Then she reveals: "I took in the persuasive speech
of the serpent, by his deceiving guile and coaxing entreaty.
For, weaving his words with viper's poisons,
he told me these fruits were sweeter than all others."
At once the Almighty condemns the serpent's deeds,
decreeing that the monster live hated by all,
henceforth crawl forward on its outstretched breast, and chew
the ground with its bite, in a war to last for all times
between human minds and the gliding creature itself,
so that, its head cast down, it should crawl low behind men's legs
and heels, as it glides and presses close upon them.
The woman, wretchedly deceived by fraudulent persuasions,
is decreed to bring forth her offspring in hard peril
and to bear subjection to her husband with diligence.
"But you, to whom the counsel of your wife seemed true —
she who yielded, overcome, to the cruel serpent —
you will lament wretched toil for long ages.
For instead of a crop of wheat there will spring up for you
the thistle and the bramble bristling with sharp thorns,
so that, with weary body and sorrowful breast,
your anxious food will cost you many sighs,
until, in the setting time of approaching death,
you are returned to the lowly earth from which you bear your body."
This done, the Lord gives the frightened pair weariness of life,
and drives them, cast down, far from the sacred gardens,
and sets them with their backs to it and shuts them out by a fire between,
in which the Cherub whirls amid a very swift blaze,
while the burning crest seethes and rolls its flames.
For them the Lord, lest their limbs stiffen in numbing cold,
sewed skins stripped from the bodies of beasts,
covering their naked limbs with warm garments.
So when faithful Adam now perceived himself
to be a husband in marriage, he bestows on his wife the name
of beloved mother; and the two offspring of his seed
their father at once names with differing names:
one bears the name of Cain; and with him Abel
tended the harmless sheep with great care,
while the other turned the earth with the curved plough.
When they brought their gifts to the eternal Thunderer,
each, as his mind prompted, gave different fruits.
For the first offered what had sprung from the fertile clods,
but the other devotes himself with a gentle lamb,
bearing in his hand the pure entrails and snowy fat,
and at once his devout offerings please the Lord who beholds them.
Because of this Cain blazed up with icy anger.
God, deigning to address him, begins thus:
"Tell me, if you live rightly and discern what is harmful,
could you not live pure of any guilt incurred?
Cease to seek your brother's ruin in your biting mind;
he will bow his neck to you as to his lord."
Yet, not softened by these words, he leads his brother to the fields,
and when he saw him caught alone on the deserted grass,
gnashing his teeth he crushes the innocent throat with both hands.
The Lord, who watched this deed from high heaven,
asks where on earth Abel may be.
He denies that he was appointed his brother's keeper.
God says to him: "Does not the voice of his blood
sound out, sent up to me, and rise to the lofty heavens?
Know, then, what awaits you for so great a crime:
for the earth which just now grew wet with your brother's blood
will be cursed for you, whom it hates, and refuse the seeds
entrusted to it, and bring forth no fruit, its plants consumed,
so that, benumbed, your limbs shaken with constant trembling,
you may forever heave sighs as though at a funeral close at hand."
Terrified, he groans and begs death from the deity;
yet it was not granted by the angry Thunderer:
for, having deserved evils, he is marked out by a branded sign,
so that no one may lawfully strike the guilty man down with the sword,
lest a sevenfold peril bring about a greater death.
At once he goes out from the face of the Lord like one lost,
turning from his home to the soil of the land of Nod;
and from among the sons whom his faithful wife bore
he founded a lofty city with the name of the firstborn.
Enoch begets Irad, and he then Mehujael,
from whom as father Methuselah in due course came forth
into the air of life and drew out the span of a long life.
But Lamech, who struck down dreadful Cain with the sword,
suffers far heavier things for slaying the guilty man;
for seventyfold penalties bind the one who deserves them.
Groaning over the deed, he reproaches himself unbidden before his wives,
of whom the first was Adah and the second Zillah.
The first bore Jabal, who as a shepherd in the grassy
fields grazed his flocks on the glad pasture.
After him came Jubal, who discovered the musical plectrum
and strings harmonious in their varied murmur.
Then Zillah bore Tubal, whose custom it was to pour streams
of bronze, and to shape iron beaten on the anvil
in diverse ways at the roaring furnace;
after him came Naamah, born of the same father.
Meanwhile Adam, not feeble in his vigorous years,
begets Seth after the death of gentle Abel.
He then begets Enosh, on whom the Lord bestowed
a pure heart. At his asking, the Lord consented
to be called upon, and received the offerings of his peaceful mind.
So when Adam had completed nine hundred
and thirty years, he fell asleep in death and rested.
After him long-lived Enosh lived through nine hundred and five
years; and Kenan, equalling him,
was longer only by five more years.
Younger than this by thrice five years, old Mahalalel
in turn lies down in death; then Jared lived,
his long life shorter by thirty and three.
Enoch, whose care it was to serve the Mighty One
and unite his mind with God, much younger than these —
if you care to add to three hundred completed years five
and six times ten — was covered by a sudden darkness,
hidden away and, by the Lord's great mercy, taken off,
and lives a happy life in peaceful time.
But Methuselah stretches out his years to nine hundred
and seven times ten, to which it is right to add one.
Lamech, born of this father, when Noah was born,
spoke thus, as in the manner of the prophets he foresees
the future and sends his thoughts into the age to come:
"This one will give us untroubled dealings in life,
and will remove the hard burden and bring back peace,
which was driven out by evil deeds and by our guilt
and by our sorrowing hands, though by their labor furrowed
the earth refuses fruit, since the Lord spoke a curse."
He lived seven hundred years and seven,
with seventy added on top, as the sum requires.
Of his begetting Noah is born, noble for upright deeds,
to give seed to an innocent age.
And he begets three sons, Shem and Ham and Japheth,
accustomed to beat the softened iron in rhythm
and swiftly forge the sparkling masses.
This prophet had now lived six hundred years
when the Lord, weary of the crimes of the dreadful world
and of men's manifold guilt through their long lifetimes,
in pity cuts short the troubles of a drawn-out life,
and set a limit of twice sixty years,
which no one could exceed under the law laid down.
Meanwhile earthly pleasure entices the holy ones
and holds captive those coming down from the heavenly citadel;
for when they see women's faces smiling in their beautiful bodies
and cling to all-too-pleasing embraces,
they begot for themselves giants of grim bulk —
by whose crimes the patience of the Lord at last
is driven to offense; and as he conceives long anger
and grieves that man was created, shaped by his
starry right hand, moved in his holy breast he speaks:
"It is my right to wipe out the sins of the guilty world
with the ocean's waves, and to engulf the whole earth,
and to drown the human race in vast floods,
and with them beasts of every kind that crop the glad
grass across the fields as they roam the lofty hills.
One death shall crush the serpents, the birds and the wild beasts,
that my anger may grow mild when their frauds are wiped away."
So Noah receives the mighty commands of God,
ordered to build an ark with double chambers,
to hold the nests of birds that would survive to breed.
And lest the timbers spring apart in splitting cracks,
he smeared the ark with the rich grease of pitch.
It was three hundred full cubits long,
and fifty wide, spreading across its belly.
But where the gables rise with their lofty roof,
it is raised up thirty cubits toward the sky,
with squared planks, to give way to no floods,
and bearing in its middle doors on easy hinges.
After God looked down from the stars on this finished work,
he addresses thus the prophet who was to be sent upon the waters:
"Climb quickly, you and your sons and daughters, into the boat
that will float on the swelling waves, for I have seen your heart
to be just, and your will, long known to me,
has deserved greater things than the present; and gather
and shut in with you gentle beasts of every kind
by sevens in pairs; of the unclean herd you shall let
two be with you; and bring in food for all these
and the food you are used to, lest, when through the vast floods
all tilling has ceased, you too should suffer grievous
hunger, food not having been provided beforehand, as you are carried over the grey
salt sea; for when the bright light of the sun
has come forth in the sky for the seventh time, I am preparing to pour out all the rainclouds
from the ethereal pole and roll forth all the springs
in a greater flood, so that the ocean, swollen with waves,
may surge, receiving the foaming rivers more abundantly
and burying all things in mud with its outpoured expanse.
For through forty days joined with their nights
I will fill the dripping clouds with ceaseless storm,
so that whatever lives may be drowned in the swelling waves."
When this was said, the Lord's commands are carried out, the old man
willing and eager, who, noble for his long age
and passing six hundred years, entrusted himself to the waves
and took in with him his sons and their wives,
trusting, though he was hidden in a narrow cave.
Meanwhile the clouds loosed all their rains,
and the abyss released its watery springs into the seas.
And now for forty days all things lie flooded.
No birds hold up their bodies on light wings,
nor does the wild beast escape the waters on a high-ridged hill;
all things are buried in the sea; one death is the lot of all.
Meanwhile, suspended over the swelling sea,
the ark, floating and hovering, protected the prophet shut within,
and as a parent preserved the seeds for ages to come,
safe from shipwreck of its own. Soon the thinning air
began to draw the rains back into the pitch-black clouds.
And now the sea shrinks as the waters slide back,
and when the boat was floating on a modest flood,
the old man sends out the black-breasted raven,
which, borne on light wings by the swift wind,
did not return, leaving the just prophet's hopes in suspense.
After it he sends a white dove over the waters,
which, wearied by its flight over the watery plain
and finding ground nowhere, returned to the kindly prophet.
And when the light of the returning sun shone
for the seventh time, he sends out the bird with clapping wing,
which, finding a grove, brought back her beak filled
with sprigs of the rich olive, just as the evening star
rose among the stars and ran before the night with trembling fire.
Then again, when seven days had duly passed,
the bird is sent out over the sea, and, gliding off
on a swift course, never returned to the shared hall.
So the prophet had then passed six hundred and one
years. In the first month following,
on the first day of the month, when the freed earth
seemed to uncover the mountains far off and send up steam —
mountains the sea had covered to fifteen cubits —
and then, when the second month had run its course but three
days remained, the earth was now free of all the flood
and gladly showed its own green.
So when the ark had come to rest on the bared mountains
which in the ancient tongue bear the name of Ararat,
the old man unbars the doors, returning new seeds to the earth,
and gladly built a festal sanctuary to the Thunderer;
and mindful of his vow, as he burns the altars with flames,
the victim was worthy, as it gives off gentle odors
that breathe out before the Lord with joyful breaths.
Then, lest the earth perish by a like peril,
the Lord does away with the flood for times to come,
ordering the swift months and seasons of the turning year
to roll their accustomed courses unresting:
only a saffron bow shall be bent in the clouds
when the bright stars shed dew from a cloud in a clear sky.
The Lord's blessing follows the gentle prophet,
namely that over all things which earth and sea bring forth
he should faithfully rule, since they are subject to him as ruler;
and he is warned to keep from his table the flesh of beasts
that have not given up their life with their blood let out:
for this reason, that in many creatures the life is lodged in it.
"But if a man is slain by iron or by a wild beast's tooth,
I will seek out," he said, "those who do such things;
they shall bow their necks in like manner, to shed their blood."
Then the Lord soon divides the children of the prophet he favored
and bids them take fertile lands, each apart,
that they might fill the empty world with crowded offspring.
The prophet receives this reward by the Lord's gift:
that as the discoverer of the vine he might taste the bright wine.
When he was soon filled with cups and heavy with sleep,
Ham mocked him — from whom the Canaanite youth
is born, who named their nation after their chief —
showing his father to his brothers with his limbs uncovered.
They, alike in piety, cover and veil him where he lay:
with their backs carefully joined, turning away their eyes,
they tended the sleeping old man, and did not see the limbs
shameful to speak of, bending their necks in tender modesty.
When the prophet, his mind now clear, learned of this work
of piety, he condemns the offender for all time,
making him last among his brothers and subject
to harsh rule, begging the strong in terror.
Then the old man died, having passed nine hundred
and fifty years, as the formula of the law provided.
His offspring, hastening to raise walls,
founded outstanding cities of towering height.
And as, pressing on with the work, they vie in building walls,
they mark them with names: Tarsus and Citium and Rhodes,
standing out with gates washed by the waves of the sea.
From here Canaan takes his name, from here Sidon rises,
thence the Jebusite, the Amorite joined to the Hittite;
the Girgashite flourishes, the Hivite, the Arkite, the Sinite,
the Zemarite, the Arvadite and Orus, and whoever dwells
within the walls of Gaza, with whom Gomorrah and Sodom are yoked,
and Admah and Zeboiim, to which Lasha is joined.
They also found Mesha, and Sephar likewise,
and the high-ridged hill that lifts its cloudy summits
where the flame of whitening day first bursts forth.
From their stock Nimrod is born, accustomed to fierce
hunting and towering with huge limbs,
and delighting to raise himself against the holy God,
fierce in the manner of the giants, whom a lofty neck
and enormous head lift high into the air.
He establishes Babylon and Erech, Accad and Calneh
among the woodlands of Shinar; then he founds Asshur,
and established Nineveh, splendid with its buildings,
and Rehoboth, and after it Calah. Resen
divides their woodlands and rises on the boundary between.
And while they eagerly vie and give names to their walls,
they come into a plain called by the name of Shinar,
and, striving to raise hollow towers to the stars,
they make no lime with which set stones are bound,
but bricks of clay are baked in a scorching furnace,
so that the walls might shine with vast buildings before
some new migration should scatter the nations apart.
Bitumen served for lime, which is drawn out like soft wool
and binds the stones together with its pliant body.
For among all of them a tongue of shared speech
spoke in like utterances and common words.
At last the Lord came down and saw the walls,
ordering varied voices suddenly to burst forth
and diverse sounds, in which each nation speaks.
At once the world is filled with settlers placed in their lands,
and the place of division is soon called Confusion.
After these comes Abram, who greatly trusted in the Lord,
whom his father begot, called Terah by his ancient name.
And Lot is joined to him, a brother of kindred blood.
When they had now grown strong in their youthful years,
they joined themselves in marriage: Lot rejoices in his bond with Milcah,
and Sarah is enriched with Abram as her husband,
though she lived into old age without a child.
Terah anxiously took them away from the Chaldean flock,
since the fields of Canaan with their leafy hills appealed to him.
But God, who would know the mind of chosen Abram,
commands him to take up dwellings in another region:
"Come now, make haste, take yourself from your ancestral lands,
and leave your kindred's houses and the thresholds you know;
for I will make you the chief of a vast nation.
And besides this I will add that whoever wounds you
with malicious words shall be cursed by the Lord's mouth
and suffer every sorrow; but whoever with kindly speech
tells of your good, may he grow greater in happy fortune."
Their home is changed, and the camp is pitched at Shechem,
which the Lord pledged to the prophet for long ages.
There in haste he raises holy altars:
climbing a mountain that spurns the breaking waves
and, swelling high, looks out on the ruddy light of the sun, ...
here too an altar is founded with piled stones
and God is prayed to; then the prophet makes his way
through lonely fields, where the land lies far from settlers;
and since it is ever parched in its thirsty veins,
barren, it brought on famine, and anxiety with it.
In this fear the fertile countryside of the Nile is sought.
And because Sarah shone with striking beauty,
she is told to say that she is bound to no husband
but is his sister, lest by chance, with savage daring,
the jealousy of an unbridled crowd should bring harm to her husband
and a grim rival should treat him as a foe.
The crowd of Canopus marveled at him as he came,
and they scan Sarah every way with desiring eyes.
And when she had been praised by the nobles and handed to the king,
the prophet is received with sweet wishes and words.
Yet the King of heaven did not wish this to be imposed on him;
for he drives out the king, shaken by many great terrors at once,
who, guilty of a harmful outrage,
rebukes the chief for saying his wife was rather
his sister, and mocking him with false cunning.
Then he bids him joyfully take his bride away with him,
with his herds and whatever he had brought from his native shores.
For God had always granted his servant, who spoke in accord with him,
great wealth and all the greatest things.
Lot too receives back whatever he had brought there,
and returning they are at last set down on their native shores.
And there, as their flocks wander, running in among each other,
the shepherds of the herds clash in strife,
because the small pastures of the two hemmed in the teeming flocks.
But the patriarch, wishing to settle the untamed quarrels,
offered his brother to take whatever fields he wished.
He gladly accepts, asking for the banks of the Jordan,
a river which long ago, swelling with waves as the Nile does,
enriched the fertile plains with its overflowing stream.
The old man receives the acres of Canaan that fell to him by lot
and settles his herds across the green fields.
But he was not permitted to establish lasting dwellings:
for the patriarch was commanded to survey with his gaze the land
which the flaming sun, returning, beholds at either end,
or the twin Bears look down upon to its farthest reach,
promised to the race to be born of so great a father.
Whoever longs to grasp their number in words
could sooner count the throngs of stars, or the grains of sand
that the sea sometimes lays bare on the shifting shore.
He goes on to the oak called by its ancient name, Mamre,
and there he dedicates a lofty altar to the everlasting God.
Soon after concord had parted the brothers,
so that each could settle his realm in the fields he chose,
four kings rise up from a numerous people
and warlike, with a great army, lay Sodom waste;
and four battle lines, upheld by twice two princes,
hurl their iron through the clouds as far as the Salt Valley.
The five tyrants abandon the war and take to flight,
and in headlong flight they hide in the leafy mountains
whatever could escape death. The victors' true names
are Arioch, Dachar, Chedorlaomer,
and Amraphel too, greedy in the prime of his years.
Amid all this, among the many things that happen in the hazard of war,
Lot too is captured with his whole family and household.
When a messenger told this with mournful lips,
the prophet rose up, and from his great flock of servants
he called three hundred attendants, adding twice nine more,
and leading them himself to war, he took up the sword again.
In the middle of the night he falls on men who now feared nothing,
routs the victors and slays many of the enemy.
More than that, he receives back his brother, rescued from such great peril,
and drags the plunder with him in a broad column.
He is welcomed with glad praise by the nobles of Sodom
and by the high priest of God, renowned for his holy deeds —
this was Melchizedek, prince and ruler of Salem —
and he blessed him, offering bread and wine —
and received a tenth of the produce as a gift from Abram. —
The king asks the victor kindly to give back the captives,
and to carry off the rest as his reward by the law of war.
But victorious valor, content with its own restraint,
accepts as its whole reward the brother it longed for.
Soon God, illumining the prophet's heart as he slept,
commands him to empty his breast of all fear,
since he is safe beneath the shelter of the unconquered right hand.
Eagerly, with the leave granted him, he speaks:
"What do your gifts offer me, for all such great words?
For long old age has come upon me and shakes my weary frame,
and, worn out as I am, I am not granted a son to leave behind at my death.
And since I have no offspring from a noble marriage,
a base-born heir will be mine, one whom a slave woman bore."
The Lord strengthens the prophet, saying:
"Do not fear, but trust; no servant shall be your heir.
For if anyone can know the stars that have no number,
or run through all the sands of the sea,
he alone will be able to reckon and count the offspring
that is to be granted you, wherever the whole world extends;
and from your seed shall be born one who will behold what is yours,
your son, and the offspring also of the eternal King:
for I am the Lord, the founder of the heavens, and I
brought you safely by my help out of the Chaldean nation."
The old man believed these things, and judged that nothing would fall short
of the Lord's words, with the sincere insight of his heart;
and, relying on him, he asks, pleading in gentle words,
for signs from God to bear in his mind and follow in his heart,
in return for so great a gift, by which he might beget a son from a sluggish
body, its limbs now chilled because his time had run its course.
At God's bidding he makes ready a heifer now three years old,
adding a lively bullock with a fierce brow,
then a ram, a he-goat, and a shaggy she-goat,
and a pair of doves, together with a turtledove like them.
Soon he splits the bodies of the beasts into twin halves,
leaving the birds unharmed, their flesh whole;
he arranges everything and sets it on the holy altar,
and places himself nearby, alert of mind and ear.
But see, in the first hours of the dark night
the pure breast of the holy prophet is struck with terror,
and black darkness rushes in, confounding the light.
Astonished at this, he receives the Lord's comfort,
as he learns beforehand of the new seed of a nation to come,
which through varied fortunes would be placed under a harsh king
of Egypt, whose name will be the bitter Pharaoh.
"For four hundred years, subject to masters,
it will serve, then be called back again to fruitful lands;
and with fortunes reversed, the people that once trembled as a slave
will wield the sceptre, curbing nations with mighty strength.
But you, when the limit of your measured age has come,
your course complete, will be committed to the tomb in your fathers' land.
For the people, torn from a home that is hostile to it,
will come here, to be given the houses of its forefathers of old.
For from where the inhabitant now rejoices in the lands of the Nile
to where the swift Euphrates flows past the regions of the Syrians,
they will hold the Kenite peoples and the Kenizzites,
the Kadmonites, and the Hittites along with the Perizzite nation;
and the Rephaim, and the Jebusite band that clings to them,
and the Canaanites will be driven from the home they love.
Moreover the Amorite, thrust out along with his ally the Girgashite,
will yield, half-dead, the fields he held to those who come."
When God had uttered these holy words to the prophet,
beneath the setting sun he gives a clear sign by lightning.
For like a flame seething in a surging furnace,
it was seen to lick up the flesh of the slaughtered beasts.
Meanwhile Sarah, long since worn out by barren years,
had now lost even the hope of becoming a parent;
and since she could not bring forth a child from her chilled womb,
she began to coax her husband toward a second
source of joy, and compels him, reluctant, to know the companionship of her slave,
so that he might at least be a father through a lowly pledge.
Straightway Hagar the Egyptian is led into the bridal chamber
and from her fertile womb bears Ishmael, the bastard son.
When with a slave's cunning she scorned her mistress,
she was struck with harsh blows and fled, wounded.
And while she hid herself, far from the road, by a nearby spring,
a messenger came down from the heavenly summit of the sky,
counseled her first, and sent her back to her masters' house,
and moreover gladdened her with a great gift.
And because she had seen the holy one shining with brilliant light,
she named the spring with a name to match.
And now Abram the prophet had completed nine tens and nine years,
when he learns that he is soon, very soon, to be a father
through the great gift of a son to be given him —
he with whom the covenants of the most high God stand in accord,
destined to be father and leader of countless nations,
receiving peaceful dwellings for vast ages.
More than that, he comes forth greater than his former name:
an added vowel letter [?] brings him honor,
and she who had been Sara is ordered to be called Sarra.
Moreover Ishmael, enriched through his father's prayer,
as prince both begets and rules twice six peoples.
After these events, when the eighth sun had come, the old man
had the males brought forward and cut off their foreskins with iron,
adding likewise all those of foreign birth.
Then, when the time of the promised gift was at hand,
his face wrinkled and he dissolved into trembling laughter,
as he silently turned the great promises over within himself:
"Will you believe that God can create what never existed
and bring forth strength from broken limbs?"
Now the sun, burning hotter, was climbing to the middle of the sky,
and the great old man was seeking coolness in the shade,
when suddenly he sees three young men standing there together.
Attentive to all, he courts the one above the rest and begs him
not to pass his servant by with hurried step as he goes on,
but in peace to deign to accept the shelter of his oak,
and to wash both his feet in cool water,
and to deign to take the bread set on a friendly table.
Consent is given, and he quickly carries out the revered commands.
Sarah too, hurrying, lets herself be seen,
and willingly brings out three measures of fine flour,
which she had set to bake in the hot vapor of the ashes.
Then a calf, its horns curving forward from a swelling brow,
is chosen, its hide darkened by no blemish,
and dishes of freshly curdled milk are set out.
And while he feeds God, present under a threefold image,
he tastes sweet joys from holy words:
"What is Sarah doing now?" (for she was hidden in the house
at that time), and the true Light repeats the words begun:
"Rejoice, mindful prophet: when a full year has passed, no less,
she will be a mother." At this the woman, glad, laughed out of sight
and despaired of giving birth from her aged body.
Meanwhile it is asked what the cause of the laughter was.
She denies that she was moved to idle laughter,
for she is afraid, and turns over her fault in her silent breast.
The young men rise, comely with equal radiance,
and gaze with all their light upon Sodom lying below.
Then the Lord, not allowing anything to stay hidden from the prophet,
declares what cause leads him to the wicked cities:
"Roused by the boundless outcry of Sodom and of Gomorrah beside it,
I have come, and I mean to see the truth" —
so that, because of the guilty mob and the horrible voice that is at work,
the two towns together might burn with lightning from heaven.
Here the anxious prophet asked, in a servant's words,
what number of holy men would save the guilty walls.
Beginning the count at five times ten,
he learns that, under the strong shelter of twice five men,
the people weighed down by vices would escape ruin.
Straightway two come to Sodom, the Son and the Sustainer,
as the evening star was already breaking forth with moist fire.
There Lot was sitting before the gates, as was his custom.
And when he had looked upon the men, glorious and alike in form,
he bowed low, worshipped them, and led them to his own threshold,
though they wished rather to lodge in the middle of the street.
He feeds them white unleavened bread of fine flour,
and then they lay their drowsy limbs on a couch.
But see, the whole raging crowd of Gomorrah rushes out,
surrounding Lot's house in fierce uproar,
and demanding the men, they wrangle with swollen mouths.
He, mindful of peace, tries to soften the raging men,
and even eagerly offers his daughters to the madmen,
so that their perverse desire might rather burn in lawful lust,
keeping shameful acts away from those of their own sex.
But his words move them not at all. The doors are broken with iron.
And while they crowd together, while they tear away the strong bars,
their eyes, shut in by pitch-black darkness, groaned.
After this, ordered to take his dear ones far away,
he invites his sons-in-law, who with dull minds refuse.
Yet, so far as his gentle mind could win by constant entreaty,
he led out his daughters, who followed along with their mother.
And while he goes forward, while he climbs the heights of the hill
opposite and wonders within himself what would follow next,
the woman, as she looks back at the citadels behind her,
grew stiff, and took on the form of salt in place of a body.
He, safe, enters the dwellings of lofty Zoar.
Soon a crash hurls thunderbolts from a horribly roaring sky,
and sulfurous flames rush down in a stinking whirlwind,
licking alike the walls and the lofty rooftops.
When all had been torn down into ash in swift ruin,
the flames were seen rising with ruddy crests
by Abraham from afar, as he pondered in his mindful heart
that no falsehood is ever joined to the words of the Lord.
Lot no less, settled in a safe dwelling,
gave comfort with tender love to his daughters,
who without husbands could not bring forth offspring.
They, when they saw that the means of having children was taken away
and their mother's honor gone, with their father alone left,
prepare a feast and bring out wine for their parent,
so that unknowingly he might have the forbidden use of his daughters.
Without delay a burden grows within the women's bodies,
and the wombs of both swell from the same kindling.
The first bears a boy, called Moab in his father's tongue;
the other names hers Ammon, with a different word.
The one is father of the Ammonites, the other the father of the Moabites.
Meanwhile Abraham departs from the place where he had settled
and crosses into the lands of Gerar with his wife and companion.
Here Abimelech desired union with Sarah
by a prince's will (for the outstanding prophet had said
that she was his sister, lest his wife's beauty should contrive
harm for an innocent man, as he guarded against a rival's anger);
yet he could not prevail, driven back by mighty terrors
such as strike the mind whenever lust is perverse:
for God tormented the tyrant by sending an avenging officer;
and when this one had broken off his sleep with a terrifying vision,
the king, trembling, his mind scarcely restored, accosts the prophet,
asking why Sarah had been called his sister, as though no husband's
bonds bound the bride who was joined to the prophet.
He explains the reasons and clears himself of the charge,
for he had told no lie: from his father's seed
Sarah was sprung, a shared line carrying down their blood.
When this was settled, the ruler gives a thousand talents
and servants, and adds gentle flocks and herds,
and acres too, spread out across broad fields,
if only the gifts might soften the guilt he had deserved.
For the king's house, paying the penalty for the sin committed,
with a host of diseases raging through them all,
had long since lost all offspring from the women's wombs.
But when the peaceable prophet prayed for the king,
prostrate before God, at once glad fertility
returned to all and filled their wombs abundantly.
He himself too, through prayers answered beyond custom in his last days,
becomes a father, and recalling the comfort of glad laughter
he names him Isaac, and carries out the commands of the high deity,
on the eighth day cutting away the covering
from his member; and when he sees him now taking steady steps,
among the kinsmen gathered from the allied stock
the father feasts and rejoices at rich tables;
for joy is greater when hopes had been despaired of.
And now, as the boy played together with the slave-born boy,
this drove the mother to swell with fiery gall,
so that she would drive out the hated slave woman together with her child —
and the old man, though unwilling, observing the supreme commands
of the Lord, thrust them both out together.
But the woman, after she had been sent away from her master's dwelling,
wanders through trackless solitudes in a remote retreat.
And now she had used up all the bread and all the wine,
sighing with weary breast over her fainting son;
she came to a well that had then been given the name
Oath, and filled the wilderness with mournful lament:
when God, moved beyond the heavens by the afflicted woman's tears,
strengthens her in her fear, and tells of great
kingdoms prepared for her son, whose death she was then bewailing.
Straightway, sipping gushing water from a flowing pool,
she rises and rejoices along with her rejoicing son.
God's gracious commands go forward: now the little boy began
to draw the bow and to shoot winged arrows.
Meanwhile the prophet, lest the leader Abimelech
should perhaps secretly plot something, binds treaties of peace,
so that, since quarrels had arisen over wells,
restored quiet might make life secure.
Oaths are sworn, and the concord of the agreed peace endures.
Then the old man, furrowing the earth with the curved plough,
filled his great hall with glad harvests,
and, praying humbly with vows to God on high,
settled peacefully in the fields of the Philistines.
There he is tested by the words of the heavenly deity,
that his only son should fall beneath the sword at the altar.
Without delay he climbs to the heights of a towering hill,
leading a beast of burden, going with his servants and his son.
And now, on the third day, when the sun shone more brightly
in the middle of the sky, drawing in all the shadows,
the old man sends away the servants and takes his son,
so that, carrying brushwood on his neck as food for the flames,
he might climb with him to the summit of the hill before them.
And now, as the flames rose, at the very altar
the boy is set, bound, his hands twisted behind his back.
And while the father hastens to cut his son open with the knife,
he watchfully catches sight of a white lamb in the distance,
which might better complete the rite with its shed blood.
After these events Sarah departs from her aged body.
And when the sons of Heth offered a place for a tomb,
the prophet would not have it so, but was ready to set a price.
Being rich, he gave Ephron four hundred sesterces,
glad to commit his companion to the double tomb.
The men of old had given the place the name Mamre.
Straightway he bids one of his servants, whom his life and faithfulness
had made distinguished, to speak a set form of words
and swear, placing his friendly right hand beneath
and joining it to his thigh, that no woman of the Canaanite race
should be joined to his son, since a wife from the stock of his kindred
must rather be brought; and if perhaps she should resist,
one would be sent from heaven who could easily soften her anger.
He eagerly loads gifts on swelling camels
and makes for Assyria, soon seeing the roofs of Nahor.
And while he silently turns over his master's commands,
he sees the excellent Rebecca coming from the spring,
who readily offers the man cool water
and invites him to her home. She tells him whose daughter she is;
he is received as a guest, and soon brings out his gifts.
When all has been explained, she sets out to marry her husband.
And now Isaac sees close at hand those who had completed the journey,
and Rebecca, seeing him, slipped down from the camel's high back
and covers her bowed head with a thin veil.
They are joined in silence and rejoice, the Lord being the author of their union.
But after the old man had passed a hundred years
and seven times ten, he bestowed gifts on all
and died, granted a place in the double tomb.
Meanwhile the son, having inherited his father's house,
lives by the well whose name was Vision.
And now he had spent four tens of years there;
with the wife we spoke of he had enriched his father's hall:
but though she shone with the surpassing star of beauty,
she was barren and for long knew nothing of a mother's joys.
But when he besought the Lord with holy lips
that his wife might conceive and bear a rightful heir,
he is heard; Rebecca swells, pregnant with twins.
She, long marvelling at the weight of her growing belly,
humbly seeks an answer from the heavenly Thunderer
and learns that two peoples within her womb
are rising toward the light of life with unequal merits.
For he who holds the first claim to the light he has earned
will be made subject to the rule of the younger and forced to serve him.
So when the children were born in an easy delivery,
the elder came forth into the air with a ruddy body,
covered all over with dark bristles.
His father called him by the pleasing name of Esau.
After him, holding his brother's heel tight in his hands,
was born Jacob, richly endowed with a remarkable mind.
The elder roamed the empty fields in hunting,
filling the rocks with the hoarse, trembling blast of his horn.
But the other, keeping to the ways of a gentle heart,
was glad to live unharmed in his father's house.
The father caressed the elder with tender love,
but the mother cherished the other with all her heart.
When the younger had cooked Egyptian lentils in water,
he pressed his brother, eager to take the prepared food,
to hand over to him the honors of the firstborn.
Meanwhile evil-counseling hunger, first of evils,
compelled the prophet to leave his native lands.
He makes for the Philistine countryside, then crosses to Gerar,
which Abimelech then held under his rule.
As he went, he saw the Lord in clear light
warning him with words not to go to the kingdom of Canopus,
but to keep to the soil, the land that the Lord had granted.
"For though you seem to live among strangers,
yet as a father whose line will endure across the vast world
you will rejoice to see nations grow from your manifold seed,
nations that will receive the supreme covenants of my word."
Then, living in Gerar with his wife and companion,
he declares that she is rather his sister, as his father had done,
lest the Philistine crowd, stirred by fickle desire,
should take up arms and carry off the prophet's wife.
But the king, looking into private places from an open window,
sees the prophet sporting with his snow-white wife,
and, seeing that they were married, binds all by law
that no one should try to seize the prophet's companion.
And now he who had once fled famine in his native land,
as he scatters barley entrusted to the softened earth,
reaped a hundredfold harvest from the glad soil.
No less meanwhile he grows rich in peaceful pursuits,
among flocks of many kinds and fruitful land.
Straightway, as wretched envy tortures their hearts,
it fouls his watered wells and fills them with heaped earth,
so that he would go far away and leave the fields he held.
Avoiding, then, the dangers of swelling strife,
he departed and stayed long in the valley of Gerar,
and when he had sunk wells with careful labor,
he found cold water from a gushing source.
Caught by the herdsmen's guile, he leaves their anger behind
and marks the hated place with the name of Strife.
Then he moves on, and again earth dug from a deep
hollow brought cold streams to light.
And because he had been thrust out by biting contention,
he rebukes their envious hearts with deserved words,
and after golden peace had broken off the grim quarrels,
he took care to give it the name of Abundant Land.
And while, shrewd as he was, he moved to fresh pastures with swift step,
he came to the hills whose name is Oath.
There he sees the Lord in clear light,
at the hour when the stars unroll the middle of their courses,
and is warned to thrust sad feelings from his breast,
since the unconquered God protects him through wars and against foes.
Roused from sleep, he gathers his chilled limbs
and, worshipping the Lord, soon builds an altar and prays.
Meanwhile the kings Abimelech and Ahuzzath come,
with Phicol accompanying them, bearing the sword,
so that the king, wishing to ally himself with the peaceable prophet,
might bind treaties of concord with clasped right hands.
He is received kindly and, having eaten his fill at the same table,
carries back the peace he desired, the danger set aside.
Next, discord arises between the brothers;
for their father, long since grown old with lengthy age,
bearing with calm mind the day lost along with the sun, and his buried eyes,
and mindful that death was at hand,
urges his elder son, on whom alone his love looked,
to take his quiver and swift arrows
and bring him the flesh of wild game as was his custom,
so as to receive forthwith the gifts of his father's tongue.
Rebecca, seeing this, lets her dear Jacob know,
urging him to bring two kids promptly
and to make haste to slaughter them for his father in place of his roving brother.
And lest his smooth body should lay bare the trick,
he is covered with skins to make him seem hairy,
and, veiling his chest and limbs in his brother's robe,
he offered the food as though he had taken it in the hunt.
Yet he did not wholly deceive the prophetic heart.
For the old man, while his right hand felt over the whole young man,
knows him for Esau by the hair, but for Jacob by the voice.
And after his hunger was stilled and the table cleared away,
he bids him come and stand nearer.
He, when he had come beneath his father's right hand with lowered head,
received the bright words of his holy-speaking father,
as he tasted sweet kisses with pressed lips.
For after he had wished him the blessings of a long life,
the elder brother is ordered to serve the younger.
Meanwhile Esau, driven through long wanderings,
was bringing the meat he had caught to his father, who had already eaten his fill.
And though he had pleased him greatly by his dutiful service,
yet he could not receive the gifts that had been intercepted.
Hence wrath and tears, and treachery sought out to do harm:
which Rebecca, seeing it in the brother's breast, reveals,
and warns Jacob to go to Haran where their kindred lived
and seek out Laban, his mother's brother,
until the passing of time should soften the anger conceived.
And the prophet's counsel is joined to the mother's warnings,
as he calmly instructs his son and, with her, equips him:
"Do not seek a marriage, young man, from the Canaanite race,
but be mindful and hold fast to the words of your dear father.
There is a place among the Assyrians, girded by twin rivers.
There lives Bethuel, our friend, your mother's father,
and Laban, his son, who holds rich estates throughout Haran
and cherishes daughters in the bloom of their years.
From that stock, I urge you, let a wife be sought,
one who draws her noble descent from our own blood."
But the young man, glad to obey his father's counsel,
sets out, leaving his homeland, and, worn out with much toil,
lets his eyes sink into sweet sleep.
And as he spreads the stones for an ice-cold bed,
he puts a very hard rock beneath his weary head.
And while his limbs are refreshed in untroubled slumber,
he sees, undaunted, with the full light of his mind,
a ladder fixed through the clouds in the clear sky,
down whose steps a throng from on high was rushing,
while another climbed from the earth to the heights above.
And while bodies were rolling down in headlong fall,
the Almighty, his face bent down, watched them descending,
and added this besides: "I am the great King of heaven,
long since your Lord, and the Lord of your father:
drive away sad fears; the land on which you have laid your limbs
is a sure dwelling for you and for all your sons under your leadership.
Now go on, be mindful, and do not abandon the task you have begun.
Under my guidance you will return to the cities you have left."
A great dread breaks his sleep and shakes all his bones,
drenching his limbs with streaming sweat.
And on top of this he says: "Here is the great house of the Thunderer
and the gate that opens heaven on its double hinge."
Soon he anoints the stone that had lain beneath his head,
and, naming it the House of the Lord, with the stone to mark the place,
he promises that he will give a tenth of his produce.
And now, hastening the journey he had begun, where the path led,
he came to a well which, alone in the vast and trackless waste,
had always refreshed the gentle flocks with its watering streams.
Here, with three flocks, under the burning sun, shepherds
were drawing the thin waters and easing the heat;
and having greeted them, the prophet asks about each thing in turn,
and learns that all those he had in mind to seek are safe and well.
Meanwhile Rachel, walking along, snowy-white of form,
was driving her father's sheep to their familiar watering place.
As soon as the young man, fresh from his brother's door, caught sight of her,
he chastely drew her into his embrace, to his kindred breast,
rolling away the stone that had covered the mouth of the well,
and at the same time revealed that he was her kinsman by blood.
Seeing him from afar, Laban, his heart rejoicing,
runs to him and settles the young man in his own familiar hall.
Nor does he allow the prophet, his kinsman, to serve for nothing,
but in return for the man's labour betroths his daughter to her lover.
So when he had worked out his wages over seven years,
he asks that his betrothed be joined to him in the bond of marriage.
Without delay Leah is given him as a counterfeit gift,
weak of eye, but the first-born daughter.
But Jacob, grieving at the deceit that had been devised,
speaks out to his father-in-law, cheated of the maiden he was promised.
Again, for the price of the other, at a separate wage,
Jacob endures long years of toil,
and, the fraud now set aside, receives the Rachel he had earned.
But God, the supreme ruler of the heavenly court,
made up for the lack of beauty with many children.
For Leah bears Reuben, and then Simeon;
the third, Levi, born with a noble heart,
took possession of the sacred altars of our Lord.
After him comes Judah, soon made the founder of a tribe.
As for the other offspring, whom Bilhah bore from her womb,
they may be learned elsewhere; now it is right to speak of the famous sons.
After these, Issachar is born as her fifth child.
A sixth offspring follows, receiving the name Zebulun,
and a girl is born, Dinah, a fitting sister for her brothers.
At last God grants his late gifts to Rachel:
she brings tender Joseph forth into the air of heaven.
So when he now had children born of both his wives,
he asks his father-in-law for leave to depart, and for what he had earned;
and when they wished to pay him a wage for his services,
they gave way, prevailed on by their son-in-law's request:
for he, wanting nothing that belonged to others, declared that he grew rich
only by the Lord's gifts, and departed,
content merely to have received both wives,
striving to secure lasting memorials for himself.
He strips rods, torn from the body of the parent trees.
The first was of myrtle; then a second was taken from the storax;
a third was plucked from the nut tree, so that little by little the wool,
smeared with the sap of the rods, might take on mottled colours.
For, hurrying to drive the bleating flock into the pools,
he marked it, tinged with a varied pattern of dye,
on account of envy, since his father-in-law had said that his
wage would be the mottled ones, a wage he had withheld for many years.
When he, thus nourished, excelled in riches he had not bought,
he stirred envy and the bitter spite of those who resented him.
And while his harsh father-in-law is shearing the woolly fleeces,
the man had the freedom to carry off all his goods
and the household gods, baked in a hot furnace,
which the Syrian believed to be deities in his native Haran.
These, however, cautious Rachel kept hidden in wrappings,
lest her father discover the offence and punish the crime.
Having set out, he crossed the river and climbed the hill
which the natives in their ancestral tongue call Gilead.
And on the third day there came to his father-in-law's ears
news of the departure of his son-in-law and of his daughters alike.
At once he calls for help from the band of his kinsmen,
and having overtaken him, long pursued, on the sixth day,
he is forbidden by the holy terror of the Lord to do him harm,
and, now mild toward his own, he demands back what he believes to be gods,
and having searched for them everywhere and not found them, he grieves.
After their complaints were laid aside and firm peace returned,
a tall heap is raised, with stones piled higher and higher,
so that the place might stand as a witness by the mound that was built,
and the boundary set there might settle disputes over the lands.
Behold, midway on the road the prophet sees lofty camps,
which God the ruler leads under his star-bearing governance, [?]
and he gave the place a name, bearing witness: "God fills these."
Meanwhile he ordered chosen young men to run ahead,
laden with gifts which he bids his brother to enjoy,
so that he might peaceably grant him return; and to him who sought peace
the other gladly assented; and with his companions and a great host [?]
around him he goes out to meet his brother, not at all hostile,
and though a crowd of four hundred men caused alarm,
the sight did more harm than the weapons, for their arms were only an escort.
So, having divided the flocks, he placed in front those
which his brother might deign to accept as a gift to him,
and at the same time, with [?] neck, he besought the Lord:
"O God, hope and substance of a boundless kingdom,
who alone are for ever the God of my father and my grandfather,
whose commands make me return from exile,
you have bestowed great blessings on your servant and made him rich;
you bade me cross the river with nothing but a pliant staff
and pass over your Jordan with humble step.
And now you see me living in divided camps,
so that by a double defence I may escape the various chances of harm.
Rescue me from these evils, unconquered one, and in your kindness
strike away my brother's darts as soon as may be, and break their iron,
lest in his fury he pierce my breast with a cruel weapon."
So when he had settled his companions and gone to sleep,
he toils in the night to overcome God, who wrestles with him;
for when his thigh was pressed, that part of his body went numb.
And when for a long time he wished to loose the hold of their limbs,
he who had struck the prophet in that mighty contest,
the Lord, after bestowing his gifts, let him go once he was released.
With his name changed, he ceases to be Jacob,
and is called by everyone "He who sees the Lord."
Though he even dared to learn the Lord's name,
he could not, for the Thunderer alone has the right to know it.
He himself calls the place after the name of the Lord who was seen there,
whose lofty face it had been granted him to behold.
And when the Lord withdrew, the night now driven away,
he goes forth, supporting his steps with a long staff.
For this reason Judea, remembering, avoids eating the sinew
which supports the joined thigh with its firm strength.
And now, seeing his brother surrounded by a gathered troop,
bowing low with bent neck, he greets his lord:
they meet and embrace with many tears...
and now more and more, in varied talk, he asks
who these are that come with him in a band, and what crowd follows.
He explains of what father his wives were born,
and by what wages the various flocks were acquired.
And at once the wives, prostrate on bended knee,
brought their tender sons forward for kindred kisses.
But the elder, while dutifully declining the gifts offered him,
kindly caresses the children of the reconciled prophet,
and gladly, with his brother accompanying him, [?]
so that in turn, little by little, they tell each other what they have done.
But since the ewes heavy with young crept along in a slow-moving column,
the prophet halted to look after his flocks and servants
and set up small huts with leafy roofs,
which it pleased him to call by the lasting name of the Booths.
He came to Shechem, which lies in the region of Canaan,
and bought for a price estates in the neighbouring land.
And hastening to build altars, he prays to God.
There Correus [?], shamelessly, defiled Dinah, whom he loved,
and robbed the tender maiden of her virginity before its time,
and, wishing to marry her, cut away his [?] foreskin,
bringing great gifts to the prophet for the bride he had seized.
Then on the third day, when wounds burn most fiercely,
[?] is slain together with all its young men.
Jacob grieved over these deeds done by his sons' sword,
declaring that the treaty with an allied people had been broken.
At once the Almighty warned the prophet to depart
and to settle his faithful household in the [?] dwelling.
He hastens and obeys God, and urges his sons
to smash the shrines of gods fashioned of hard metal,
and to put on garments under a snowy-white covering.
He himself hides the gods, which are nothing, in a hollow under the terebinth,
and he sees the mighty Lord speak to him his familiar
words, saying that he would be a prophet of the God on high
in the rich lands which the Lord had promised to Abraham.
He himself named the place and consecrated the stone,
which in reverence he drenched all over with flowing oil,
and he raised a dwelling beneath the roof of the tower of Gader.
Meanwhile [?], worn out by grievous pain,
becoming a mother in death, she brought forth Benjamin from her womb.
For besides the sons born of his lawful wives,
the prophet fathered children by substitute mothers,
and gladly acknowledged, from the allied stock of Bilhah,
distinguished Dan, whom Naphtali follows close behind.
Others Zilpah soon bears, Gad and Asher.
He obtained this as well, which he had known he did not deserve:
to see his father's face with so great a family;
so that he who had been born of an aged mother
might rejoice, honoured with twelve grandsons.
So when at last, through twice ninety years,
the great man's life had been drawn out through a long age,
he is released and goes forth, shining, from his weary body,
to see the holy dwellings, [?],
in which, reclining through the ages on a star-studded couch,
he invites the snowy-white righteous to carefree joys.
And now the brothers resolve to divide the dwelling places they had marked out;
for since, within the narrow bounds of the land, they could not
contain settlers whose many flocks kept increasing,
the elder took Mount Seir, beyond the fields of Canaan,
and, being very rich, took for himself fertile pastures.
Jacob, coming after, does not leave the realms of Canaan,
so that his pious mind might always delight in his fathers' rites.
There Joseph begins his remarkable deeds,
shining among his brothers with as great a distinction
as the moon gleams among the small stars of heaven.
When he was now reaching seventeen years of age,
he was tending his father's flocks in the grassy meadow,
younger in birth than all those whom, from noble
marriages or from a slave concubine [?], his father had begotten.
And because he flourished, conspicuous among the band of brothers,
he stirred his brothers' hearts with the chill of envy.
His father, loving him above the whole line of his sons,
cherished him, so tender among the sturdy bodies of his brothers,
and so that he might be more conspicuous among them all,
he clothed him in a flowing garment of many colours.
While he was serving the Lord from his tender years,
one day, his eyes closed in peaceful sleep, he sees
himself among his brothers binding sheaves,
while they reap the grain in the middle of the fields,
and his own sheaf rising up tall, its point erect,
while his brothers' sheaves bowed down beside it [?].
When the young man innocently related this,
he stirred their uneasy hearts to anxious turmoil;
with a fearful muttering, calling him king and lord,
they let slip that a lonely spot for a crime would not be lacking.
And to rend their gloomy hearts with doubled anger,
he reveals to his wise father the dreams he had seen,
with all present whom the bond of blood unites.
For he seemed to see the rosy sun,
and with it the moon with her flickering light,
and with these ten stars and one rising together,
and bending their necks low before him as before a lord.
When his father had heard this with a sidelong look,
he soon admitted to the anxious brothers that he was to be worshipped.
At once the young men go out, and for their father's flocks
seek out valleys watered by a river, through flowery meadows;
sent to them, he sets off and wanders among the silent thickets,
until a certain young man pointed out to him the remote places
which the band of brothers had chosen when they changed pasture;
when they could recognize him from afar by his many-coloured garment,
they contrive an ill-fated plan, though their tongues disagree.
The decision is reached to destroy the brother hated by them all,
and, once he was dead, to report that wild beasts had torn him,
while in fury they mutter among themselves with blustering murmurs:
"Let us see whether dreams can ward off death."
One gentler [?] rejects this with calming words
and urges them in their rage to sheathe their cruel steel,
saying it was better to plunge him into a stagnant pit.
At once he is stripped and, naked, [?] in the cold.
Meanwhile a man accustomed to trade in Sabaean wares
was driving camels to carry heavy loads,
hurrying to take the harvests of Arabia down to Canopus.
So when the hope for the younger brother had been dashed,
Judah says it is better to sell Joseph for money.
Their father is deceived, and seeing the garment dyed in blood,
he judges that he was killed, suspecting no fraud.
[?] tears his garment with clawing hands,
and wraps himself in black clothing of haircloth.
Stricken with grief, the father searches for the son he has lost,
whom Pharaoh's eunuch had long since bought and kept,
a man accustomed to load the tyrant's gilded tables
with dishes and to delight in the din of a great kitchen.
Meanwhile Tamar gives birth, while the joys of her sin
bring her pleasure, and her womb is filled with twin offspring.
Of these, the boy who first earned the light of life
thrust out and put forth his hand, which the skilful woman
ties with a scarlet thread; soon he is drawn back into the womb,
and, their order reversed, the other is at once born,
taking first place, who had been second by lot.
This one, since he had once been set apart by a boundary,
bears the name Zerah; the other they called Perez.
The faithful protection of the Lord of the earth watched over Joseph,
not allowing him to live subject to a harsh law.
For the master mentioned earlier entrusts everything to his servant,
and not in vain hope; for the gentle Lord from on high
abundantly increased everything the young man looked after.
Yet he did not keep the favour of harsh Potiphar;
for since his eyes shone in a striking face,
his mistress, sorely smitten, begs her slave to lie with her.
But the boy shuns the foul deed and refuses
to defile the sacred marriage bed with shameless guilt.
But the woman, hopelessly lost in forbidden passion,
tries out soft approaches and watches for her moment.
One day, when she found the house empty and him alone, she presses him,
and seizing him by the hand urges him to lie down with her.
He so swiftly slips the garment from his body
and escapes from between his mistress's arms.
The woman cries out and draws boldness from her crime,
shouting that the precious honour of her chastity had been violated
by a young man confident in his good looks, who, in the wanton heat of his youth,
was burning with desire and trying to climb into his master's bed.
She even addresses her husband in a mournful voice,
and wants the innocent accused to suffer the punishment she chose;
he, thinking it true, shuts him up in a cruel prison,
in which the king's ministers were already being held as punishment.
The keeper of the prison soon treats him with a kindly heart,
and, seeing that he is innocent, entrusts to him the prison in his charge.
There, as it happened, two men, whom the grim tyrant,
stirred by black bile, had shut away from his lofty hall,
were imprisoned, dreading punishment in their anxious hearts,
and while they stole some sleep amid their troubled cares,
they saw dreams foretelling things to come.
When [?], with clear-sighted eye, saw them downcast,
he asks the reasons and makes them reveal their secret.
At once the man who served the tyrant his usual wine
tells what he had seen in the drowsy night:
"I saw a vine, leafy with green shoots,
as it creeps along and hangs from its twining tendrils,
and [?] three branches [?] among the vine leaves,
and golden grapes hung in nectar-sweet clusters.
Then the king's cup, from which he pours his mellow drinks,
foamed with the new wine that my right hand had pressed,
and my lord took it and held it in his outstretched palm."
Then the young man plainly reveals all that was hidden:
the three branches are three days, after which he
will recover and regain the favour he had lost,
and will mix for the gracious king the cups he saw.
"Only do this in return for such service," he says,
"that when you have gained the confidence to speak,
you take away my punishment, imposed for no crime.
I am said to be of the Hebrew race. For, sold [?]
through my brothers' crime, I, though nobly born, went into slavery."
After this the chief of the bakers begins to tell what he saw:
"I seemed to carry three baskets on my head,
filled with royal dishes and lavish fare,
which countless birds seized and carried off in their talons."
At these words, speaking what was true enough but harsh,
he declares that the man will soon be slain by the cruel sword,
and his severed head fixed on a tall stake,
for the birds at once to tear with their savage beaks.
Everything the young man said is fulfilled, and soon
the one is restored to his post, the other cut down and his body mutilated.
Meanwhile, as time slipped by through two years,
the stars were again turning on their eastward courses,
when the ruler of the Nile saw these dreams:
for it seemed to him, as he gazed at the pleasant river,
that he saw seven heifers with sleek bodies
grazing the lush grass on the green banks;
after them others, hideous with leanness, came up,
and though, sluggish, they barely held together on their bones (a wonder!),
they swallowed the fine heifers with gaping mouths.
Dreams are joined that agree, with matching meanings;
behold, he sees seven ears of grain from fruitful seed,
and others thin and empty of [?] seed
(dreadful to tell!) devouring the crops as if [?].
Saddened, he by no means keeps this vision to himself,
but in alarm ordered all who were skilled to come,
asking what meaning lay in these hidden things.
And when the augur of Memphis, being consulted, was silent,
the man who, long since freed from prison, served the wine
says that through the interpretation of the young man Joseph
he had returned to the post he had lost, and his companion had been killed.
Men are sent in haste to bring the prophet swiftly,
cleared of every charge, out of the foul dungeon,
and, shaving his unkempt cheeks and the hair that had grown long in prison,
to make him flourish again in his former beauty.
So the upright man, when consulted, gives this reply to what was told him,
and explains that the cows foretell years,
and interprets the light ears as seven years.
For thus the signs of what is to come were set out in figures:
that for seven years the earth would be bountifully fruitful,
and that dire famine would prevail for an equal time,
during which the earth, utterly dry, its veins parched with thirst,
would wither the pale grass in the dusty furrow.
"For dreams that are joined in a double vision
God, the Thunderer, ordains to stand sure [?].
Rather, while there is time, while a remedy can still be sought,
choose [?] someone who, foreseeing these things,
may appoint overseers and, raised on high, govern all Egypt,
and demand a fifth part of every harvest,
so that the plenty first given by the fruitful land
may sustain the barren years when the crops are used up."
The nobles receive the prophet's counsel with applause.
The king himself too, at last, his heart calmed by heaven,
raises to high honour the man who had told him the truth,
and orders him to go as governor through all the cities.
Then he crowns the prophet's finger with a gleaming ring.
Soon he wraps him in linen robes with a saffron mantle;
a flexible chain is placed around his neck [?],
and the new ruler stands high on a chariot,
and a loud herald [?].
Moreover a wife is chosen for him, whose name was [?],
whom Potiphera the priest had begotten of a famous line,
and by her he soon becomes the father of two children.
The elder is called Manasseh, the younger Ephraim.
Then the prophet, illustrious on his high seat, collects
all that a time of hunger could scarcely have gathered,
keeping the granaries full, so that when need required,
he might bring out the stored grain for all who asked.
Afterwards, when dire famine, spreading over the whole world,
forced the terrified people to eat whatever could be chewed,
the people cry out and demand food from the king.
He orders the noble Joseph to give grain to the sorrowing,
Meanwhile Jacob, having already mourned the death of his son,
sends ten young men from his numerous offspring
to buy grain for themselves at a price in a far country;
but Benjamin, the youngest of all, he does not allow to go,
lest, being weak, he should be unable to bear the hard labour.
And when they had reached the walls of the land of Egypt,
they bowed down to the ground and greet their brother,
marvelling at him seated high on a lofty throne,
yet they do not recognize him, seen after so long a time.
When the prophet looked on them, his memory alive,
he rebukes them and terrifies them, already afraid, with many words,
saying they had come to [?] what supply of grain there was
and what men held the rich lands under their rule.
They protest that they know nothing of deceit, and confess
that once there were twelve brothers, sons of one father,
who had a notable household; of them all, one,
the youngest, was looking after his father's work,
and another had long since perished by a death well known.
They, fleeing dire famine and hating the land of Canaan,
which dooms the seed to a meagre yield,
were seeking goods for sale and grain to bargain for.
The prophet speaks, swearing by the ruler's name,
that the young men must be shut in harsh custody until
they produced the brother whom their gentle father kept with him.
For three days they are held, stripped [?], under the guards' watch,
and then, released, they left one behind to be held.
Nor [?], their hearts breaking with hidden grief,
they recall how just were the trials rising against them,
since, having striven to sell their innocent brother in a forbidden bargain,
they were now, late, paying the penalty before a judge.
[?] adds weight to their words, recalling the truth,
and that the crime had been committed by them in haste against his will.
The prophet is moved by this, and, hearing his brothers' recriminations,
he turns away and weeps mournfully with silent eyes.
Meanwhile, from the midst of the circle of brothers, Simeon
is taken, a faithful hostage for all who were leaving.
Then the young men take the grain they had asked for,
and the mules are burdened, weighed down with the load they had obtained.
And now midway on the road, as one of them loosens the cords of his sack,
he lets his brothers see the money he had found.
They all do the same, and soon, finding their payment,
in amazement they vie with one another in praising the noble lord.
And now as they cross the threshold of their native home,
their father rejoices at their return and asks after one.
Learning everything, he takes the money and the gifts,
lamenting bitterly that now another son is gone.
Then, when the food had run short and the grain they had brought
forced them once more to buy provisions at a price,
no one had any mind to make his way back to Memphis
unless their father bade the youngest brother go with them.
When, groaning much, he refused to let him go anywhere,
Reuben, with a pledge of good faith, asks for his brother,
confidently entrusting his two sons to his father.
Judah follows and declares that they cannot return,
citing as witness the words of stern Joseph.
When the aged father, now more yielding, had heard this,
he gives up the young man, bathing his face in a flood of tears.
They depart, taking with them sweet-scented frankincense,
joining incense and resin with terebinth,
carrying honey amid the fragrant scents,
and double payment, lest any mistake be entangled in the matter,
since the coins had been hidden in their closed sacks.
When Joseph saw them in his splendid hall,
he orders that they hold a joyful feast with him.
They came [?], however, and in anxious guilt
guess that they have been summoned by some contrived trick,
because the money they had counted out earlier and paid to the prophet,
placed in their bundles, they had not been able to return;
yet, innocent of theft, they were bringing it all back,
and had never before been in the habit of living on [?] treasure.
As they say such things, the steward checks them with his words
and assures them that he knows he has been cheated of no money:
if some gain had brought the men profit,
no one should call it his own, nor the prophet's, nor the king's.
Simeon comes out to meet them all and presents himself.
And while he provides water for the men and fodder for the mules,
the prophet enters, surrounded by many soldiers,
and at the sight of him the brothers bring out their dutiful gifts.
When he had gone round them all with gracious words,
he asks whether their father is in good strength and health.
After they said he was safe and living well,
Joseph declares that the prophet holds fast to God, for the gift [?],
and always keeps to what is right.
And as though Benjamin were not known to him,
he questions the young men, and at once [?]; then
he prays God for every blessing on the boy, to God's praise.
He can neither hold back his groans nor stop his tears,
but, overcome with tender feeling, [?] himself in an inner room,
and in distress seeks relief for his overwhelming grief.
Afterwards, when he had taken his place at table, the servants set out the food.
He eats, and with easy talk he draws out their hearts,
and, glad to set out the portioned dishes man by man,
he hands them round and sets a larger share before one brother alone.
And when, now that they were full, their desire to eat had been checked,
they loaded the mules with a heavy burden as before;
the money they had paid is hidden, now in the usual way,
at Joseph's command, and a gleaming cup is hidden
among your things, Benjamin, more precious for its workmanship.
And now they had set out on the road and were not many miles away
when suddenly a royal troop surrounds them, caught off guard,
seizes them and holds them fast, demanding the glittering cup;
they declare that whoever is caught by the charge will become a slave.
They agree, and all together they open their loads,
uncover the cup that was sought, and leave their brother behind,
and they go to Joseph, and as they tell what had happened
they at once lay out the commands of their dear father.
Moved by their pleas, the seer orders everyone to withdraw
and begins to speak, revealing himself by the name of Sennarum [?].
They stood frozen, rigid with fear, and, condemning themselves
in silent guilt, held back their words in dread.
Soon he coaxes the guilty men, calls them nearer,
and charges them to carry words that would please their father:
what is, what has been, what is said to be coming soon;
urging the old man to move, he bids him gather his flocks
and come down [?], and offers the hills of Arabia to those who come,
so that, since the land would stay parched for five unbroken years,
he might feed all his kinsmen [?] of the world.
The king hears these words of the man with a glad heart;
Thara [?] asks him to bring the throng of his dear ones,
and orders Lothus [?] to hand over grain free of charge.
The men are given wagons, grain, cups, bread,
and mules sweat under the great loads they carry.
Five robes are given to Benjamin and five to his father,
