and three hundred coins struck with a stamped die.
But the other young men, honoured with a lesser reward,
receive cloaks of snowy garment [?Melchae].
When the father learned of this and of the gifts sent, [?]
he breathes again, and hurrying to leave his native land
he makes for Egypt, which borders the fields of Arabia,
leading out under his fatherly rule young men numbering five
and seven tens, as the record of Genesis has laid down.
And while the company hurries on with eager effort,
Judah runs ahead, flies in front of his brothers' column,
and tells Joseph that his father is not far off.
He eagerly mounts his chariot and goes out to meet him,
and, on seeing his father, welcomes the longed-for company.
Then he quickly returns, at full speed, to the king's court,
reporting that shepherds are on their way, so that the throng of his dear ones
may live apart in lands of fertile grass.
The ruler of Memphis himself also presses the seer
and bids him settle his brothers in rich fields.
After this, at the request of Sarram [?], the aged old man
speaks slowly of how many years he has been granted,
what his house is, and what reason brought him to Canopus.
And the excellent leader, with much praise [?] ...
nor meanwhile does he fail to send gifts in return,
worthy of his own, and he gives the leader a great talent to carry,
with which the court was enriched by the sale of grain.
And when the people who came to buy had no more money,
the crowd of Memphis vied in bringing their flocks
and, destitute, bought grain, Joseph setting the price.
Stripped of these as well, they hand over themselves and their estates,
receiving seed so that the crops might grow green again.
Only the priests' property was not taken from them;
the leader chose to give them the tyrant's [?] grain free and not to sell it.
From then on a levy of a fifth of the harvest is laid on the people,
a rule that remains and is kept by fixed law.
Meanwhile, weighing the span of his completed life
and pondering what was to come, Jacob makes his son swear
to lay his limbs in the tombs of his forefathers.
He grants his plea, and with his right hand placed under his thigh
he makes his pledge, while Jacob touches the top of his pliant staff.
And with his grandsons placed on either side, the old man
soothes them with words, while he gently gives them kisses.
He began [?] — a wonder! — the right hand consecrates [?] ...
Ephraim, the elder by birth, is touched by the left.
By the old man's foreknowing mind the elder is made to serve the younger,
and the first hope gives way to the second place.
However much he wished to pull apart the crossed hands,
Joseph still could not call back the holy words.
And after the seer had confirmed fitting blessings on the boys,
he gives Shechem to his son, and his own sword, and his arrows,
so that, more renowned than all, he might rise to lofty honour.
Then he calls his sons and hands out rewards to them all,
utterances that would long endure, and to his sons' offspring
he assigns, for long ages, what had not been granted before.
And he founds twelve tribes, named after them.
When all was done, now blind in both eyes,
the seer departed from the earth in his earthly body [?] ...
and gave over seventy days to mourning,
while the throng honoured the tomb of the dead.
His sons, too, mourned [?] for seven days
with abundant tears, and Joseph granted peace
to his brothers, unharmed, putting aside his old anger.
He himself, too, when he had now passed a hundred years
and ten, measuring the time left before his approaching death,
tells his brothers what the course of things to come would be,
when they would be able to turn back and leave [?]:
only let them carry back his buried ashes and bones
and [?] to be buried with the remains of their forefathers.
So at last, after the bright years of a long life,
he died, went to God, and left his body behind.
EXODUS.
Meanwhile, as the ages ran their varied courses
and a new generation [?] rose from the stock,
the sons died off [?], and the offspring of those who came after,
and the land of Memphis raised up new and different kings.
Neither any memory of Joseph [?] nor the merits [?] of the prophet availed,
once so greatly loved. But by the gift of the holy Lord,
who protects his people, many
bodies were born, and the ranks thickened into a vast cloud.
When the king of Egypt saw that they were to be feared,
he addressed his companions in these words, stirred by eager anger [?]:
"Look: a people once captive, content with the food
that a sparing hand held out to them—look, it now calls up cohorts
in a long legion, and it swells not with arms alone;
it is our superior in fighting valor, and it wears threatening looks
even in subjection. What if it should now take up weapons
or ally itself with our enemies? Under what weight of war
would Egypt fall laid waste, and what vast ruins
would our lofty cities make, their walls torn down?
No—rather let them be broken by a hard lot of toil
and raise immense citadels on massive foundations,
so that hope of their lost freedom may not return to idle men."
When this was said, he set skilled men over them,
so that they would build new walls and towers, and, straining,
lift menacing gates to the sky. Driven by these misfortunes,
they founded several towns with sweating labor:
Rameses, then Pithom, and On, famous for the name
of the Sun. But—a marvel—the more they lay under the grim
burden of toil, the stronger all their youth
shone forth, as though they were resting on holiday.
The grim king of Egypt grew more and more alarmed
and doomed to destruction those who did not yet fear his commands,
ordering [?] that, when the pregnant women bore their young,
[the midwives] should kill and destroy the males, and that no punishment [?] would fall
upon them [?] if, bound by oath, they abandoned the despised infants [?].
Among these women was Puah, with her companion [?].
But they, with the fear of God planted in their timid hearts,
scorned the ruler's threats, and, when ordered to appear,
said that the Hebrew women, needing no help,
were used to bringing forth their ripe offspring quickly.
For these words they earned the Lord's favor,
rejoicing to establish themselves in their familiar homes,
as they revered the Lord and praised him with all their heart.
The ruler's command was changed, and the people were ordered
to drown newborn boys in the stream of the Nile.
The crowd obeyed its ruler, plunging the newborn into the river.
Amid these upheavals a Levite, having taken a wife,
fathered a son radiant with a beautiful body
and striking features, and he refused to destroy, together with that great beauty,
the man he would become; and lest he be killed,
he cherished him in hiding until three months had passed.
But fearing punishment, should the deceit he had committed come to light,
he sadly sent him out exposed, where the roaring currents
could carry him downstream, though he had no oarsman.
His sister watched him from afar with keen sight,
as far as following eyes could keep him in view,
so that she could tell their parent the fate of the exposed child.
But meanwhile [?], walking happily and seeking pleasant [?] waters,
the king's daughter, accompanied by her attendants,
was dipping herself in the calm river and bathing her body.
She saw a small boat on the swelling waters
and ordered her maids to bring the prize she desired.
They eagerly—as joyful youth is ready in the young—
brought back the child set in the little boat and, placing him before her,
made the girl rejoice with a mother's feeling.
Wishing to keep for herself such sweet
delights of beauty and the surpassing grace of that fine brow,
she openly ordered that a woman of the Hebrew people be summoned
to be his nurse, and the care of the boy's hunger [?]
was given to her. The sister, with no deceit now, called the anxious
mother, to whom the ruler's daughter would return her own child,
to her joy, the mother being given the name of nurse.
The boy grew and swiftly advanced to the years
that flourish in the first bloom of youth, and, given over to the palace,
was regarded as a true child of Pharaoh's daughter;
and he received the name Moses, because he had been
rescued from the murmuring waves, floating in a little skiff.
But he, prompted by his nature and following his heart,
set out to visit his kindred people throughout the towns,
who were fretting in sorrow under the harsh yoke upon them.
By chance, in the middle of his way, he saw a man of the Egyptian people
with loud shouts beating a groaning
Hebrew; and, loathing the injustice of his lot,
he looked all around, and, seeing no one present there
who could act as a witness and reveal what had happened in that place,
he struck him with his heel and buried him, laid low, under heaped-up sand.
Next he saw other men of the Jewish race threatening
each other [?]; and while he eagerly stepped in,
helped the weaker side and restored the peace,
he was met with words hurled from an angry breast:
"Why do you swell with lofty neck, as if you wielded the scepter
of a high prince and written laws rang out with you presiding?
Or perhaps you mean to destroy me with sudden death,
as you killed the Egyptian youth in yesterday's light?"
When these words had been spoken, talkative rumor carried them
to the ruler's ears, and the king in anger drove the young prophet to flight.
Leaving his country, he came to a deep well
in the land of Midian, where the priest
Jethro lived, who had fathered a brood of seven daughters
and filled his house with a numerous line.
These carefully tended the soft sheep entrusted to them
and drew water [?] from the hollow spring;
but by chance shepherds drove the weak band, the timid sex,
far away; and since they did not dare to stand against them
or to raise ready hands in resistance,
Moses defended them, brought them to the flowing waters,
refreshed the flocks, watered to the full, and sent them home.
The girls returned, to their father's great surprise,
earlier than usual, and, speaking readily at his command,
summoned the young man and brought him to their father's threshold.
Jethro, measuring his tall limbs with a keen [?] eye,
and his spirit greater still than his looks, rejoiced to join him to his daughter
and foresaw grandsons from that excellent stock.
For Zipporah diligently bore Gershom in a swift birth
and afterward brought forth his brother Eliezer.
Gershom signifies one born in a foreign land,
and Eliezer one snatched from the anger of a harsh ruler.
Meanwhile the ruler died, and the captive people,
crushed by evils, with many laments pressed the Lord
to turn his kindly gaze on them and protect his people;
and he, mindful forever, turned over [?] within himself his gifts,
promised long ago to the good in sleep [?], which at the beginning of time [?]
Abraham had heard would come to his descendants, and with him
Jacob, who then [saw] the ladder [?] and was chosen for holy things.
And now the oppressed race saw God, merciful, pouring down protection from heaven,
as it begged for peace from on high.
And while Moses was driving his father-in-law's woolly sheep
through the countryside alone, he came to the summit of the sacred hill
which the Hebrew tongue calls Horeb.
There he saw a bending bush shining with a conspicuous blaze
of flames, yet not burned by the fire.
Stirred by the strangeness of the thing, he was eager to find out
what fuel could make such bright fires rise.
And as, trembling, he [?] silently drew so near,
he was forbidden by the glorious voice of the starry Thunderer
to hasten forward with quick steps; rather he was made to halt
and at once to take the coverings off both his feet;
and he obeyed, because of the sacred heights of that ground.
Soon fear entered his senses, and his eyes grew dim
from too much light, because it is not lawful
for anyone to look upon the Lord, and he turned away his face and gaze.
Then a voice rang out, in which the glorious King declared
himself the God of the patriarchs, whom we have long called
the leaders of believers and of life. Then he added this:
"Now the prayers of my people are known to me and seen with my full sight,
a people that builds cities of vast mass
and, driven by the hard sweat of toil,
exalts the wealth of Egypt and kingdoms not its own,
cowering with a slave's mind and racked
by constant pain, long subject to the will of wicked men.
And so I have come here, descending from lofty heaven,
to protect my own and take them from the seat of Canopus—
I, the giver of great riches and of a fertile land,
which now, rich in manifold produce, the bold
Canaanite holds, and the Amorite joined with the Hittite,
with the Perizzite band and the Girgashites following,
and which the Hivite youth also tills, spreading over it [?].
There honey flows in sweet springs from a rich stream
together with white milk. Meaning to give these gifts
to my chosen, I appoint you their leader; I command you to go
before the king's eyes and report what has been commanded.
And lest, trembling at the outset, you falter in the deed,
I will always be with you. And when freedom has returned, you [?]
will come to me on this hill, exulting in heart and eyes [?]."
When the Lord had thundered this, at first the prophet
had little confidence. Then he asked what eternal name
the Lord bore, so that Judea might know the token
of the ruler set over it. The Savior answered thus:
"I am who I am—so you shall say—and he who lives above the stars
and is God of your fathers from the root of your line:
God boundless everywhere and throughout all nations,
creator through the ages of the living, not of those who lack the light.
This is my name; declare it [?] to those gathered together,
who may then let the words pass through peaceable ears.
And entering together into the hall of King Pharaoh,
you shall say that the Lord of the Israelites has commanded from on high
that for three days, through the desert fields,
the Jewish host should march and offer fitting gifts
in sacrifice to the holy God and keep the rite of their ancestors.
For the proud tyrant will consent to release my people
only after disaster and plague, which will be sent again and again
from the depths of heaven, varied with many perils.
And further, when leave has been granted to you
to take the journey commanded, then let each woman ask
her neighbor or acquaintance for the things of rich worth
that soft Egypt now possesses, and take what she asks for,
so that the host, to be led through the shapeless fields of the wilderness,
may leave Egypt emptied of its noble spoils."
After this the prophet asked for signs that might strengthen
wavering minds, if they should not believe that God
could have been seen with the eye, speaking such radiant words.
He was told to let go the pliant rod at once
and release it from his hand; once the ground received it,
a foaming serpent gathered itself into a coil,
striking terror into the leader; ordered to seize it by the tail,
he brought it back and restored it to its former shape.
Then, hiding his hand in his bosom, he brought it out
snowy white, and again covered it and drew it out, and it
was restored to its own appearance. Then he was instructed,
if these should seem slight, to pour out water taken from the river
and change its clearness into red blood.
Still the prophet resisted, saying that his speech was feeble
and that his voice, tied in knots, could scarcely come out,
which veiled the secrets of his heart; in short, that he had nothing worthy
that the minds of men could rely on and follow.
He was rebuked: no one, unless the Lord grants it, speaks out
with polished thoughts, nor do the mute break long silences
unless [?] the Lord loosens the bonds of the tongue—
he who opens the ears of the deaf and the eyes of the blind,
and who clears with pure light the sight of those who see.
"Go," he said, "and speak, trusting in full speech,
noble in eloquence, with thought well-rounded into words."
But while he kept asking God and begging that another
be put in his place and substituted for him, he roused to anger
God, renowned for his kindness, who, stirred, said:
"See, there is your brother, eloquent, with polished
lips, and known to me, born a Levite
of that tribe, whom they call by the name of Aaron."
At once the prophet departed and told his father-in-law
that he would go back and wished to visit his brothers
born of the Jewish race. Jethro gave way
and, their affection unharmed, bade him go in gladness.
Eagerly he took his sons and wife with him
and set out on the journey commanded; and, weary from travel,
while he was restoring his strength, lying in the cool shade,
behold, an angel of the Lord came and threatened death.
But Zipporah quickly [?] searched out a sharp flint
and diligently cut the foreskin of her tender son;
and when she had cast herself down before the feet of the holy one,
"Let this blood from the little one's wound be stanched," she cried.
At her words the holy one departed to the stars.
And now the prophet was treading the sands of the barren desert,
when, at the Lord's sudden command, Aaron
came to meet his honored brother at the sacred mountain,
and, joined together, rejoicing, they exchanged kisses;
and it pleased them, in flowing talk, to open their minds
each to the other, about what must be done and what had been done.
At once both joined sincere and firm faith
to the Lord's word, and, going on together,
they told the elders they had summoned what [?] was to be
and what God had commanded; and when the signs had been performed in order,
the people believed that the longed-for remedy had come back to them,
and, bending the knee, humbly worshipped the Lord.
They went on to the king, who saw nothing with his blind heart
and did not believe in God, whom he said was scarcely
known to him; he held the people down under harsh law
and fierce command; the burden of labor grew,
the work was doubled, and a huge load was added
of raw bricks, which the sun's torch bakes.
He even took away the straw that was usually mixed in
to bind the cracking earth and the wet clay,
so that the people, worn out by evils, would rather lose heart
and suffer exile [?]. As they, spent with grief,
were driven on with harsh blows, they poured out
reproaches on the priests themselves, crying that they were afflicted
all the more bitterly, now that, by their reckless words,
they had procured wretched slavery instead of freedom.
When the gentle prophet had reported these words
to the eternal Lord, he received these words in reply:
"See, I have decreed that you shall be a god to King Pharaoh,
and that your brother shall zealously serve as your prophet
and obey you. You shall tell your brother what you have learned;
he shall declare it to the king, so that he may take care to release the people."
And now the holy prophet had spent twice forty years
of peaceful life in mortal flesh.
While they longed to soften the king with holy speech
and performed new signs, nothing moved him: not the slippery serpent
made from the rod thrown down, not the rivers
changed into red blood, not the moving water
fouled with grim stench from the dead fish—
because the profane minds of men, equipped with sinister chant,
were skilled in performing like deeds.
Indeed, they too made frogs creep forth
wherever there was land or water, and these were produced in like manner
by the magicians' chant; and these frogs, all croaking
with rattling voices, the prophet labored to drive away,
only not allowing them to be absent from their usual rivers.
This was granted to the king, if he wished to escape the plague,
through the prayers of the old man as he entreated, so that it would then be clear
that no other god reigns: the next day's light
returned to the sky, and all of them perished by one and the same death
and, heaped together, rotted with a bitter stench.
Gnats swiftly sprang up over all the bodies
of beasts and men, and the earth as well was filled with them.
The Chaldean band, having attempted this too, confessed
that it was the hand of the Lord, and gave up its vain effort.
After this the cynomyia poured in—which is called
the dog-fly—and at the prophet's nod it filled every
place, spreading far and wide, unknown only to the soil of Goshen,
which was then the land given over to the Jewish race;
wherever it went, it brought unending torments.
Then indeed Pharaoh, overcome, ordered them to depart
and to move their steps wherever they wished to go,
and to serve God with their vows; and he likewise begged
that the present, overwhelming evil might leave the fields
of Egypt and that God at last might be more merciful.
No delay: sudden death was dealt to the swarms
and killed them all at once. But the horny hardness
that had been in the king returned; soon a plague was sent
on beasts of burden and flocks alike, and deaths followed,
while Judea lost nothing. Then empty ash,
taken from the hollow of a furnace, was flung toward the stars
and raised dry pustules over men's limbs
and hollow blisters, and, leaving none exempt,
they brought torments on every kind of flock through the fields.
But a renewed form of evil pressed in vain upon the sluggish
king, so that the praise might be all the loftier
of God who varied so many wonders: behold, amid the fires
that the lightnings hurl, and the rumblings of high heaven
that crash at the Lord's command, there rushed down from the stars
menacing hail, whirling its freezing missiles everywhere,
which flew thick as from a rock [?]; and men who lacked
the shelter of roofs it battered [?], their bodies crushed,
and killed them and all the cattle; and, splitting the bark,
it crippled the forests and killed them as their inner bark withered—
a hail never seen before and unknown to ancient ages.
The wheat crops, their blades not yet grown,
and the spelt it only laid flat on the ground; for the rest it buried,
which, scattered in the soil, the harrow had not yet brought forth.
This too lost its force at the prophet's request,
as clear daylight returned, because, with a broken heart,
the ruler had begged in his weakness, confessing
his own crimes and declaring that God on high is just.
But see, once again his heart grew hard with mad thoughts—
a ruler who lived on to bear worse losses—
nor did he believe his companions about the downfall of perishing Egypt.
Yet he granted a limited leave to go [?]
to men stripped of the goods that serve life's needs.
The prophet would not accept it and demanded all their property
and their herds of beasts; but just speech is not welcome
to unwilling ears. For this he was driven out,
and his brother thrust out with him. Then the south wind came
with a mighty blast and darkened the day, and through a gloom like night
brought in countless masses of green-backed locusts,
which devoured whatever moist with sap they had found
among the leafy canopies, and the lush grass on the turf.
These were then destroyed, at the king's fearful request,
and, heaped together, were drowned in the waters of the Red Sea.
When the grim king had spat these out as trifles,
night descended and held them all, and vast storms
shut in and confined the people; and for three days
they remained hidden, and no one saw his neighbor
or could rise from his helpless bed,
while the [Hebrew] band enjoyed a radiant, open world,
untouched by any evil. Indeed, as they ran to and fro,
the dogs were harmless and silent, and, their barking suppressed,
they fearlessly licked their legs, wagging their tails—
dogs that at times, casting off all fear, are savage even toward their masters.
Yet the king's resolve did not yield to these losses;
raging, he rebuked the prophet and threatened him with death
for wanting to sweep away the cattle and all their property.
And now God had darkened the night with a pitch-black mantle,
planning a hidden blow amid thick deaths,
when those whom nurturing mothers had brought forth
in their first births died a sudden death, all within a brief moment,
from the very throne of the king, and then all
of every stock—men, cattle, and wild beasts.
At once immense grief raised dreadful cries;
every house roared, the cities resounded with lamentation.
Then indeed all pressed hard to drive out the people
that bore the Jewish name, as though it
were the cause of their evils by its deserts; and wealth and every possession
was handed over, and no loss was thought to come of it;
and countless herds of cattle went with them as they went.
So they departed, with God leading them, who went on before,
and on straining shoulders they carried their means of life.
And now the world had spent four hundred years
and forty more besides, if one reckons the sum
of the time elapsed since, out of concern to obtain grain,
Jacob came to the cities of Egypt to stay;
when these were completed, God at last took pity from on high
and, worthy of praise, took his people away from their untamed foe.
That [?] day is reckoned the first festival of the Passover,
and the joys of a night consecrated to God are celebrated,
and seven blessed days, as each year comes round,
bring unhurried rest, and every care is set aside;
no one turns the soil; free of the curved plough,
labor sleeps [?] ... and slaves rejoice
in equal freedom, and the whole business of life
is to join hearts to God, to recline on spread couches,
and to bring in abundant foods, which in its rich fields
the happy earth produces. And a white lamb is taken,
when the twelve months that make a year have run their course,
unblemished and the tenderest of the whole flock: this all together
the law requires to eat and to set on the holy table
with its bones unbroken, and with its blood to stain
the doorposts as a cleansing and so to gain a life kept safe.
A common law binds all; and those bought with money
and those used to hiring out their hands put off their foreskins
and take festive food from the flesh of the lamb.
Nothing may be left over; if a small company
has not eaten it all, it is right to join with a neighbor [?].
The loaves lack leaven, and soft flour,
mixed with spring water, is shaped into thin rounds,
which in their ancestral tongue they call azyma [?].
These rites are performed by all as the years return [?],
once fourteen days have run their course
in the new month, as men discern with reckoning as their guide.
And with anxious care they bind up their flowing garments,
alert, as if trumpets were sounding and war were being waged,
and their armed hands carry stout staffs.
They also take a stalk of pale hyssop
and with devoted hand dip it in the consecrated blood,
and, shaking it out, they gladly sprinkle the doors,
so that the noble liquid may dry on their dear doorposts,
which bars entry to the evil one who assails holy things.
And now the line had come down to the fifth generation [?],
when, making for the wilderness, the people dear to God
came to the Red Sea, carrying the bones of Joseph
taken from his tomb—he who once had said with truthful lips
that the Lord's serene regard and kindly right hand
would come from heaven and bring them freedom.
Then they came to Succoth and left Etham behind,
with Christ showing them unknown ways through trackless places,
who, when at fresh morning he spread light from the stars,
flew before them and furrowed the heavens with a snowy cloud,
and when night hid the sun, he shone through the darkened sky
as a gleaming radiance, with the bright hair of a comet.
Then they made for Pauleum, next to which lies the land of Migdol,
bordering on Baal-zephon opposite.
Here the Lord stripped the king's mind of fear,
sharpening his swollen thoughts and fierce spirit,
so that he would claim that the people he himself had released
were in fact fleeing, and would move his ranks headlong
to war, believing that with easy effort he could overtake
men driven by wandering and slowed by trackless ways.
So he eagerly roused his battalions to war, as if for a trifle,
driving iron-clad chariots, which, on flying axles,
a threefold crew drives, while one rises to hurl the swift spear,
now crouching low, now lifted high into the windy air,
full of terror and cunning; for, driven by frequent lashes,
the horn-hoofed steeds lay low the ranks that stand against them hand to hand
and add their pounding to the seething wheels,
which the hoof, urged on, sets turning with its varied leaps.
And now, hastening on his way, he had brought his chariots,
[?] for war, to the curving shores of the Red Sea,
when the Jewish band, suddenly turning their eyes,
looked back and saw the vast ranks and armored men
gleaming over all the plains; and, hemmed in
by an equal weight of twofold fear, as they saw the sea and the enemy
set against them, they turned on the prophet with harsh words
and said: "What great confidence was this, leader,
in a strength you never had, to destroy your kindred people,
to make them follow you, and to set the Red Sea before them,
trapped as they are? Why, in vain, take us away from hated Egypt,
who bore burdens that were sorrowful indeed, but safe?
Would it not have been better to endure Pharaoh's grim hardships
and his deadly laws? Was not that slavery
better than a freedom which, exposed to treachery,
prefers what it formerly endured and counts it sweet
whenever worse things, never seen before, come after?
We said this long ago, when you called us to vows
to be paid to the boundless God: it is safer
to live there as we were used to, and to bear the slavery
of a troublesome yoke, than now to lie down in death
among barren plains, in a land forsaken,
while in our trembling plight we are terrified by sea and foe."
But the prophet, overcome by no fear of what was happening,
and rather foreseeing what was to come, spoke these words [?]:
"Let go your gnawing cares and put on calm spirits,
my companions, and look with steady gaze
at how great a salvation is brought to you from the lofty stars,
granted by God on high. Those whom you see
pressing upon you in dense column—after this day, to look upon
will not be granted you, for the hour of their death is pressing upon them.
For God fights as a warrior with his lofty right hand
and governs those subject to him, while you keep your lips silent.’
When he had said this, the outcome followed his words.
For the angel who had flown before the camp of the men withdrew
and placed himself behind; and then the tawny column took its stand
at their back, and with a boundary set between it divided the ramparts
and the sites of the camps; and God poured a dark night
from his shining throne, and an unexpected peace soothed those
who raged for war and banished every disturbance.
O happy beyond measure, you to whom God sent defenses
from the lofty stars, for whom the shining heaven serves as a soldier,
and the nights come sworn together into battle!
Then God’s commands bade the leader bring out his rod
with outstretched hand and look down upon the vast Red
Sea. When this had been duly done,
the south wind came, and, using all its blasts,
through the silent night it drank up the seething waves
and dried the sea, so that a path opened through the midst
might lay out an unharmed course across the opened waters,
when the retreating deep had laid bare the thirsty sands.
So when the sea had hastily withdrawn, the wave,
curved into the shape of a mountain, stood round about them
and received them in its wide bosom and sent them through the deep.
Pharaoh, believing this allowed to him too, pressing close behind,
goes in and treads the sea floor; but suddenly the slow
wagons groan, and the horn-hoofed horses, leaning forward
with their whole chests to the ground, vainly push the loads with their knees,
which, their axles bound fast, could not be moved at all.
At once, bloodless, bound as if by an immense fetter,
straining to attempt a hasty flight and turn back again,
they goad their yoked horses in vain terror.
Upon these wretches another thing, greater and far more dreadful,
is heaped, and strikes their senses numb.
For the sea, which is wont to dash its wavering billows together,
joined the divided waters, mingled the swelling waves,
and sank all Egypt to the bottom.
But the Jewish band, seeing the floating bodies
of men from the enemy’s side, and the chariots swimming,
and the arms, and whatever is hurled slantwise at a foe,
looked up and feared God, and with faithful heart
trusted the Lord’s command and revered the prophet,
as they sang sweet canticles in the words of Moses:
“Let us sing to the Lord our God,
to whom belongs glory, mighty with honor;
he adorns himself with magnificent deeds,
as the swift chariots of the Egyptians,
with their horsemen joined and their heavy throng,
he slays in the streams of the Red Sea.
The mighty helper of my salvation
has borne his people out of the midst of the deep,
guardian and father and true salvation!
This is he, this is my Lord and my nourisher!
Him will I hallow with conspicuous praise,
who is the God of my father.
Him will I acknowledge with lofty voice,
who waged the war and overwhelmed the strong,
worthy of the name by which God is called.
Like stones and heavy lead
he buried in the vast billows the troops
which the king of the Nile, gathering them to arms,
menacingly proclaimed sharers in the spoil,
as he unsheathed swords against our throats
and whirled and brandished the drawn steel,
saying: ‘I will seize them as they flee,
I will divide the spoil and crush the vanquished,
and with the glory of a famous war
I will hold the palm my merits have won.’
While he recounted this and trusted in himself,
he prepared destruction for all his men.
None is like you, Creator,
greatest in deeds, prince of princes;
you have given mighty aid to your own,
so that the nations of the Philistines fear,
the Edomites too and the Moabites,
and the Canaanites tremble at their ruin,
until this people, redeemed by you,
climbs the conspicuous mountain holy to God,
an heir with everlasting trophies.”
This, repeated in like measures while the circle applauded,
the mothers sang, with the prophet’s sister leading the words,
beating tambourines with their fingers as they sang in harmony.
Then, fearless now that they had seen the host of wicked Pharaoh
overthrown, they made their way through trackless places
which of old were called Shur, and through the dry heat
they wore away parched days; for three days
the lamp of the sun scorched them with its fiercer rays.
Weary, they come to Marah and see waters
welling up with a bitter taste; sipping them with weary breasts,
they fling them far away, for the heavy water
tormented their stricken throats with its bitter savor.
Because of this flaw they mark the spring with a name,
and with a dense clamor demand of the prophet flowing
streams that could soften the burning heat.
He entreats God; for by what license could waves
be brought forth, unless the Lord sent them from his starry hall?
At once he takes a piece of wood, with which he sweetens the bitter
draughts, and suffuses the flowing waters with honey poured in.
There God, with the scales balanced in weighing,
gave just laws, testing the leader, as he spoke thus:
“If, mindful, you take all my words into a sincere heart
so as to do the things that are fitting for life,
bearing God’s commands in your heart, nothing grievous through all your days
will you suffer, nor will the burden of losses
or of savage disease weigh upon you; you will be far from every
evil disaster that laid waste fierce Egypt.
For I am the Lord, who heals hearts
and can make them whole.” After this they came to Elim,
watered with springs, twice six, which happened to flow
among leafy palms that with lofty tops
waved seventy crowns through the clouds.
And after, with camp pitched at Sin, rest had been taken from the worn [?]
roads, then, journeying on the fifteenth day
of the second month, they hurried through shady places,
they groaned under extreme hunger, while with loud voices
they rebuked and harassed their leader: “What so great a cause
of evils was there? Or what could there be? What could prove
more grievous than dire hunger, than burning breath
in parched throats, and death at hand,
which, when delayed, weighs more heavily than one that presses close?
Would that a single lot had given us death
while we were settled in Egypt, when the supply of food
was plentiful for all, and no one muttered privately
that he lacked nourishment! Now we live here,
where life is heavy even when there are no hardships.
Can anyone, then, amid the barren sands
endure the hateful day, and, parched, bear
the burning sun, which no shade tempers?
Rather, if our perils stir your feelings,
aged leader, we beg you: give back the Nile and Pharos
to your people, and permit the men who ask it
to take up all their labors again from now on, since it is our
judgment that nothing can be sadder than food cut off,
and that it is pleasant to serve with a full belly.” After such words
the prophet speaks, with Aaron as his partner in speech:
“Why does it please you to hurl words with such unruly tumult
and harass your leaders? Why demand food
which only he can provide who made the stars?
Yet at the setting of the sun’s lamp you will see
that God exists, by whose gift bread for you
is sent from heaven; who, after you were long entangled
in dusky Mareotis, now sends you joyful to the fields.
So come, and at the first light of the returning sun
taste unaccustomed food, the heavenly manna.
For the people’s quarrels, which our deeds do not deserve,
are aimed rather at the Lord, who is wont to feed
whatever he nourishes, and draws out the ages with long sustenance.”
When he had said this, the Lord shone forth from the cloud on high
in brighter daylight and promised heavenly food
to all, which a harvest that knows no blight
brings forth, and whose seeds no rust destroys.
Then, when evening now shone from the saffron sky,
quails fell thick from heaven like snow,
heaped in a heavy mass, and filled the level plains
and the site of the camp, while all marveled.
Moreover, when the light returned at first dawn,
manna gave snowy food, which in fine grains,
like coriander seeds, flowed down from all the stars.
This the men, as commanded, gathered by hand with a fixed
rule of gathering, lest anyone should perhaps prefer to store more
than the measure of fair food that suffices for each
single day; nor did vain cleverness [?] anyone
to have laid up more than was right at home; for in the warm sun
the meal rotted and was spoiled by worms of many kinds.
This alone two days could not spoil:
what the day of preparation brought out to be eaten on the feast day,
which God commands to be holy, and that men undertake
no labor whenever that day comes round,
which they call the Sabbath, granted to leisurely rest.
Moreover, this was thoroughly known to all:
that on every seventh day none of the food came down
that the heavenly harvest holds; for men, going out with keen care
through the countryside and the level plains,
saw nothing but grass waving in the gusts of wind,
and returned to their dwellings with empty laps.
And lest only those should see God’s memorials
to whom the food of the honeyed gift was sent,
some of it is shut within the protection of a golden casket,
for the band yet to be born and to come hereafter to see,
and, revering God, to marvel at the food of their forefathers.
After this they moved the standards, and the long column was led out
to [?], a place which, burning in the sun and lacking water,
made the people utter biting words
against their leader as they demanded water; and not with murmuring alone,
but they nearly proceeded to violence; for the priest,
fearing stones would be hurled at him, sent up on high
his words to God and implored rivers for the dry sands.
At once, prompted by the sentence of the great Lord,
he bids the elders likewise go before him;
then he takes his familiar rod, with which he had known
how to halt the waves and part the sea with a wall in the midst,
and makes for Mount Horeb, which rises vast
and lifts its holy head to the neighboring clouds.
There hard flint had shut in enclosed waters —
over it the Lord stood and summoned springs
by the same working of power with which he set out
immense rivers through the whole world and poured out the seas.
Commanded to strike it, he strikes, and suddenly the rock
bursts and pours out rivers [?] with surging waters.
The crowd runs to the waters, vying in a mass,
and countless flocks rush in and relieve their heat,
and, once they are filled, strength returns to weary bodies.
So the place itself takes its name from the cause:
Temptation, because the people were in two minds,
wavering in heart whether the Most High,
the Almighty, dwelt among them, and because the rough crowd
had wished on their leader the curses that anger conceives.
There Amalek, drawn up in warlike troops,
routed the Hebrew columns; to ward off this disgrace
Joshua swiftly takes with him the chosen strength of the fighters;
as he goes with iron-clad hand into the war he has taken up,
the leader helps him with vows and prayers and climbs Mount Horeb
with hastening step; Aaron, joined with him,
and Hur flank him on either side, and his limbs, worn with age,
shrinking from toil and not strong enough for the task of standing,
they steady with a stone set beneath, and they place a hard seat
under him and spread it for the leader; then they hold up
his hands as they droop and sink, so that the prayer of his palms
might be joined to the pleadings of his heart; for often, falling
under their aged weight, they made the contest doubtful.
When the hands placed beneath had steadied them on every side,
the enemy lines gave way, and the fields were filled
with the slaughter of men, and of so many thousands none survived.
That these things had been done at God’s command, the prophet
wrote down in a book to teach the times to come;
and at once he built an altar consecrated to God,
addressing the holy place in faithful words:
“My sure hope is God, whose protection alone
has always given me aid, who with strength concealed
and hidden hand drove back the warring [?]
and slays the Amalekites and their troops with all their youth.”
Meanwhile Jethro learns of his son-in-law’s deeds
and comes in haste, rejoicing to see with his own eyes
what had been told him. And he found him beset with labor
beyond measure, as he heard all the cases
of a crowd beyond number; and having prayed to the great
God, he sacrificed beasts; then by his counsel
he brought it about that tribunes should be chosen from the people
and other ranks besides, which the soldiery receives in due order,
so that the legions might be governed by a fixed law
and settle the lesser disputes, while the great quarrels
should be judged by the leader alone. When this had been duly done,
Jethro sought his own home and left his son-in-law.
Meanwhile the third month, in the swift changing of the seasons,
had come round, when through the lonely fields
the Lord’s column was led to Mount Sinai.
This the prophet quickly climbed, driven by the voice
[?] and the warnings of God; soon, prostrate, he hears:
“These words spoken to you, remember to tell to all:
you have seen, O men, what portents Egypt endured,
while care for you holds me, and I gather you all
and carry you, as though led along the path of the wings
which the prince of birds spreads as he furrows the clouds.
And now, if my words make their way to your ears,
so that what is commanded is done, and your hearts in harmony
cleave to just law, I will hold you forever as a people
distinguished by rich possessions, and set you above all
nations, so that you may reign in strength through the whole world.
For all this earth is mine, and whatever anywhere
is brought forth is ever subject to my eternal right.
You [?] a kingdom made glorious by my right hand,
and a holy nation to me, which will prolong its days.”
He, mindful of the command, repeated what had been said
to the chiefs of the people; and the people trusted the noble words
and submitted their hearts to the great Thunderer,
saying that they would carry out the glorious commands.
After this the Lord, from his lofty seat, prepares something greater
to establish, and sends the prophet to the duties
familiar to him, and bids all with flowing water
wash away stains of filth from clothing and limb,
and the men to sleep apart, so that, pure in mind and body,
on the third day God might be seen from the lofty stars
by those stationed far from the mountain, which no one, standing near,
was to touch or tread; the cattle were ordered to be driven
into the far deserts, lest the penalty meant for the guilty
fall upon them, which comes by stones or iron, when a missile weapon
is hurled by a forceful hand, or blows send stones flying.
When this was done, their bodies stained by no blemish,
the people gaze toward the hill, as dawn first
gave its blush on the third day, the stars withdrawn.
Now lightnings flash, now from the lofty stars a great
roar of voices is heard, and a stormy cloud
hangs poised in its mass, and with an awesome blare
a trumpet repeats terrible sounds, and, fenced by the rampart
within the camp, the sorrowful people tremble, and the steep sides
of the holy mountain, witnessed by God from heaven, smoke.
And whoever was a priest chosen out of the people
stays far from the mountain, which only devout Aaron and Moses
have the right to climb. Then with everlasting utterance
God gives commands to endure, in this order of the law:
“I am the Lord who, freeing you from peril,
brought you out of the land of Egypt, and bade the hard labor
that the burden of slavery imposed come to an end.
Let your hearts worship me alone, and fashion no idols
for yourself, nor bow down and worship a god that is made;
nor believe that the stars which shine in heaven
are divinities, nor likewise marvel at anything on earth,
or that the grey waters of the flowing sea conceal.
I am a jealous Lord, repaying sins and crimes
upon fathers and then upon their offspring to the fourth generation;
abundant in mercy, repaying greater and grand rewards
which just men have earned, who, embracing my commands
deep in their hearts, keep them and follow them in mind.
Revere the name of God. Keep the festal Sabbath
with your children and servants, and gladly lay aside
all labor whenever that day returns to the world.
In twice three days the Lord made all things
that flourish on earth and in heaven and in the swelling sea;
on the seventh, his mighty works completed, he rested;
hence that festal day flourishes, hence it is always [?],
always honored, and hallowed by the Lord’s kindness.
Give honor, my son, to your parents, that you may
have lasting life on earth, which the mighty God
prolongs from his mighty seat. Do not love adulteresses,
nor kill a man, nor wickedly swear
false oaths; commit no theft,
nor, as a false witness, support a litigant by fraud.
Restrain your mind and your eyes from another’s wife,
and shrink from whatever your mind warns you is not yours.
Let altars rise built of heaped-up earth,
where it is lawful to sacrifice devoted sheep.
But if you should resolve to raise them from a mass of stones,
keep iron far away, since they become defiled
when smoothed by a craftsman’s hand; and you are not allowed
to climb them with a ready step, lest you uncover your nakedness.
Whoever is a slave, born of your own kindred,
let him bear the yoke of slavery for twice three years;
then let him go free, carrying his rewards with him,
his wife sent away with him, if she is not yet seen to have borne children.
But if he already rejoices in children and the name of father,
he must leave his wife and offspring to his master,
while he himself is his own man, freed from his master’s bond.
But if he clearly prefers to remain a household slave,
let him be placed before the holy doors, his master standing him there,
to suffer the wound that a slender awl pierces
through the soft ear, and remain so [?] forever.
To sell a daughter to a foreign people is not lawful
for a parent, but the right remains within his own people;
yet it is by no means lawful to send her away as a slave.
If she displeases the master to whom she was sold,
the money shall be returned, whatever the price assessed,
so that she may return to her father’s threshold.
But if perhaps she is given to his son, it is fitting that he
treat her as his own daughter. If the son would rather
lawfully take another, as is permitted him, the garments that cover her limbs
he shall openly provide, nor afterward deny her her due,
if she has been known to him in intercourse; or, if these terms
are not ratified by the man, he may release her to go,
and not reclaim the price that was paid. Whoever with a cruel wound
strikes [?] and lays a man low, let him lie dead by the same
death by which he kills; but if the harm
was inflicted rather by chance, the Lord giving the man over
to another’s blows, there is a place able to shelter
one who deserves pardon, the Lord graciously granting him safety.
But he who by guile hews living limbs with the sword
and of set purpose rejoices in blood shed
is guilty of death, vainly seeking the sanctuary
consecrated to God most high; for he shall be taken from there
and, set far apart, cut down with the unbending sword.
And he who insolently reviles or strikes his parents
falls into a capital crime, to be atoned for by death.
No less is he sought out for punishment who perhaps by deceitful
craft treacherously steals one born among his ancestral people
and rejoices to hand him over for money received.
But if a quarrel has been stirred up by words
and someone, struck by a fist or by a thrown stone,
recovers his usual strength, no guilt shall cling;
yet what the physician’s care has cost must be paid.
He who with a blow of the rod kills outright his maid or manservant
does not escape the penalty that clings to him.
But if the slave dies after another day,
there is no guilt, since the master has lost his price.
But if perhaps a quarrel boils up between two men
while they burn with stirred-up bile, and one of them strikes
a wife swollen with a child conceived,
his hand stretched out to deal a blow, and makes the coming birth
be thrust from the mother’s womb before its day,
he shall make good the offspring with a price the husband assesses,
if its form was not yet complete and fashioned.
But if the infant died with its features fully formed,
he shall fall by a deserved death. Eye for eye taken
shall every guilty man repay, giving tooth for tooth;
he shall give hand for hand, and foot likewise,
whoever cuts off a foot; and burns made by flames
devouring fire shall expiate; wound shall be given for wound;
bruised limbs are appeased by a bruised body.
But if anyone deprives his manservant of sight, taking his eye,
or his maidservant, let him allow them to go free
wherever liberty calls; or if fragments of a tooth
have been knocked out by his hand, let the injured one take consolation,
weighing the gift against his wound.
But if a bull [?], rejoicing in his mighty neck,
still a stranger to the field and free of the curved plough,
gores anyone with his horn, let him be crushed with a heap of stones,
and, buried, to be eaten by no man’s tooth,
let him give his limbs to the earth to decay into liquid,
leaving no penalty on his innocent owner.
But if he was accustomed to strike his neighbors with his crescent brow,
and the owner, long warned, has heedlessly not restrained him [?],
let the owner lie dead for the killing done by the ox, and the bull be slain.
But if a milder sentence demands a price for the one slain,
let him pay whatever the assessment requires.
This too any man may rightfully demand for the killing of his son
or daughter. If a slave has fallen by the blow
of a bull, the master is bound to pay
thirty coins, and the savage bullock is put to death.
But if anyone wishes to sink a well with a deep pit,
digging the soil right out, let him soon close it with a cover,
lest, if some beast should roll down the slope,
he pay the damages, the owner demanding the price, and must buy
the flesh of the fallen beasts, a slender consolation.
But if perhaps an ox kills an ox with its curved horn,
let it be sold; let the price be shared by the two,
and let them divide between them the flesh of the slain bull.
But if its vice had already been well attested,
the owner shall give back beast for beast in place of the one lost,
and the innocent man shall take the limbs of the slain bullock.
Whoever steals a calf, let him be compelled to return five;
let whoever carries off a lamb pay back twice two.
It is lawful to strike down a thief by night with the sword
as he breaks through the doorposts and bursts the barred threshold.
But if he is caught when the sun has risen with its light,
the guilty man is ordered to repay twofold what he took.
But if this is beyond his wealth and means,
he shall be sold, to make good the theft by the labor of his hands.
If anyone’s beast strips [?] a crop or a green vine
or crops it bit by bit with gaping mouth,
let him at once measure out acres of fertile land
of equal yield and extent; so he will make good the damages
that were done before. This rule binds
those also who sweep whole fallow fields bare
and reap leafy vines, the branches consumed,
so that they lose in like measure the fine things
they held in their own fields. For if the crackling fire,
which from a little kindling is wont to catch the brambles,
the dry stubble, and trunks stripped of bark,
has consumed another’s crop or vine with its heat,
the charge recoils upon the one who started it, through deserved losses,
so that he repays whatever the guilty flame devoured.
A deposit must be returned: if the treacherous hand
of thieves has plundered it, when the culprit is found
a double sum is paid; but if the one who took
the stolen wealth stays hidden, a sacrifice alone
shall free the keeper from guilt, since he will be clear of fraud.
But if the deceiver is exposed in lying craft,
let him render twice the weight of the deposit before a judge.
This measure must also be kept in cases concerning cattle,
so that what has been carried off by wicked theft
he must restore whose watch was slack.
But if the mad fury of wolves tears the tender flock,
the dispute is calmed when the carcass is shown.
But if someone lends two bullocks to draw carts,
let the borrower not claim they perished under an enormous load
if he himself was present, goading them as they went.
This holds also for the rest, whom the loads imposed weigh down.
But if he loses the swift animals he has received,
whoever drives them, it is right that he bear the whole loss.
If he lost them when they were hired out for an agreed wage,
he shall set them against the price of the work, promptly assessed.
If anyone takes to himself the use of a virgin not betrothed,
he shall join that same woman to himself as wife with a dowry.
But if the mind of the girl he took does not agree to marriage,
let him give her father gifts suited to the bridal chamber.
It is wrong to harbor a sorcerer. Harsh death shall slay
one who mingles with a beast in the act of foul intercourse.
Let life leave men who revere the shrines of demons,
since it is right to bow the neck to the Lord alone.
Let no one wrong a stranger by word or hand,
because Egypt took you in
when you left your native soil and former home.
A woman whose husband has died must not be despised,
but rather cherished, and boys bereft of their parents too,
lest the guilty [?] suffer like penalties
and, snatched away by a swift death, leave their own behind in terror:
for God hears and helps afflicted hearts.
To one who asks, lend the use of the money he requests,
setting aside any fee, far from shameful usury;
and do not hastily press the anxious debtor to repay what he took.
And if perhaps he entrusts the very covering of his body
and hands it over to you as a pledge for the coin,
return it before the sun hides his head from the sky.
I am a merciful Lord: I readily hear such as these.
All of you, cease to curse foreign gods
and leading men, who will hold the reins of the people.
From your first fruits bring devout gifts to the Lord;
and whatever child you beget from the first seed of your wife
you shall consecrate to the Lord, after the seventh sun has
measured out its high path, so that you may be a holy offspring.
A beast killed by the tooth of ravening wolves
let no one eat: let him reject what is unfit for the table.
You shall not believe tales told to you which no supports
of credibility uphold. Nor wish to speak falsely as a witness
with wicked mind. Nor, adding yourself as one to the many
in an assembly, strive to prevail as a guilty man,
so as to condemn the poor and lowly on a trumped-up charge.
Rather, if perhaps you see a beast straying
that belongs to one whose heart is not joined to yours, bring it back.
And if beasts of burden are bowed beneath a heavy load,
raise them, and straining, lift them with both hands in turn.
Do not lay low an innocent man, for he is righteous of heart.
You shall not take gifts to plead for an anxious guilty man
and a worried defendant, since such gifts soon blind the eyes
and corrupt men's words and every judgment.
For twice three years let the vigorous farmer press on
with the rich clods, since the seventh year must
bring slow leisure, in which every poor man may take
what has grown in the open, and gladly leave
what remains to be eaten by wild beasts as they roam the glades.
While the swift year rolls round in its endless circuit,
you must keep feasts divided into three kinds;
for seven days it is right, rejoicing,
to eat soft unleavened bread of wheaten meal,
as I told you long ago, in the first month of new fruits,
when you had full freedom to depart from Egypt.
Let no one come before my face empty-handed.
Know that the firstfruits of your works and the beginning of harvest
are a feast for you, whenever you have scattered seed on the field;
or when rest is joined to the year that has run its course,
all things being finished which the toil of labour produces.
Let every man mark out three times in the year
in which he may present himself before my face.
For when the glad possession of the land
has been entrusted and given to you, the nations subdued, know
that only unleavened bread is to be placed on my altars;
that manifold beasts and the red stream of blood
profit your feasts nothing, and that the fat [?]
must not last through the wakeful night into the hours of light
of the feasts that return whenever the care of sacred rites comes round.
And let no tender lamb be cooked in its mother's milk.
Behold, from the heavenly citadel I send a starry minister
to take care of you, who with great strength
will cherish you on your way to a land which, glad with rich fields,
flourishes green and pours out sweet streams of nectar.
Make ready to hear him, and trust his sacred words.
He is joined to you and will remain faithful,
keeping an everlasting name on the heavenly height.
Come now, join your hearing to holy words,
and take up my command with a sincere mind,
that you may be a people dear to me, a blessed nation,
and a lofty kingdom of God, a race exalted forever
in all the lands which the sun, returning,
beholds on either side, embracing the world with its warm axis.
While they are of one heart I will cherish your people and resist all
who prepare to make war on you; the Amorite will yield to you,
and the fierce Hittite, and those whom the best of lands
now sustains, a land soon to pass to you as its tiller forever.
Take care not to bow your neck to forbidden shrines,
and in fear, relying on them, adore hostile gods.
Rather, overthrow profane things and shatter all idols
with their inscriptions, and blot out the names engraved,
that you may serve God, at whom all things tremble.
Soon I will bless your food and your flowing springs,
and remove the plagues of disease from your body.
No one in all the people, lacking a son, will grieve
that the name and honour of a father are not his.
I will grant long days, so that a wider limit of age
may lengthen the span of the life you long for.
Before your battle lines grim terror will fly,
and wasps with poisoned sting will run ahead,
so that your standards may be feared by warlike companies,
and easy victory may come over the fierce nations.
Yet once they are subdued I will make them dwindle little by little,
lest the land be empty of men, and [?]
an excessive throng of raging beasts increase.
With your soldiers spread abroad I will make the borders
of your land and dwelling extend, from where, with red marble,
the ocean seethes, slippery with windswept waves,
as far as the Philistine sea and the land that lacks
a human tiller, and to where, famed and with great throngs,
the Euphrates flows, clear with glassy waves."
When he had thundered these things, the Lord bids Aaron and Moses
climb the hill, and seventy men of noble age,
and bow their necks from afar
to the eternal and supreme God; for he lets the leader himself
hasten near, who, carrying out the holy commands
of God, at once builds a lofty altar
beneath the towering mountain, rising into the empty air:
twelve stones, which seem the full number of the tribes,
he sets close beside it. Here he brings forward [?] bullocks
from the herd [?] and sacrifices them on the holy altars;
part of their blood he pours out upon the altar,
another part he drips into bowls, and the thronging people
he sprinkles with a light dew, and unrolls the book
that keeps the records of the eternal God. After
the docile people had declared with one voice that these were dear to them,
he climbs the swelling hill with slow effort
and sets the aged elders and his brother on the summit.
Together they behold a stone gleaming with brightness,
on which the footsteps of the starry King had stood:
its name is sapphire; and here a white heaven is seen
stretched along the ridge's back: revering all this,
they offer lofty praise and partake of food.
Meanwhile the prophet, having told the elders
to stay seated there, has Joshua join his steps with his own
with peaceful heart [?]. Hur
and Aaron he leaves to his people, to hear the disputes of contending men
with even scale and to speak the words of law.
When he had reached the many ridges of the holy hill,
a shining cloud glides swiftly from the ethereal sky
and, embracing the mountain, covers it, and hides the prophet
apart from his companions for twice three days of sunlight.
And now the seventh day had opened the snowy heavens,
when the Lord addresses the prophet from the midst of the cloud.
Shining amid wondrous flames, he begins to speak,
and gives the prophet commands over four times ten days,
that he might know what sanctuaries are worthy
of the most high God; and he orders these lofty works to be built
of wood strong forever, which no age destroys.
This he lays out in wondrous ways, and a ductile plate
of gleaming gold overlays the measurements commanded,
joining twin rings with smooth rounded turning
on the right side and the left, where holy things are worshipped.
Then from smoothed timbers he fashions the ark,
in which the commandments of the everlasting Thunderer may abide.
Moreover, he causes [?] to spring forth from ruddy gold
and sets them facing each other where the altars spread,
with equal splendour of wings and like flight,
as though they were moving nimble feathers into windy clouds.
And besides, many other devices of new things
were made in wondrous ways; whoever wishes to tell them
will sooner count out the sands the sea rolls.
But neither how many their kinds nor what their names are
can a law bound by metre bring forth in speech,
while the prophet fashions ladles, bowls, and mortars,
and makes engraved dishes to be carried for offerings,
and the stands that are placed beneath the lamps [?].
Now whatever covers the sacred ark from above
or veils the doorposts, he dyed with blazing [?].
Moreover, robes are woven with a mantle [?]
for Aaron and the pious priests who offer
sacred gifts in the house of God; and flashing gems
are fixed to the folds, marking six names on each,
distinctly, of the tribes from whose body the people come,
marking each single name on noble gems.
The first place: emerald joined to topaz;
sapphire follows this, with which the carbuncle burns,
and jasper flourishes and glitters amid tawny gold;
the third, with ligure [?]
and amethyst, which shining purple dyes.
Chrysolite is the fourth, with onyx joined to beryl.
Added is the venerable sign of the heavenly King,
which a plate of gleaming gold holds, formed upon it.
Moreover, linens of snowy weave [?]
are ordered to be gathered in loose folds and put on the limbs
and to hide the private part of the flesh,
lest the priests, while carrying the sacred things, uncover what is shameful.
Among these things the whole order of sacred rites is unfolded:
what gifts lighten sin, or what victim, struck
by the blade, falls and brings God's holy wrath to an end.
For whoever among men touches the sacred altars
is made holier, his heart cleansed of blemish.
That a lamp should hang always from the high coffered ceiling,
kindled, and conquer the night with its light,
God's decree proclaims, lest perhaps darkness make dreadful night throughout the holy altars.
And at times the juice of liquid olive is set out,
sanctifying the flesh of men, as it flows from the crown
of the head and drenches the limbs with thick ointment;
add incense too, whose light breath is made pleasant
to the nostrils and sprinkles sweet airs upon the senses.
Then, that the structure of the great temple might shine
and surpass all buildings in its adornment,
God gave the craftsmen most skilful minds and the greatest
of endowments, and put every art into them:
to Ahisamach's son of the tribe of Dan, and Bezalel joined with him,
whose illustrious lineage was from the tribe of Judah.
And that the Lord's words might be well known to the people,
the prophet receives twin tablets carefully formed,
given by God, which with holy thumb
and matching fingers the glorious hand of the King had written.
Meanwhile the people, settled in the camp laid out for them,
groaning with gnawing heart that their prophet
had now long been absent and was nowhere to be seen,
murmur. In their madness they keep demanding of Aaron
perverse deities for themselves; and he, as they raged
and pressed him long, ordered them to bring and hand over
the ornaments which daughters and daughters-in-law wear in their ears,
since their native beauty is thought to have
too little splendour, and gold hangs from a shameful wound.
When the people had heaped this up, he cast it into the fire,
and then, drawing it out softened from the furnace flame,
he blended it and formed a calf with grim brow,
and said that the coming day would be a solemn feast.
Then, as soon as the morning star brought forth
its white fires and shut the night out of high heaven,
the Jewish band rises and gladly keeps the ruinous feast
and floods their breasts with many cups,
and in frenzy leads exultant dances.
The Lord sees this, high on his lofty citadel,
and orders the blameless prophet to descend quickly,
saying: "Run down swiftly and leave the mountain,
leader of a perverse people and master of a folk
whom profane things delight; Judea has sinned greatly
under you, its chief, despising holy deeds.
See, those who under your leadership were permitted
to loose the chains of untamed Pharaoh and go out from dark Canopus
stand as transgressors before a bull's face
and, instead of God, celebrate the limbs of a counterfeit calf,
and now call it the deity of their freedom.
Do not turn aside my anger, nor stand in my way,
while I send on them deserved terrors and fitting ruin.
And do not fear loss, as though the power taken from you
were at once to pass to the height of another.
There will be given in the lands a nation unknown to you,
far mightier in arms, which will be victorious with you as its chief."
Terrified at this, the prophet, prostrate, worships the Lord,
speaking thus: "Why does your anger now go out
with such commotion against your people, whom, groaning
under harsh rule, Egypt let go in great fear,
while it fears you, great one, while the strength of your lofty right hand
terrifies the wretched tyrant, his neck broken?
And now, O Lord, what will the crowd of Canopus say,
deprived of its captives and hostile to the people
which it now sees to be yours, except that you, mighty God,
favouring them in vain with your accustomed kindness,
led men out to be slain in a desert place,
as they drag out their deaths among vast wildernesses?
Lofty one, be gracious to your own, and show a serene face
to one who asks; for who, when you are angered, can live
on earth or in heaven? To you alone runs
whatever dies and whatever lives. And at last let there return
to your mind, venerable one, the gifts you prepared
for Abraham once, and then for great Jacob
and pious Isaac, men whom their service adorns as blessed
because they pleased you: swearing by your own strength,
holy one, you promised that their offspring would be in your care,
unconquered King, to grow dense with numerous youth
and countless ranks, like the stars of great heaven
and the starry gems that sparkle in the vault of the world.
Why do your promises totter? Why does no one possess
the riches of the wealthy land, and your prophet lingers an exile,
he to whom you promise streams of honey and rivers of milk?"
The Lord is moved by these words and casts out all his anger.
Then the prophet descends the lofty hill,
bringing back the tablets written with the Lord's law
inside and out alike; for the holy page
was set on the back as well; and as he comes out in haste,
Joshua is startled by the people's immoderate cries
and thinks this the clamour of a crowd at war.
But the prophet sees not wars, but hearts sodden with wine
sending manifold cries up to heaven.
And now, having passed the threshold of the camp, the leader
sees the dances of the reveling people seething,
and sees the gilded calf with swelling neck,
which the crowd gazed upon as if it were a heavenly father.
Then, enraged, as he conceives a hot anger,
he breaks the tablets, rising with his whole body into the blow,
and melts down the calf, thrown on the hearths, and then
casts it into the water, and taking from those streams
orders the stunned people to drink; then
in his offence he sharply rebukes his brother for having listened
to those seeking vain things and provoking God to just wrath.
He, begging for peace, confesses the people's crime,
making himself free of any share in the guilty deed.
But the leader, preparing to punish the crimes of the mad crowd,
orders the Levites to run through the whole camp
and bare the sword and strike the bodies they meet
everywhere, though they be of kindred blood.
Eagerly they run through the byways they know
and charge the groups that meet them, and swiftly,
avengers of the Lord, they slay about three thousand men,
to whom, as it were, you might add twenty thousand more for their zeal.
These things done, the prophet goes out to his people now gentler
and entreats the eternal King for the people's crime,
speaking thus: "The throng of your people has sinned,
unconquered King; the hearts of men seek more than mortal things,
worshipping images of dumb beasts.
To these they have made vows, and believed gold to be a god.
And now, O Lord, if you deem me worthy of the prayer
that I make and pour out to you, forgive the guilt,
which you alone can release. But if a greater punishment
awaits them and the sentence of death holds them all,
blot out my name, holy one, from the heavenly page
which your venerable hand has written, to which the world is subject."
As he prays, God's favourable answer soothes him:
"Whoever, a sinner, wounds me with forbidden crime,
coming against me, him the page of the holy book
does not hold, and his guilty name will be blotted out from it.
But you, make haste, and from here pursue the course you have begun,
and assign the promised places to the throng in your charge.
And lest anxious care should touch you on your way,
a messenger will always go before you as you go.
But their own deeds weigh down those whom crimes darken,
men with stiff neck and swollen mind:
therefore I do not walk with you at your side."
The people received these words in sorrowful guilt,
and groaned with streaming tears for such disgrace,
putting on soiled garments of black thread.
The good prophet, in his words, bids them lay aside
their sad attire and their mourning, and he earnestly entreats them
to take heed lest perhaps God's anger be greater
if he should chance to be offended by a like crime.
These things done, he brings out the tent prepared for him
and pitches it apart from the camp, and fittingly gave it a name
from the Witness, whose sentence is true.
As he entered the threshold made for God, all the men
vied with one another to see him, and they in turn
rejoiced to step forward or to stand facing it:
when suddenly, dreadful to see, a shining cloud glides
from heaven and floods the top of the high temple;
and while the pious prophet goes in and while he then returns,
Joshua always kept himself hidden in the house of the Lord,
never going forth. But the prophet holds his accustomed converse
with the Lord, and asks for what had never before
been granted to mortal man: that he might see
face to face the venerable face of the blessed Lord,
and that God might always accompany the leader on his way,
however much a heavenly messenger might guard him.
It is granted, and God begins in lofty words
what must be done before the grace of so great a gift
could feed eyes accustomed to look on worldly things:
"Come now, make haste, climb the threatening rock
and plant your step there; and while my glory
passes down from on high and returns, beneath the rock's vault,
shaded by my right hand, stay there, until, passing by
in swift course, I withdraw the shade of my divine palm.
Then you may see only the hindmost legs
of God as he passes: it is not lawful for anyone to see his face
among the number of the living, whom the earthly air sustains."
These things are done as commanded; soon he shapes anew
carefully hewn tablets like the first, for the divine laws,
and, alone, approaches the height familiar to him
from his usual journeys, and does not allow anyone
to come near the mountain, and drives away from there even
the woolly flocks, since such things border on guilt:
holy things in no way cling to what is corrupt.
Then, enjoying the longed-for words of the Lord,
he learns what will come upon his people, and of his own accord he speaks up:
"O Lord, whom generous mercy makes great
in heaven and on earth among your own, you, gentle in your heavenly hall
and alone mighty, and likewise most just,
equally indulgent to the peoples whom the glad world
holds everywhere, confessing the Lord with their whole mind:
you relieve all from wrongdoing, you can pardon
whatever is wicked, since you alone are without crime;
you are likewise wont to punish deadly guilt
upon the offspring, the sons of fathers and the sons of sons:
remain with us, God, in your surpassing power.
For this fierce people is proud with stiff neck;
if you forgive the sins committed by anyone's crime,
we shall live as yours through the ages." Soon from his hall
the holy Lord of heaven declares what he had commanded before:
that when the people had rested after wounding wars,
looking to leisure, it should know only marriages
allowed from among its own people, lest perhaps
a wife taken from outside should ensnare the unwary minds
of men with deceitful cunning and teach profane rites.
And now four times ten suns with their swift light
the prophet had passed here, and had taken no food,
bringing back a fasting breast to the vast camp.
When they saw him shining with the torch of a brilliant flame,
the men's gaze feared him, and his brother was in awe,
turning his mortal eyes away from the shining light.
But the prophet, unaware that the honour of a sudden power
had shone upon his consecrated person, learned from the people's fear
that the blaze of that immense light must be veiled,
lest the Jewish band turn away their ears along with their eyes.
But whenever he went to the peaceful words of the Lord,
he took off the [?] linen of the transparent veil.
Then, with metals offered by the people in rivalry,
and fleeces dyed with Sidonian dye,
he completes the sacred house with exceptional skill.
The Lord on high filled it with a cloud he sent,
so much that the prophet could not pass
the holy doorposts, though the veil lay open
across the whole threshold and no guard stood in his way at the doors.
Whenever this cloud had moved off on the shifting breezes,
the camp was moved; and night, wont to return again,
shone with the great light of a red flame,
as the flying crest blazed and showed the presence of God.
LEVITICUS.
When the temple, plain to see far off in the trackless wilderness,
had received its finishing touch, the care of the sacred rites soon
fell to the priests: by what rite each offering should be made acceptable,
which victim should take away sin, or which, when slain,
should bring well-being; what gifts the powerful man, and what the poor man, should lay
at the altar, and what benefits a pair of turtledoves would bring,
or a dove matched and joined to a dove like itself.
But, a marvel: in a moment the entrails of the slaughtered beasts
were snatched away by devouring fire sent from the high heavens.
Meanwhile two young men, vigorous now in their strong years,
believing in their foolish hearts that it was allowed them,
Nadab and Abihu, the well-known sons
of the prophet Aaron, kindle a fire with sacrilegious rites.
Their death was not long delayed: for lightning from the sky
flashed out above and, in the midst of their prayers, killed
the insincere men, while their father mourned bitterly.
Then the bodies of the cold dead are laid in a tomb.
Yet soon the father ceased to mourn the buried,
and so did all their brothers, for the prophet forbade the weeping
that had been allowed the people: for the fiery blaze,
flying from its heavenly seat, had shaken all
the men with the terror it struck into them, and they saw plainly
that God, who was not absent, must not be scorned.
Amid these events the priest learns from the voice of the Lord
that wine is forbidden to him, and honeyed strong drink to his sons,
so that, whenever they worship the Lord at the altars set up for him,
no breath sent out from a wine-soaked chest may give offense.
A rule sets apart the common food of the people
and declares what may be eaten and what it is not right
to take, a custom which even our own banquets
keep under heavenly law: that the vulture shall not become food,
nor the raven or magpie, nor the [?] buzzard,
nor the keen-eyed hawk, nor the kite with its hooked beak,
and other things that are hard to name in measured verse,
so that unclean things, heaped up in the stomach and settling there,
may not by their touch make the harmless innards foul.
A woman who empties her womb in lawful childbirth,
if she bears a boy, is unclean for seven days
in her whole body; but when the sky has turned
to the eighth day, on which it is the custom to cut the private parts,
the boy's foreskin will be removed, and from then on she will stay apart,
now delivered, for thirty-three days more,
so that she may not boldly defile, by sight or by foul touch,
the altars on which offerings are burned in holy worship.
But if her body, once it has conceived, brings forth a girl,
by keeping twice that time she will incur no fault;
and when it is completed, she will at once vow her gifts:
either two turtledoves, or doves alike in their plumage,
or a lamb of white fleece from the gentle flock,
so that the priest by his prayers may stanch the flow of blood.
The appearances and signs of diseases are taught as well,
especially those that leprosy produces, which over the whole body
