drenches the sallow flesh with pale corruption
and covers the whitening skin with deadly spots,
so that, since it sometimes flares up through the Lord's anger,
by this remedy it may take flight and leave the body
of the man who prays for his offense and brings a gift,
[?] poverty, which in triumph often outdoes the rich,
since the Lord drinks in the vow of the simple man.
And yet no great expense is required for healing:
for the whole law prescribes the offering of two young birds and twin lambs,
so that a ewe is joined to the young one,
with fine flour, over which a stream of oil has been poured.
These the rich man can offer; but the gifts of the humble man
remain humble: for he will slay at the altar a young one
that is thriving, with a year of twelve months completed,
and some of the holy meal, which he mixes with oil,
or two turtledoves, or perhaps doves alike.
Moreover, since idle pleasure often makes sport of men's sleep
by night, if by chance seed drips
from the member, the body of the sleeper becomes foul
and remains unclean until the evening star, bright in the sky,
goes before the night with its glad light;
and men whom dreams have darkened do not only disfigure their own bodies
with a foul stain, but also whatever they touch as they go about:
for this reason it is right to bathe the limbs in a river,
so that purity may quickly return as the guilt ends.
Indeed, it is right even to break earthen vessels
stained by such a man's touch, but those made of metal
to wash, and to draw off the filth in a glassy stream.
Under this law even lawful intercourse is purified.
Then, once the troublesome stain has been removed from the limbs,
the priest will lend his help when, the sun having returned,
the seventh dawn has shone out among the crimson stars,
if the man comes to the altar supported by a pair of turtledoves,
guilty of sin and bound by his vow, or with matched doves.
A woman who, as the month runs its course, has her monthly flow
is defiled by the moist discharge that comes from her womb,
and whatever she touches she stains, until the seventh day passes
with the return of the morning star; but if the harmful flow
presses more heavily and the order of its fixed time breaks down,
the appearance of the ailment is no different, and the end of her guilt
will be the same, if she brings to the holy altar a gift
of those birds which are known to have pleased the Lord.
Meanwhile, after the sons of Aaron, men of rank, had perished [?] for their crime,
the mighty Lord makes this known:
that since the altar has hangings let down from veils stretched before it,
and the sacred ark too is veiled,
at fixed times the priest should go back and take his place there,
bearing holy offerings, because there the holy
Lord abides, to be seen in a white cloud;
yet in such a way that he slays a calf for his own sin
and then, for the congregation, sacrifices two like goats,
with a lot cast, so that one may wander off astray,
bearing the offenses of sinners and hiding them away with itself,
but the other may be slain for the Lord at the peaceful altar,
to bring the best benefits of the heavenly gift.
A beast or bird that has died without its blood being shed
is fit for no diner's table:
the reason is that in the blood of many creatures lies the life.
And also, if a beast is killed by the blade
and they let the saffron-red stream flow from its cut throat,
it must be covered with earth, lest left unburied it bring harm.
Next the Lord teaches which unions are guilty
and which gladden hearts bound in equal harmony,
and this ordinance, arranged in set measures, explains them:
first, a mother is not fitting for the bed
in which she lies as a wife, and let the dutiful mind of her son
know no such use of her, save the devotion owed by a son,
since she has at times clung in a father's embrace.
In the same way a sister born of the same mother,
or a granddaughter, whom you behold born of your son or daughter;
let no aunt, on your father's side or your mother's, be joined
to you more closely in foul affection, nor let guilty lust stray toward a daughter-in-law,
or the wife whom your brother has; let a daughter not know the use
of a man that her mother knows, nor lie in the same bed,
mingled with one man, and so disgrace the names that join them.
If a stepmother should become pregnant with [?] offspring,
as one who is joined to her stepson... And to hold two
sisters in one embrace is a thing at odds with the law;
or the woman whom your neighbor, joined to you as one of your people,
has taken. Let no son be given to serve the mighty idol,
lest the name of the Lord be profaned in a forbidden act.
Let no male be mingled in obscene love,
nor disgrace your own sex; nor let any four-footed beast
know monstrous couplings with wife or husband:
crimes for which nations of every kind
have offended the mighty Lord, and the land shows its wrath
at all of them, and spews out the filth with which it is stained.
But when the reaper shears the ears of wheat,
or when the vintager cuts the golden grapes,
let no one gather it all, so that a part may be left for the needy,
the last that remains. Let no one tell a lie,
nor be willing to serve theft, nor to ruin a brother,
nor to swear an oath over an unjust matter.
Let it not please you to harm anyone or to keep what has been stolen;
nor withhold from the hired man the price of his work,
even for one night [?]; nor be willing to curse the deaf
as deaf, nor reproach anyone for a bodily defect.
Let a judge's decision never lean further
to the left side or the right, since the person of a poor man
and of a distinguished man ought to look the same
to those who, with the scales set before them, can discern what is right
with a teachable mind. Next, rein in a swollen heart,
lest you become hated while you look down on everyone.
Do not hate your brother either, if silent anger drives you,
but rather rebuke him and lay the matter out openly before him,
so that he may avoid his former misdeeds and reform his mind.
And when the right to do harm has been put in your hands,
lay aside your resentment willingly and soften all the anger
that, long gathered in your silent breast, has grown strong,
lest you yourself become the master and avenger of your own grievance.
And as you will desire what is pleasant and useful for your own affairs,
so ask it for your brother, lest your mind be at odds with itself.
Keep this, you men, and hold fast to the holy law.
Let the beasts yoked and harnessed to your wagons
be alike in body, and do not join a bull to a horse
as you guide the reins; nor scatter grain among the green vines
when you sow; and let no garment of yours be of mixed colors,
woven in different ways or with two kinds of thread.
If anyone loves a slave-woman bought at a separate price [?],
before the right has been granted that release confers on slaves
and freedom has been given, he is free of a deadly charge.
If a girl not joined to a husband has been of one mind with him,
if she has yielded easily to intercourse without a struggle,
God is appeased by offerings, if from the gentle flock
a votive ram is slain at the Lord's altar.
Whenever shoots are grafted onto a wild trunk,
by no means pick the fruit until three Decembers have passed,
but consecrate it to God most high; for the fifth year
will give you the right to eat it as lawful food.
Refuse to be a slave to auguries, and shun listening to omens
as if they were true; and do not make straight hair
glow red with curled locks, or clip the beard,
or mark the skin with iron, or put brands
on the body's limbs, which are never gentle to them.
Let not your daughter be sold by you to smooth-talking adulterers
or handed over to a shameful bed; and avoid the men
who heal by incantations; and summon a fitting penalty [?].
If a young man has not risen for an old one, and if
a boy has not risen for any bearded man, since one greater in age
asks the respect that is paid to a father's years...
Let the measure of your bushel never be short,
nor keep a balance that cheats by half an ounce.
The just God requires justice in every act.
And those who seek answers from ventriloquists, reject.
Let no one, for the sake of the dead, be eager to shave his beard
or to bare his head, or to defile his fair brow,
or choose anything that would make him uglier.
A woman whom a night-roaming adulterer has possessed
is unworthy to marry a man who would take her afterward;
and she who has been sent away by the decision that brings divorce,
let her not know another's marriage chamber; and the pure priest
will in all things keep bright the shining oil
with which the crown of his consecrated head was first anointed.
Let a wife from his own people, known to him alone,
cleave to him, and let him avoid a widow or one guilty of lust,
lest his offspring be stained by a forbidden mother.
And if anyone bears any blemish in his body,
he will not be worthy to undertake the holy duties.
Pure bodies are pleasing, not smeared with foul blemishes,
such as womanly wantonness [?] has, when offerings are consecrated,
which each person has vowed at the altar according to his means.
Moreover, it is by no means lawful to join veils [?] together;
for they are filthy with stains. The ruler on high is pure.
If the daughter of a holy priest has been given
into the authority of a husband from outside, let her by no means
touch the first offerings by eating them; if, her husband dead,
she has come to live in her father's house, let her take,
without anxiety, the food her father takes, and the bread in her turn.
But if anyone, unknowing, lays his hand [?] on holy things,
for his fault let him bring a fifth part more to the altar.
Let a lamp hang before the sanctuary from the lofty ceiling,
so that through the night its oil may give a flaming light,
lest, when the day has run its course, it mingle pale shadows
in the house of the Lord and hide the holy altars.
Meanwhile two young men are stirred up with hot bile:
one was a Hebrew, the other born of Egypt.
And while, seething, they hurled insults at one another,
the worthless Jew did not fear to blacken with his complaint
the boundless name of the Lord, carried away by anger.
For this crime he was dragged out beyond the rampart of the camp
and set in the middle of the plain, and at the command
of the Lord on high he fell beneath a shower of stones.
God goes through the holy laws and sets them all out.
Whenever a needy man wishes to take another's money
by leaving a pledge, if he has made over his land to the man
whose help he seeks, let him promptly repay what was lent him
once his hand has grown rich, and let him take back
what had been transferred before; if all his life long
he has remained needy, he becomes free in that year
in which rest and sweet relief are granted to all.
But if by chance someone sells a house in the middle of the city,
let him repay within a year the money entrusted to him,
lest, once the time has passed, he lose the property.
Yet money must be given into the hands of those who ask for it
in such a way that interest does not afterward exact a tangled little profit.
Whoever is poor and cannot bear the meager needs of life
and endure hard days, and thinks it better
to submit himself to a master, putting his freedom aside,
let him not bear the yoke as one born of a slave-woman,
but as one taken on to work for a fixed wage,
until, when the time has run out, he returns free,
at the time when rest is granted to all things together.
And if he is sold away as if under a master's command,
let his next of kin redeem him, or, if he is not at hand,
let any fellow tribesman, when bidden, carry out the transaction
for his brother and lift the slave's yoke from the man.
For if he has been sold for lawful money,
he will serve until the time comes in the longed-for year
in which all together take back the rights they had given up.
Or, if the total of the years was small, let him make it up
by his own labor, which he has rendered with the work of his hands.
So let him go off wherever he wishes, and take back with him
his children, free and secure, together with his wife.
The one who stores up such commands in a sincere heart
will have tranquil peace, which no wars with their uproar
can disturb; and rest granted through long years
will fill the granaries with fruit of every kind.
Even if a fierce enemy draws his weapons,
he will be driven back by a small fighting band and will depart,
however vast the battle lines he leads to war.
But the one who shuns the lofty commands of God
will be driven by the terror of death, as if an enemy were hurling the sword,
and in headlong flight will hide, trembling, in the city.
Then at last famine, with pale diseases, will
beset him, and though he is full he will think his mouth
is fasting, and he will always be afraid, as fear keeps returning.
And if he pleases to go out through the double gates
wherever his feelings lead him, the dismal wilderness will confound him
as he goes through fields deserted on every side,
and he will fear still more grievously the plundering wolves and the beasts
that roam the countryside, fearsome with tooth or claw;
and though the spring crop springs up from the earth's rich soil,
it will bring forth no tender ears on its stalks.
Then a father will crave his children's limbs as something sweet to bite,
and a mother, from hunger, will send down into her belly
what she once fruitfully bore. Then the victor, exulting,
will put chains on the captives, and flashing flames
will lift their ruddy locks over the great houses,
as the cities are turned to ashes, cities that, given over to foul deeds,
strong walls once surrounded as a defense.
Inscriptions will fail, the emblems of varied [?] praises;
and what was once beautiful will be torn down and perish,
so that God, ever to be revered on high, may be loved,
he whom idols cannot reach with their false worship.
Next, what valuation in drachmas should hold for vows,
whether a woman or a man has been given to the altar,
God's written ordinance set out: whether one older in age,
or a boy or a girl whose years are not yet mature,
or a house or an estate, or whatever is dedicated in the mind,
when the mind, untroubled, gladly entrusts itself to God most high,
or when it is driven, shaken by anxious dangers;
so that error might not become entangled in these matters [?],
part remains set out in detail, part is entrusted to the priest,
so that his judgment also assesses the tithes of the produce.
If someone wished to keep back a beast, a field, or a house,
it was within the giver's right: then let him pay at the altar
the surcharge that the agreed coinage adds to the price.
NUMBERS.
Meanwhile the year had turned in its accustomed round,
running back along its own tracks as the months unrolled,
since the young nation chosen by God had left the shores
of the Nile and had at last departed from the sands of Egypt,
when God, shining, spoke from his star-studded throne
and commanded the prophet to bring sure orders to the leaders of the tribes
and then to number the whole people,
setting aside the boys and those whom greater age
now shows to be exempt from the burden of anxious war,
so that he might learn the total from twenty years upward.
Eagerly they go over their troops, the count running through them all,
each his own, and quickly they report the names they have inspected,
which stand recorded for the twelve tribes.
Together these made six hundred and three
thousand, if you take care to add as well five hundred
and five times ten; and then the reckoning of the houses, man by man,
showed twice six thousand chiefs.
But the Levites, for whom the care of the Lord's sacred rites
alone remains, he forbade to be added to the people's total.
Of these, seven thousand Gershonites were chosen for God,
with five hundred added as well; Kohath, separately,
makes twice four thousand, with six hundred more added close by;
but the third, called Merari in the ancestral tongue,
presented twice three thousand and two hundred.
Since different charges of the sacred things and of God's temple await these companies,
the camps keep them apart in this way.
The first skirts the sea; another stretches toward the south;
the third faces the icy breezes of the north.
But where the first flame of the coming day reddens,
the household of the illustrious prophet pitches the greatest tents.
Next he prepares to single out the boys born of the first birth
and to consecrate them to the Lord; they fill out
twice eleven thousand, if you add as well twice a hundred
and seven times ten; and in exchange for them the priests are permitted
to take a drachma and assign it to the sacred uses of the temple,
as though the divine altar released them as bought.
Forthwith, as those assigned to the service of the sacred things,
they choose from the band of Gershon, from Kohath, and from the so-called Merari
twice four thousand, with five hundred joined to them
and fifty more besides, whom he ordered separately to carry
or bring out the furnishings of the Lord's house.
So, with the camp now pitched there, they took their rest;
and it was decided that those should be shut out beyond the threshold of the gate
whose limbs the dire wasting of disease had corrupted,
lest, placed among the healthy, they should spread contagion,
while hidden dangers wander through the hot veins.
Likewise, whoever is jealous of his wife in his silent heart
and has no witness to reveal it, if a stealthy adulterer
has defiled the once-chaste marriage bed,
let him go quickly to the priest and present before him
the woman he believes has sinned against him. And let him bring white flour,
made from barley, to the sacred altar,
neither smearing it with incense nor moistening it with rich olive oil.
Then the provident priest is to take water from a spring
in an earthen vessel and tinge it with a little dust,
which he takes, bending down, from the midst of the temple's vault.
Soon he will make her bare her head and hold in both
palms the offering of the memorial rite,
and the elder will make her drink the waters that carry the curses.
If she is free of the crime,
she remains unharmed, with an easy mind and a calm face.
But if crimes lie hidden deep in her silent heart,
the woman will swell with the sudden bloating of disease,
and her shameful thigh will melt away with rotting flesh.
Moreover, she sharpens the curses of the jeering people,
as with easy laughter they reproach the sin she has committed.
Amid these laws: if anyone resolves in his mind to lead his life by a chaste rule
and longs with watchful heart to fulfil the obligation of a vow,
so that bodily indulgence may have no power in him
until the appointed end,
let him willingly deny himself the wine that is made, and refuse all
the drinks that the care of drinkers is used to turning into wine
with warm waters, whether with honey or with fruit,
when they renew clear draughts from pure springs.
Let him shun grapes and bite no grape at all,
whether it drips with the juice of wine or dries in the sun
into a raisin, shrivelled at the wrinkled edge of its split;
indeed let him avoid even the liquor of sharp vinegar,
sipping sober cups from running streams;
and let him who is enrolled under the vow wear his beard grown thick
the whole time; and let his unshorn crown
keep its flowing hair; let him have nothing to do with visiting tombs,
his fathers' graves, or a sister's pyre,
so that his holy dignity may remain intact. If by chance someone, laid
under the same roof, should loosen his limbs
in death, it will force him to be defiled as though unclean.
He, then, is to pray for pardon with gnawing cares
and shave off the hair grown long on his unkempt crown;
and when the bright day has shone forth at its seventh rising,
let him offer turtledoves, or doves white with like plumage,
so that his fault may be lightened through the priest's words
and prayer; yet let the time be forfeit
during which he had abstained before, and let him take up again
a fresh beginning, running once more toward the vows he longs to fulfil,
so that by his merits he may reach the goal he seeks.
When all this is done, and he holds his reward secure
in his possession, let him offer lambs alike in their white fleece,
yearlings that have completed the course of a year;
let one fall as the price of the reward he sought
and lighten his sin; let the other, now of spotless body,
and a ram, be laid down for the offerings of peace.
He is also to sprinkle snow-white loaves with oil,
along with whatever the solemn customs of the ancient rite require,
so that he may once again take up the cups he has gone without.
Come then: whenever you wish to sanctify the people at prayer
with your blessing, ask it of Christ in these words:
"While the right hand rests, bent down, upon the heads of men,
may the Almighty, shining, bless you from the court of heaven,
and may he be your guardian through the ages;
may God lift his shining face over all your heads
and be merciful forever;
may the Lord also raise his countenance to look upon you again
from his glorious throne, and give you peace as a mighty gift."
Meanwhile the prophet, ready in all
God's commands, adorns the Lord's first house for the united camps
and anoints it with rich olive oil;
and whatever vessels of the holy house gleam, wrought of silver or gold,
he washed in the same stream.
Then the wagons, already yoked, which the tribal leaders had given,
he divided along with the horned oxen for fair use
and gave to the Levites: two carts, each drawn by a pair of bullocks,
were handed to the first troop, the Gershonites;
but the company of Merari, with twice four oxen yoked,
received four carts for carrying the things
made for the sacred rites of God; for Kohath alone,
receiving no such gift, bore its loads upon its shoulders.
Meanwhile the leaders of the tribes, bringing devout gifts,
were assigned separate days; for the people's columns
number two thousand five hundred and twenty,
to be led by twelve men; of whom, first in order,
the tribe of Judah vowed its gift, with Nahshon as leader;
in it he gave vessels splendid with gleaming silver,
which together, counted in full, make a weight of twice a hundred
and ten, filled to the brim with snow-white fine flour
steeped beforehand, by the custom of the rites, in a stream of green olive oil;
and then a calf and a gleaming lamb
and a ram as well, joined by a white kid
that takes away sins; two bullocks of like brow
together, which serve the rites joined to peace;
five rams, and he-goats and lambs following
in like number: these make up the first gift.
After this each tribe gladly, on separate days,
gave its gifts, nowhere differing from its brothers' offering,
if the total is reckoned equally across all the vessels.
But in the dishes blazing with engraved gold
there are a hundred and twenty pounds by weight.
When the prophet had dedicated these splendid instruments of worship,
he heard the Lord speaking in the holy house,
as he shines in ruddy splendor above the lofty roof
and gives the teachings of the law between the cherubim.
Likewise the lamps set in another part
poured out twice six flames, which a bright row
made to glow each in its place, while the golden lampstand
spreads its arms and holds up its separate lights.
Meanwhile the band of Levites that handles the offerings
is enlisted from twice twenty and five years,
and whoever has completed the Lord's service for five times ten
years is to be free from the duty of serving,
and a young man is to take the old man's place and attend.
Their bodies are made pure with the light sprinkling
of river or spring, and a blade of sharp iron
trims their hair, if its full growth has become unclean.
Then their garments are washed with zeal and care,
lest any contagion should ever stain the hidden body.
Meanwhile men from among the people, pursued by grim anxiety
over their guilt, confessing it with conscience as witness,
entreat the leader whether they might celebrate the sacred Passover
on the customary day; he holds them off for a little while
and, relying on the Lord, prays for his commands,
and reports the order: that those stained with guilt may rightly
keep the solemn day and renew the worship
which the joyful night calls to mind when the year has run its course.
But if a man free of guilt neglects the people's feast,
and no business of travel keeps him far from the temple,
he incurs a capital charge: this law is the same for all.
After the devout prophet had completed all the duties
befitting God's temple, he soon set the columns in motion
and fills the fearsome trumpets with mighty blasts,
which he had earlier made of silver at the Lord's command,
a thin sheet being bent into a smooth round tube.
And he gives a short signal with the windy blast,
with the ranks drawn up, so that at the first call the trumpet
may gather the expectant lines at the holy oracle.
At this the first division of the camp sets out in haste, the one that
stretches toward the dawn and the first light of the sun.
And when the trumpet sounds again, let the column go forth
that faces the light south wind from the opposite quarter.
Then the third blare of the horn gives the signal to those legions
that hold the camps bordering the sea,
and after them the young men facing the north pack up their baggage.
But when the Levites, chosen for the divine duties,
hold back the columns, the sons of the prophet Aaron,
already high priests then, had the fitting task of blowing the trumpets
and setting in motion all that was assigned to God.
Advancing first into the long wilderness, they come
to the place called Paran to make camp; here the prophet, in friendly words,
entreats the young Hobab, son of Reuel,
a native of the land of Midian,
to walk along with them and come to the promised kingdom,
where sweet honey would flow abundantly from full
combs, along with a great river of snowy milk.
But he, reluctant and lingering a while in two minds,
prefers to turn his course back to his ancestral home,
in no way won over by the words of his kinsman's pleading:
"Why," he said, "do you go off another way? Turn your mind here,
to where the kingdom of the Lord calls us, a kingdom ever rich,
ever honored, that totters under no ruin.
And yet what cause, so harsh and unknown to us,
moves you to seek again your homeland and your father's people,
whom, far away and long ago, your mind seeking better things,
you left behind, and the desert parts you from them with its intervening sands?
In all that time no thought ever stirred your feelings.
There might have been a reason then, since you would more justly
have longed for these things when there were no drinks
running in wandering streams, and they burned beneath the hot star of the sun,
and when an uncertain road and an unsure hope of the future
shook us in our ignorance. But now, at the very end
of a modest labor, when the happy kingdom of God
shows itself and draws near, you waver in your mind like this,
as though I were urging on you something worse than I wish in my heart.
No: rather, young man, give yourself back to your dear kinsman,
and finish the journey you have begun and complete the task you took on,
so that, as soon as the Lord has settled us all in the homes we long for,
you may take hold of better things
and, placed among the leaders, be greater in your deeds."
From there they depart and leave the mountain of God behind them;
and the camp followed the ark, guardian of the heavenly teaching,
after the third morning star had risen
into the high heaven and night was left behind,
so that, with the Lord's holy things always going ahead, there might be
due rest for the people as they traveled under their heavy load.
Then first the prophet, as he diligently gives the signal
to the leading columns, speaks these words in supplication:
"Rise up on high, O God, and swiftly scatter the enemy's
thousands; let those who prepare to make war
against your camp flee, O God, and those who with violent heart
hate you, highest Creator; for you have power by your everlasting word
to lay low strongholds, however firm."
As he speaks, a bright cloud covers him, and with its veil it shades
the crowded column and the immense ranks.
But the people, unruly, as they rolled savage mutterings about,
hurled the insults of a raging tongue even against the Lord.
Because of this a lofty tongue of fire glides down
from the heaven above and devours people and camp
up to a certain point; but the flames flashing grimly
over that harvest of punishment were quenched by a prayer pleasing to the holy
ears, which dissolved them into white ash,
while the devout prophet toils with bowed neck
and implores the boundless God over so great a crime,
and says again that he is unwilling to bear alone
the people's constant uproar, with a heart worn out in vain.
But the Lord God gives the prophet his accustomed comfort
and calls for elders from the kindred host,
seventy together, whose united judgment
and number might easily break the anger of the quarrelsome,
since so many harmonious hearts of prophets alike
would bring the divine oracles as though with one mind:
yet these, when they had uttered like words to all,
withdraw and speak again in the manner they used before.
Likewise two young men, staying in another part of the camp,
speak most certain things with divinely inspired minds
and prophesy in prophetic speech just the same,
Medad and Eldad; and when a messenger brought this to the ears
of the leaders, Joshua presses urgently
that Moses restrain and rebuke them, as though they told the truth in an unlawful utterance;
but the prophet at once, in gentle
words, reproves him and teaches that to check out of envy a mind sent from heaven
is not the part of faith.
Next they come to Hazeroth and, with a vast rampart,
pitch camp, as though they feared war by night.
Here the devout prophet's sister and brother swell with pride
and seethe with envy: "Why should the wife joined to the prophet
be an Ethiopian, and why should one man alone claim
the honor common to the siblings? For they too
received the records of the highest God and his glorious commands."
The prophet, attentive and gentler than all, hears these words
in silence, with an innocent mind, and renounces anger.
Yet the Lord, from his lofty throne, does not allow
these untamed passions to go further, but rebukes them
as they stand before him and, enclosed in a clear cloud, declares:
"Whoever among you, of your kindred people, is a prophet
will see true dreams, his mind rather keeping watch,
in the middle of the night, when men's lulled senses
relax and God gives the joys of his holy word;
while I speak and fit my discourse to suitable words,
how could he behold me, and see my face and eyes
close beside him, which no living man can make out?
But this is not the way when my true word
is given to the prophet who is faithful in all my house,
while he binds his heart to my lawful rites.
He is able to stand before my face
and look upon God and behold him with clear sight.
Nothing is ambiguous, and no riddles
are woven into my words: I show myself with open face.
He, then, was able to behold the glory of the reigning Lord
and perceive the light invisible to mortals;
and could he not set gentle peace amid your passions
and do away with your bitter whispers?"
Hardly had he said this when, the cloud suddenly withdrawn,
the Lord's anger came and, seizing the trembling Miriam,
struck her and covered her whole body with leprosy.
Seeing this example, Aaron, terrified, began:
"Spare us, I pray, Lord, and turn away your harmful anger,
and pass over my sin and our sister's.
We did it unknowing: what strikes our limbs
and lashes our senses, let not death be sent to follow it,
the avenger of wickedness; guard us and take thought for us!"
Without delay the prophet gives his heart to his brother's prayers,
asking the Lord with suppliant vows for remedies
against the deadly plague, which, spread through all the limbs,
was tormenting his sister's flesh with its cruel bite,
as he cries out: "Such a penalty exceeds the guilt!
O God, take away our fear and heal the disease."
At once it is granted; but the woman, thrust out of the camp,
lives in exile and, having endured the wasting for seven days,
recovers her limbs unharmed, with a joyful face,
and from then on is held in the people's accustomed honor.
Then the Jewish host, pressing on toward the promised rewards,
moves its standards and next pitches camp in the fields of Paran
and builds its walls with a secure rampart.
There Moses, urged by the heavenly voice, sent
twelve young men, who, as we said earlier, were
the leaders of the tribes, to explore the land and cities of Canaan
quickly and report their findings to their comrades.
They set out and make for the forest called Hamath,
and, having crossed the wastes of the desert, they survey Hebron,
which the fierce peoples of Sheshai and Talmai held.
When they came to the valley, which was then planted with figs
and sweet apples, and with those called stony apples,
or rather pomegranates, and was green with the joyful vine,
they bring fruit from it to serve as a token of their good faith,
and also from other fruits that the rich field had produced.
They cut a huge cluster from the pliant vine shoot
and carry it back, straining under a pole laid crosswise;
and, after forty days spent in anxious care
had at last gone by, they report what they had seen,
adding terror as they tell of walls raised
to a vast height, and of huge peoples lifting
their heads to heaven, as when many an oak
with ancient trunk reaches up to the starry sky.
At this the people's spirit is broken; stricken with bitter feeling,
they groan in sorrow and wet their faces with a flood of tears,
saying: "O men ever worthy to be
spoken of with praise, whom no sight of evil so great
ever terrified, and whom, when life was done, their own familiar land laid to rest!
Them no grim soil scorched with burning sands,
nor long-endured thirst, nor the crumbs of manna,
sweet indeed, but soaked in gall, since it does not nourish the limbs,
afflicted with a heavier hunger: to it only the quail
is added, and it wastes the body with meager food.
But when we lived long ago in the land of Egypt,
no such dismal food tormented us, when sweeping up fish
was sport, and we set the whole Nile on our tables,
or stripped the windy sea of its varied throng of swimmers
and stretched our bellies with joyful feasting.
We were rich in flocks; we in all the fertile gardens
plucked unbought melons and cucumbers, wont to swell the belly,
biting into them with greedy mouthfuls.
There garlic and onions, there the sliced leek
fed us and, when we were full, refreshed us with drowsy sleep.
Come then, put an end at last to these hardships.
Turn the standards quickly, bring these troops back to the Nile,
and appoint a distinguished leader from our own kindred people,
one who will put the concerns of our safety ahead
of his own or of our timid chief's, who, following the words
of a fearsome God, as he says, has left us wretches
stranded in desert fields and set us against an enormous enemy,
so that, helpless, we suffer things worse than the fear of death,
while a beloved wife is slain, while a virgin daughter
is led away and serves as a captive to an arrogant tyrant."
With these words they plan worse things; for the frenzied mob
seizes stones and, rising with their whole bodies, poise them to throw.
But while they tremble in advance, while they steel themselves for the crime,
the leaders tear their garments and, rushing forward,
fell prostrate to the ground in fear and implore them all
not to hurl foolish reproaches, in such uncertain circumstances,
against heaven and the throne of God, nor to think
God's promises too hard for his decrees; then Caleb,
with faithful Joshua beside him, prostrate, pleads thus:
"At the time when it was decided to explore the distant lands
and to report to you on the enemy's homes and what we had seen,
the first leaders out of all the tribes were chosen,
men of known good faith, who could by no means
speak at variance or deceive their fellow citizens with lying talk.
And now, if the same respect for our name
still stands, and we utter no empty words,
believe what we have found out; for what confidence could lead us
to deceive our fellow citizens, when we follow the Lord's answers
together with you and go through everything in the same way?
What some think fearsome, while white pallor sits
on their faces and their senses waver, seized by dread,
is in fact empty, because God's mighty commands strengthen us
and do not allow us to be conquered or driven back, even if giants
lift their necks on high and oppose us with troops of dense soldiery.
The land lies open to us, which, after these ruinous fields,
we rejoice to have explored and found blessed, a land that flows
rich with a great stream of milk and with a flood of sweet honey.
Only do not part your hearts from the holy God,
nor hold back your hands in fear; for those who follow
God's standards, never vanquished, victory serves and enriches."
When this was said, at once from its high seat
the venerable majesty of God came and flooded the people, the elders,
and the assembly with wondrous glory.
Then the Lord announces his grim anger
and a final destruction, by which the vast nation would perish
amid desolate wilds and a land left behind,
except for only two, spared the dreadful plague,
whom a shared strength had made firm in like conduct,
seeing that nothing could contend against God's commands.
However much the prophet, trying to avert this by prayer,
entreated with gentle pleading amid fearful words,
lest the Canaanites, uttering foolish words in vain,
should loudly proclaim that the people had been helped by no power,
the people that had been desired and chosen for the Lord's rewards,
he still could not bend the dreadful sentence,
which flies forth under fixed law; for no one
was allowed to see the fields granted to faith alone;
for within forty years the warrior people
perished and left the lofty kingdom to their sons.
Meanwhile, armed and spurred on by foolish designs,
a legion rises up and on the topmost summit of the hill
sets its standards and charges headlong against the enemy in its way.
And because the Lord did not strike fear into the warlike squadrons,
it is defeated and, its soldiers routed, turns its back.
Foreseeing this, the prophet stayed in the camp,
keeping the sacred ark within the protecting ramparts.
Meanwhile a certain man among that people, on the festal day,
while gathering sticks, a scorner of the eternal law,
is seized and, by God's holy command, put to death
with hurled stones, so that the forbidden deed might not spread.
Moreover, so that a watchful mind might often remind men
to turn their thoughts to the Lord's eternal admonitions,
a hyacinth-blue fringe with a knotted cord is attached for everyone
and marks their garments with a recognized border.
Next a source of evil arises from a forbidden act:
for Korah of the Levite tribe, and with him Dathan
and Abiram, believing in their mad presumption that all were permitted
to offer burnt offerings with holy incense to the Thunderer,
assailed the prophet with arrogant complaint.
Nor was their death long delayed; for, its hinges bursting,
the earth opened and sent them all down to infernal Tartarus;
with them, perishing together, two hundred
and five times ten, who were bringing God offerings he had not commanded,
behold their own deaths, the whole crowd gathered together,
and their flocks and whatever had belonged to the guilty;
and as though one death were coming on all alike,
the people scatter, trembling with fear, and try in vain
to flee the fire from above and hide themselves.
Moreover, when the next day came round, they did not fear
to seethe with uproar, and they are at once crushed by a great slaughter,
and by the same death there fall twice seven thousand
and six hundred men; and had not the prophet,
seeing such peril, entreated the Lord with winning prayers,
a greater punishment would have avenged that unspeakable guilt.
But when calm returned after the fearful turmoil,
the golden pans with which the young men, under an ill-omened sky,
had earlier offered God unaccustomed offerings,
Moses breaks up and skillfully beats them all into thin plates,
dedicates them, and puts them on the altar of the Lord;
for whatever is brought to the Lord
and set before God's lofty face becomes holy.
Likewise, so that a distinction might be made between the high priests
and the tribes, he asks for a rod from every
chief, until the total had reached twelve;
then the prophet sets apart one in the name of Aaron,
lays them out, and leaves them in the midst of the Lord's dwelling.
And when the stars had glimmered out before the returning sun,
a thing never known before, as the people gathered in wonder,
is seen, and it revealed the Lord's great honor.
For the rod, smooth before and cut off with iron,
the rod of the chief Aaron, with no nourishment from the earth,
blossomed and put forth nuts from a stock already dry.
To the records and commands of the sacred law it is added
that a heifer, whose hide will gleam tawny over all her limbs,
be slain before the Lord's doors, and her body burned
with fire, and that the ash born of the burnt flesh
should purify bodies defiled by a foul touch,
when it is sprinkled over men's limbs, joined with a sprig
of hyssop, so that with a light stroke it may scatter drops
of river water and wash the infected with clean water.
For whoever touches dead bodies with his hand,
or under whose roof a lifeless corpse lies,
is stained with defilement and darkens the eternal temple.
Indeed, even vessels with open mouths
are all defiled; and then whoever touches a bloody wound,
or the bones of men, or the tomb of one buried,
can make himself pure again on the third day or the seventh,
if, having prayed to the Lord in the silence of his heart,
he brings gifts, cleansed by the water of the healing branch.
Meanwhile, as the Jewish host marched through the desert fields,
it came to Kadesh, and the chief buried his sister
after her death; and great anger flared up,
because the region, parched with thirst, yielded no streams
from cool springs, and because all mouths were dry
and bodies burned under the scorching sun.
Considering this, the Lord commands the prophet to bring out his rod
and touch the rock with a double stroke.
Yet Moses, striking it with a doubting heart,
rebukes the people, saying: "Alas, you who are fierce of mind
and hard of feeling, can any rocks run wet
with streams and send forth living springs?"
As he says this in agitation, he deals slow blows with the rod.
[?] rivers burst from the stones.
Yet the Almighty rebukes the hearts of the hesitating prophets,
reproaching them: "Since your judgment
lay in a wavering heart, and your mind, not firm,
does not see that I can do all things, and pays little honor
to the command of the Lord on high, which you ought to have trusted before
the ranks of Judah, declaring your faith
that there is nothing God cannot do: for this reason it is not permitted you
to lead the people to the homes long promised and the fruitful land,
nor to take up these great gifts."
Meanwhile the people reached the fields of Edom,
through which Moses, eager to lead his peaceful ranks,
asked passage in calm words of the king,
a savage man, swollen with pride in his strength, and preparing for battle.
Avoiding him, however, the people reached Mount Hor,
on which, after very many years of a life run to its end,
Aaron is buried, and he left his well-known insignia
of festal priesthood to the priest whom Moses set at the lofty altars,
Eleazar, the eldest of all, as mighty God
had commanded, choosing him as minister for the altars that pleased him.
There the Canaanites, trusting in their manifold youth,
struck boundless terror, with a heavy defeat,
into the Jews, as they turned their bare backs in flight across the fields.
But still they take heart, and with the Lord's favor
they lay low the enemy's wedges, set fire
to their strong cities, and triumph with boundless glory.
But though advantages flowed and things went as they wished,
there was still no lack of sidelong grumbling and murmurs
hurled at the holy prophet, as each with fierce
voice laments Egypt, rich in its abundant endowment of land,
now left behind their backs, and the Nile, fruitful
in crops, and always [?] with a carefree tiller.
Almighty God, punishing this with evenly balanced judgment,
brought forth ranks of vipers from a poisonous source,
which laid many men low, while, slight though the wounds were,
they swelled their bodies with deadly venom.
But the people, groaning mournfully, praying prostrate
at the prophet's feet and telling of the common deaths,
with acknowledgment of their wrongdoing stored in every heart,
receive the longed-for cure, as the Lord saves them.
For the upright leader, bidden to fashion a swelling serpent
of yellow bronze, hung it from a tall pole,
so that whomever the horned snake had pierced with its roaming fang
might shed death by turning toward the hanging serpent.
From here the people came to Oboth; then to the fields
of Achina; then to Zered; soon it crosses over to Adar.
Now they are in a green plain, where the Amorite, tiller of a pleasant home,
dwells and feeds on rich fields.
There is a well there, clear with glassy water,
beside which the Lord, speaking with holy word,
ordered Moses to gather the people in a dense throng,
that they might draw the flowing waters and the gleaming wave.
Then in divine song all of them had
one harmonious voice, as they sang praises to the Lord in this hymn:
"The boundless Lord has sent us streams
and taken away all the people's burning heat,
for the well lies open, full to its depths,
and gushes richly with cool streams:
the well that mighty kings once made
when they ruled mighty nations with the reins
and pressed down fearful subjects with their scepters,
that it might lie open for their own use,
all outsiders kept far away.
This, given by the Lord for our salvation,
has filled the living with refreshing waters."
When they had sung these songs to the King of the stars,
they break camp and leave various places behind them.
Led to King Sihon when their course was run,
they rout in mighty combat the ranks opposed to them,
which he, mocking the words of the harmless prophet,
had marshaled, vainly vaunting himself in the empty praise
of the Amorite race; and that race, subdued in harsh war,
lay prostrate, though long fenced about by mighty cities.
Jazer too, laid waste in a similar war,
crushed, took up the yoke and surrendered many towns,
begging for the leisure of longed-for peace.
When rumor reported these things to the anxious Balak,
who ruled the peoples and cities of the Moabites,
he is shaken by a heavier fear, and he courts the prophet Balaam
with honorable entreaties, that by his words he might hinder
the people achieving such deeds and wholly check the course
of the warriors; since whatever he prays for, prostrate,
the Almighty hears, and brings every grim thing to pass.
He refuses, saying it is not right for him to utter curses
against a people marching always with the Lord as its leader
to its own home and kingdom, and that it seemed far
more just to pray for things fitting their merits,
since the Lord, appearing in the night,
forbids the old man to give Balak the answers he sought.
But after the messenger, dismissed, had brought back such words,
and his care still gripped the king, he anxiously seeks out
chosen princes and once more to the prophet's door
sends envoys asking for what had already been asked
in vain, since the words of God fight against it.
Yet the prophet set out, mounted his she-ass,
and matched his pace to those who went before.
Behold, in the middle of the road the Lord's angel presents
a drawn blade thrust forward, and, facing her and pressing on,
terrifies the beast, who, startled, with a swift leap
swerves aside, flees, and wanders over the field.
While the prophet turns her about as she scorns the reins in headlong fear,
and struggles with tightened reins,
and digs in with his heels and lashes her with a sharp rod,
there among the leafy vines, its coping fallen,
a half-ruined wall set in the way of the hesitating ass
blocked her advance; she pushed his foot against the stones,
crushed the old man's foot, and stung him with sharp pain.
Then the messenger swiftly stands against them in another place,
on a very narrow way, where a slender path led,
leaving no way around on any side.
The beast saw him gleaming with drawn sword
and, in great terror, fell down; ordered to rise,
she is beaten by her rider, who curbs her with many a welt.
When she had suffered deeply, she suddenly spoke out,
as God loosed her speech into unaccustomed words:
"What have I done, what have I deserved of you, that with many blows
you drive me so hard as I stumble? Did I ever refuse you the back
you are used to? Did I ever in fear shy from my burden,
or throw you headlong, so that you slipped headfirst over my sloping shoulder
and went rolling, flung down over my neck?"
As she spoke these words, the priest, provoked,
answers harshly again and again and seethes with great anger;
and while he rages furiously, the angel soon shines out
plainly and addresses the prophet with holy voice:
"You are beating an innocent beast, and now for the third time,
who flees from me headlong and lies dashed against the ground
for this reason: because your path is not
pleasing to God most high, and now you stray far with wandering steps.
And had the beast's course not carried you away
as she went off in another direction, this hand would have laid you low
with a hard wound of iron and driven home the cruel sword,
so that, with you struck down, she would have been kept safe by me."
At this the prophet leaps down and, bowing, worships the holy one,
and grieving for his offense, begs to return and to live.
Dismissed, he hastens on and fulfils the duties he had undertaken,
intending to speak the words the Lord would dictate to him.
And now, completing the road, he reaches the city of Moab
and sees the king, conspicuous amid a dense throng of soldiers;
he observes him asking for help with fearful voice,
and he prays to the Lord at seven altars;
at once he sacrifices fine bullocks and choice sheep,
entrusts all the offerings to the king,
and in the silent night receives God's judgment.
Then, unfolding it, he terrified the king with these words:
"I was summoned from my native mountains by Moab's prince,
from where the coming day and the clear light grow red,
where the land lies enclosed by the twin streams
of Tigris and Euphrates, so that, savage with bitter words,
I might wish unworthy things upon men whom the Holy One on high,
the Almighty, protects, and to whom he assigns a rich land.
These, then, it is right for me soon to view from the hill far off,
and even now to make out the longed-for faces
of a blessed people, whom alone the great gifts of God
attend, and which, set apart from the nations and sharing nothing with them,
receives from a gracious deity the homes it longs for.
Who, then, has searched out the glorious offspring of ancient Jacob,
or been able to count the people through?
Rather may my life end among them, leaving
its bodily dwelling, and rest joined with the just,
and may my offspring live with such a stock!"
When he had said these things, Balak, his senses numbed,
collapsed, and he rebukes the prophet for speaking words contrary and discordant,
and bids him climb a lofty hill,
to see a small part of the people across the fields below.
Again the prophet adds these words in measured speech:
"Let my words at once sink into your ears,
ruler of the people of Moab, and come as a witness!
God is unlike men; when he has spoken the truth
he does not make his words void or utter any threat in vain.
He who sits enthroned on high bids me pray for great gifts,
as I do; and I will hallow God's people with my prayers,
a people from whom all pain and toil of labor will flee,
for God is its partner and ally, who drives back
all hardships, granting the gifts of enriching peace.
Behold its prince from the holy star, the ruler
of heaven and earth: for he is worthy of your honor,
he who led out the people, long groaning with bowed neck,
from the kingdom of bitter Pharaoh;
a standard-bearer second to none in the praise of virtue,
he cherishes a single kingdom and trusts in no augur.
He chants no spells and grasps at nothing vain.
At an appointed time it will receive, secure, the happy words
of God on high, and its perfect strength
shall become Jebusite by the might of the Lord Most High.
This people springs forth as when, through lonely fields,
a lion strides proudly with his maned neck,
and does not seek again the lair of his accustomed forest
until, grim, drenched in thick gore and laden with prey,
he has terrified the green mountains with his threatening roar."
This too the king rejected, stung with great anger,
and asked the prophet for a third utterance on a different hill;
from its summit, when he saw the people encamped
throughout their camps, he brought forth words from a teachable heart:
"Lofty and great are the houses that the seed of Jacob
possesses, and they raise their roofs in matching dwellings,
like the cedar and the gleaming wood that tosses
the glory of its leaves and pipes whispers through plaintive branches,
or that flourishes gladly, planted along the banks of a river.
These the Lord has built and raised up to the lofty stars.
From their seed one day will be born one who brings laws
to all peoples, glorious in an everlasting kingdom,
whom God in mercy summons out of Pharaoh's Egypt,
conspicuous, matched by none, without a peer.
He shall rule the rebellious nations everywhere,
hurling many darts with deadly right hand.
Then, when he lies couched like a lion,
he stretches himself out openly once sleep has slipped away; then he shakes off
his slumber and at once returns to waking deeds.
And who will make him halt again with a touch?
Whoever praises your renown in holy utterance
shall be blessed; but whoever speaks against you
brings curses on himself from his windy mouth.
These are the things of which the Lord commands you to be warned by my voice,
a word which no one may lawfully break,
nor any man change, nor add anything besides,
however great a talent of silver you might give me to carry away,
and your riches, and a weight of boundless gold:
gifts avail nothing; what is spoken stands fixed."
This done, he makes for his own home and leaves the king
astounded and groaning bitterly at the harsh words.
But meanwhile the Jewish host, flushed with success in war,
runs riot and thinks holy the altars it had conquered,
and celebrates heathen idols in unlawful worship,
idols once devoted to Baal [?] and to mute Peor.
Hence God's immense wrath soon rises up, and then
he orders the chiefs to be led out to the open plain
and, turned toward it, bids them face the light of the returning sun,
and so expiate, attentively, the guilty deed.
The prophet hastens to do this and bares the sword,
pursuing innocent and guilty alike with roving blade.
Meanwhile a certain man, exposing a kinsman's disgrace,
that he had contracted an unlawful marriage with the Midianite people,
brings before all and before the prophet
Zimri and Cozbi, guilty of the same offense.
Phinehas, swiftly seizing a spear, strikes them,
and by just atonement stays the immense plague,
which had carried off to death twenty thousand men
and three thousand more, as the Lord's weapon ran through them all.
For this deed the prophet receives the sacred altars
and took up the lofty honor of the Lord.
Meanwhile the youth sprung from a new generation
is enrolled, and then, counted up, is recorded by number:
youth that, flourishing in its first bloom, was already clothing
its cheeks with soft down, glad in its twenty years.
Its total then came to six hundred thousand
and twice eight, with three hundred more added besides.
This generation earned blessed homes by the Lord's gift;
straightway the Almighty bids the prophet turn his standards
against the hostile foe and press on with the war begun.
Against them they march with twelve thousand men,
to which every tribe had sent its share, each counting out
a thousand warriors from its own troops.
Phinehas leads them as commander, carrying the holy vessels
and the terrifying trumpets into battle, as was the custom;
and eagerly, with his chosen soldiers, he at once cuts down
the Moabite ranks and kills all the kings,
pressing on the backs of the routed; he slays the prophet Balaam
and brings back spoil from the conquered nation.
But because after the war he was dragging ranks of women
in a captive column, he is admonished by the chief's orders
to spare the life of the virgins alone, as they deserved,
and to cleanse the men's bodily stains in running water.
He likewise divides the spoil among the whole people,
and gave the Levites a share of the gift, as was their due,
for pious care kept them always in the Lord's temple.
First-fruits too are rendered to the eternal God
from all the things brought back from the conquered nation.
This done, the tribe of Reuben and half of Manasseh
and Gad ask for the fertile settlements of Gilead,
a land easy for flocks: for, rich with abundant grass,
it lay green and grassy beside the river Jordan.
Though the leader refused them in fearless speech,
thinking they were changing their minds for fear of the battles to come,
he nevertheless grants and allows it, provided that with all their soldiery
they bear arms and help their allied cohorts in the wars.
Until now harassed by the shapeless sands of the desert,
the people had moved their arms forward to the river Jordan,
which, as it wanders smoothly among green glades,
leaves glorious Jericho behind with its gliding stream
and flows on, and then mingles with the open sea.
There the holy prophet, seeing death
approaching him and the end of his days at hand,
the term written down for his time in the world, while he stays there
gathers the people, assembled in companies and crowded ranks,
and enriches them with this gift of words:
"If you wish to lay the hostile nations utterly low
and to keep calm peace for the ages to come,
fear God, and store him in your hearts with all your mind,
so that he may always be joined to you in unbroken love;
he it was who, when you long mourned with your necks bowed down,
lifted you from your chains and freed you from the prison of Egypt;
who set clouds between you and the enemy
as he pressed on you in your fear and bore down on your exposed backs;
who gave you, in safety, a cloud as a sign by day,
and wiped away the pitch-black night with clear light,
so that, set on an unknown path across the earth,
you might be upheld by God's elements, changing themselves
as the dark night comes and as the stars shine in their course.
He too laid bare the ocean, which is wont to surge forward with ebb and flow
and is ever restless, wherever the untraceable blasts of the wind
carry it, and left dry sand,
the land sweating blood-red, the reddening shores,
so that he might lead you, hemmed in by a double peril of troubles,
with walls raised up on either arm,
the sea divided, as it hung in a cloven wave.
You saw what care the high divinity then showed
around you, while the enemy, flying behind, urged himself on
and sought a like road through the windswept sea.
But he, unable to cross the swelling waves,
fell, and is rolled among the wet sands.
You, whom soft Egypt had made rich with spoils,
conquered the shapeless lands of the desert, where no houses may stand,
under God's protection, while he at once sent streams [?] from the rocks
and sent down manna from the shining heavens.
And quails, falling by night in great clouds,
filled the plains that lay round your pitched camp.
Long use did not wear through the coverings of your feet,
nor did your clothes perish from mould or wear on the body;
weary age destroys nothing that is about you.
Hostile battle lines give way and cities lie open:
the Lord is your standard-bearer, sending swift terror
and weakening all who stand in your way.
And now, since we have come to the waters of the sea-like Jordan
and the land already lies close and joins us,
the law written out by God on high, I call the stars to witness
and whatever shines in the lofty hall of the Lord,
that you be willing to keep the heavenly law which the Thunderer's right hand wrote
with all your senses and all your heart.
It commands nothing hard or harsh. All is just,
gentle, pleasant, and suited to long life,
since it commands that whatever no one likes
done to himself, he should take care to inflict on no one.
Love the sabbaths. With a sincere heart cherish
those whom one law holds and one Lord presents.
He will want to do nothing forbidden who loves all
as equals under the law of birth. Let the Passover each year
be kept in power with its night of vigil, and for seven days
let it bring unhurried leisure, bound to no care.
Let father and mother be dear and always revered.
Beware of forbidden marriage with a foreign nation.
Scatter the idols and turn away the baleful divinity [?]
which savage nations brought forth, as they worship dead
gods and set up offerings in shady groves.
Moreover, whenever the hoarse trumpet gives the bloody signal
and the war-calls lead out the bronze-clad squadrons,
dedicate the houses you have built and your joyful vineyards,
and let a man join a lawful marriage with the customary festivities:
for wars at hand always make men's fortunes
uncertain, and no one can grant himself the span of his life.
Keep the unwarlike at home: a wounded spirit often
unsettles brave men. And at every time of war
spare the suppliant and subdue the proud.
Take care, men, not to cut down a wood rich
in noble fruits; cut down the barren groves
in time of war. If by chance the body of a slain man
is found lying uncovered, it shall be the Levites' duty
to cut off a heifer's foot, lest God be the mighty avenger
of the innocent. If you wish to take a captive woman to your bed,
the law fully permits you to keep her under your roof:
to shear her long-haired head and cut her nails,
and to grant thirty days to her tears as she mourns
her dead and slain elders, from whom she was born,
and only then to bind her to yourself in lawful marriage.
And if, once her chastity is lost, the captive displeases you,
let her lay down the yoke of slavery and leave her master.
If by chance one man has married two wives
and does not keep his union with each with equal care,
the children of the scorned wife shall by right hold a double share [?]
of all the goods that the parent's care has produced.
Bury condemned men, and lay all the slain
in tombs: for the earth is denied to no one.
Let a woman by no means put on a man's garments,
nor men those of women; forbidden dress brings guilt.
If anyone wishes to take the unfledged young of birds,
let him not carry off the mother with her brood. Whoever builds a roof,
let him take care that the workman does not tumble from on high.
Let the vineyard not bear heavy clusters, made fruitful twice,
nor let your harvest be reaped with double ears of grain.
Shun Gentile men; and whatever is alien
in morals or worship, the holy law drives far away.
Keep away unclean harlots, lest they bring the wages of a night
they have sold to the eternal sanctuary of the Lord.
Whoever shelters a runaway, let him not return him to his master,
lest the master cruelly torment the captured man under the harsh lash.
Let no one gather a harvest grown in another's field,
nor seek to press wine from grapes that grew
on his neighbour's portion; it is indeed lawful to pluck
grapes and ears of grain, but not to take away the whole.
If a wife driven from her home happens to marry
another husband, and afterwards is widowed by losing him,
let her not return to seek again the partnership of the bed that spurned her.
Let no one send away a new bride before the year is complete.
Nor let a mill be sold, which, hollowed with twin stones,
whirls round in a circle and breaks the grain.
Let no one pay the penalty for another's crimes.
Let him receive forty lashes on his back
who fiercely hurls abuse with foolish words.
Let the mouth of the threshing bullock not be bound.
If by chance a man has died with no child begotten,
and has a brother living, let the surviving brother bring the widow
to his house and beget children, lest, with no offspring,
the house be left empty and the line, now void, fall into obscurity;
but if the man refuses, let the woman at once plead her case
before the elders and invoke the law that compels the reluctant.
Whenever treacherous quarrels turn into a brawl
and drive men, gnashing their teeth, to blows against each other,
let no woman throw herself into the midst of them, nor
seize the private parts of another woman's husband.
Whoever devoutly does these things is touched by no
plague of evil, and fears neither wars nor burning fevers,
nor knows a barren year when the months have run their course,
but rejoices in peace throughout his whole life,
as God grants him riches, God who gently looks down on the crimes of the world
and punishes them in the time of wrath."
With such words the prophet pleaded, and he charged all
the Levites, who have the care of the venerable hall
and of God's sacred rites, to read the commands of the eternal law
constantly to everyone, so that the fear of God
might be more ready in the hearts of all men,
and also to keep the tablets, smoothed from twin stones,
which hold the ten commandments to be feared throughout the world,
shut away in the inner chamber of the holy ark.
This done, he bids the son of Nun come forward,
and by God's judgment gives him the right to rule the people;
and so that the Jewish band might gladly overturn the altars
and the lying gods, he puts his words into a melodious hymn.
THE SONG OF MOSES.
Let heaven give ear and praise God,
the heaven that spreads its veil above the stars;
and let the earth, divided by the swelling sea,
lend its ears and take in the sounds
which my speech, the messenger of the mind, utters:
as the earth is wont to drink the rainy dews
when, through the burning flame of fierce heat,
the crop wastes away in the dusty field;
the grasses smile and the world brings forth,
and the parched ground, split by many gaping cracks,
drinks in the fruitful rain clouds.
For I have called upon the name of my Lord,
to whose glory it is fitting that deserving servants
render honours and praises.
Truth clings to his words,
which flourish forever in strong youth.
His right judgment and just ways
entangle travellers in no windings:
nothing is unjust, nothing crooked.
The Lord of blessed faithfulness
does not repay guilt in full measure of its deserts,
although a race faithless to its covenants
swiftly works its own punishment.
Alas, people doomed to sorrowful death!
Is this what you repay to the Lord our God,
to him who prefers to be called father,
while he gives his servants the name of sons,
though he rules all things with eternal power
and could destroy you with sudden death?
He established you, he created you,
he who holds you now and will hold you hereafter.
Remember rather the everlasting age
and the things that live on after death and burial;
inquire into the years that the course of the future will take up
and the things that are to be created anew.
Or if your mind grows dull, entreat your father,
who will at once teach you everything,
or ask one of the elders:
he will scatter the cloud and give light.
When the Lord, ever high above the stars,
had given the world its divided peoples,
whom Adam, the first father, begetting them,
gave over to anxious toil upon the earth [?],
as the word of the eternal God had commanded,
he set a limit and a number to the nations,
such as the starry hosts possess.
The people of Jacob clung to the Lord,
whose inheritance is assigned to him himself:
for it lives as the heir of the Lord God,
alone, sufficient and steadfast in itself,
in a land that lies denied to dwellings,
panting under the hot flames of the sun,
watered forever by no streams.
There God, drawing out the guilty,
struck them at once with a deserved plague
and soon gave them holy healing,
placing them under his right hand, as a bird labours
to shelter its chicks beneath the cover of its wings,
as we ourselves are wont to keep hidden the central light
of the eye, through which we see,
lest any chance blow should harm it.
For those whom the Lord alone took from the enemy,
he who set up the heavens and made the earth
prepared food of many kinds,
which the earth bears when watered by rains;
the rocks gave streams of honey
together with flowing rich oil;
the udders of the flocks gave milk for food;
the fruitful earth produced harvests of wheat
and wine from juicy grapes.
Yet filled with these streams, the youth
in drunkenness exults to deny the divine power
whose gifts have enriched its reign!
Worse, following pestilent rites,
it prepared rich altars for demons.
The eye of the Lord God saw these things
and prepared a death fitting their deserts,
scattering the guilty and driving them far away,
since it seemed more right to him
to prefer an unknown nation to the deserters.
Fire flashes from the mouth of the Lord,
which, as it ranges through the whole world,
blazes out, dreadful even to the underworld.
It lays low the pastures and destroys the crops
and whatever has sprung from the scattered seed.
The stars shine and the mountains blaze
when the Lord is stirred to just anger
and strikes the fearful with his burning dart.
Ghastly pallor will kill their bodies,
the pallor that comes upon the starving breast.
Some the winged birds will carry off;
some the beasts will devour with their teeth;
some, wounds harder than iron
will make mourn for their children destroyed;
so that at last Judea may cease to think herself
rich as though by her own gift.
A wounding enemy will destroy her,
while a thousand flee and fear one.
But the Lord returns serene once more,
as in his gentleness he at once calmed all his anger,
far unlike the gods of the guilty,
whose vineyard is the vine of Gomorrah,
all too fruitful in gall-bitter juice,
more deadly than all the venoms of asps.
The time of death now hastens, see,
in which the Lord, the avenger, restrains all.
And now ask your pestilent gods
to be present, to help, and to lighten your punishments,
so that healing may come back in answer to your prayers.
I alone am the Lord, see: I alone
am the founder of life and the judge of death:
mine is the right to spare, mine the right to strike!
No mightier judge of the heavens
exists who could rescue from death
one whom the hand of the Lord restrains.
And as I raise that hand through the starry heavens,
I shall say: "I shall decree it for the everlasting ages,
drawing my sword bare from its sheath,
which, as it whirls among the trembling enemies,
shines white with flashing lightning,
deadly to those below and fearsome to those on high."
Rejoice always with the Lord, O heaven,
whom the whole sky and the angels praise,
and the nations, joined with his people as equals.
For the Lord bursts forth after long anger,
and, while he strikes the wicked from above,
he spares the submissive and preserves the godly.
After the prophet had sung these strains worthy of God,
to see from the summit of Mount Nebo the land
given to the people whom he had governed,
he climbed the lofty ridge, and then, his task done,
he died, his body covered by no tomb.
His life lasted twice sixty years,
fearless in all things and happy in its course,
broken by no misfortune and subject to no disease:
indeed, even at the time of his setting, his eyes kept
their fire, clear in their untroubled sight.
JOSHUA.
Meanwhile the Lord, deigning to approach Joshua,
promises that he will be raised high by mighty gifts,
and bids him cross the ford of the pleasant Jordan
and pitch his marked-out camp on the enemy's bank;
he is to found new homes in a remote part of the earth
and settle the people in rich places.
He also learns the nations, each by its own name,
as far as the great mountain that its people call Lebanon,
and on to your banks, you who glide down in your sloping course,
Euphrates, who part the Persians from the Syrian border,
or to the sea that heaves, swollen with wind-driven waves.
For besides his outstanding strength once battle is joined,
which strikes terror far and wide into peoples pale with fear,
the Jewish soldier trusts in the Lord's protection.
The Lord granted him a remarkable reward from the stars
and enabled him to take rich lands without a wound.
"Come now, take up the cares of a man," God thunders,
"so that the people may soon take possession of the kingdoms given them.
And do not turn your eyes away from the book of the law,
so that you may stay safe and never be bereft of the everlasting Lord."
At once he addresses the scribes who carry out his orders:
the people are to gather provisions and suitable weapons,
for he is about to lead his strong cohorts to the wars close at hand
when the third dawn's streak tints the world crimson.
He also addressed the tribes who stayed beside the Jordan:
they were to leave their flocks and children in the lands they had received
but wage the common war, and then, once the peoples were conquered,
return home; these were the peoples they were to drive out under the Lord's leadership.
Eagerly the tribes join their wedges and merge their columns,
ready for every hardship and seeking it with swords and prayers alike.
Meanwhile he orders young men chosen from the warlike host
to track out what places there are, what men hold them, and where the nation's walls stand,
and to report swiftly what they have seen.
While they survey the rich estates in the heart of the land,
they slip through the unguarded approaches of the city
and secretly survey the site and houses of Jericho.
A harlot takes them in, a woman long known as Rahab,
secretly hides the frightened men, and soothes them with earnest words.
When this was reported to the king, with menacing threats
he demands the men in hiding, but she, speaking with a steady mind, says
that both had long since left through the double gates,
though she had secretly covered them in a hollow among stacked wood.
The king's men search for them along every byway
and, as though an enemy were pressing, shut the city gates.
But once the tyrant's search had ceased, the harlot
turns to the young men and spoke like a prophet:
"I know, brothers, what rewards the Lord
has bestowed on you since he first brought you out of dark Egypt:
how in the middle of the sea the water, held up in a swelling flood,
stood for you like a huge wall;
or how, across the empty sands of the barren desert,
snow-white manna supplied you with the food of heaven's dwellers;
or how the fearsome kings who lived beyond the roaring streams
of the Jordan fell by your sword
and left their ancestral cities to you, the victors.
Why say more? Pallor has seized our minds and hearts;
no one takes up weapons or trusts in the curved bow;
no infantry packs its bronze ranks for battle;
no four-horse war chariot flies on its iron-bound wheels.
To you, young men, true victory is given, to you
by the King of the stars, who made the earth and the heavens.
And now, young men, promise me on oath
that when the walls collapse and the ramparts are laid low,
my safety will be placed and entrusted in your hands,
so that I may not become a captive, along with my family and household,
my parents and my dear ones, whose welfare weighs on me."
They agree, and she is told to keep at home all
whom she wishes to live along with her, and as a sign
to hang cords of broom carefully from her window,
so that when the army pours through the captured city
the wool, dyed crimson, may be seen.
Eagerly they cross the ditches and reach safety
on the hill of Aisamo [?], lying hidden for three days,
so that, while hurrying back too hastily to their camp,
they might not run into pursuers coming from another direction.
The harlot, assured of her own safety, carries out her instructions.
The leader, too, informed by the young men's report,
swiftly breaks camp in the valley of Shittim and from far away
speeds forward, and he encourages their spirits by giving all of them rest
for three days; and he urges the scribes to tell the people
that when they see the sacred ark carried before them
and the priests advancing behind the lofty altar,
they should promptly and eagerly raise their standards and leave a space
of about two thousand cubits, and should purify their bodies
in running water, since they were to stand before the face of the Lord.
Meanwhile the leader, honored by the Lord's favor,
shines out, outstanding and worthy of Moses' line.
And now the priests, ordered to cross the river,
dip their bare feet at the edge of the bank;
then the twelve tribes, as they were told, provide chosen officers
to pick gleaming stones from the middle of the riverbed,
so that twelve stones taken from the wet sands
might bear witness that the river was dried up for the people to pass.
They also set similar stones, alike in number and kind,
in the middle of the channel, where the moving water
washes over them and floods them, slippery, with its roaring current.
Then the tribe of Reuben crosses the stripped riverbed;
Gad follows, with the half-tribe of Manasseh hurrying along,
and they send forty thousand men to the war.
Suddenly the flood that used to run down the river
is held back, and the course of the waters is bridled as if by ice;
the lower part of the river flows swiftly away
and vanishes into the ocean, plunging into its vast tide,
from the region that holds the body of holy Moses
to the boundless sea with its restless waves.
And when they had crossed the Jordan in their crowds,
the ice is loosened, softened by the sun's warmth,
and joins the banks, drained before, with the stream once more.
When the tyrants on the other side learned of this,
their spirits sank; no one was held firm by courage.
Then the leader made knives from twelve stones,
and with them, as he had been commanded, he circumcised the people.
For during forty years in the desert this great people
had borne strong sons, now numbering many thousands more.
They are given a long rest, so that a scar, slowly closing,
might ease the sufferers' painful wounds.
Next the Passover is kept, and the white manna is withheld
from people now rich in grain, which an abundant harvest everywhere
offered to the people as they eagerly reaped the wheat.
Unleavened bread of snowy flour feeds them in their joy.
The feast of the holy night is celebrated in the open field
in the month of new fruits, after twelve days had passed.
From the gates above, a crowd of frightened people looks down on all this,
guarding their camp and walls with picked soldiers.
Meanwhile the prophet catches sight of a man threatening with a sword
and gladly hurries to meet him,
saying: "From which side do you come?
Are you one of ours, or rather of the Phoenician race? Tell me."
At once he is granted the answer he longed for,
as the exalted God declares: "I have come down now
from high heaven: I am he for whom a glorious army
serves throughout the stars, and under whose command it lives."
At this Joshua rejoices silently, his joy mixed with fear,
and falling to the ground and worshipping God, he speaks thus:
"O Lord, who have deigned to leave your boundless throne,
what do you bid your servant hasten to do, what tasks to undertake?"
He is told to loosen the straps on his feet at once,
since he had set his feet on holy ground.
He also sees that Jericho, strong with walls and firm with barriers,
will fall, and sees the fierce nations
and the death of the kings whose ruin goes along with it.
