Swiftly he surrounds the walls with his whole army,
placing the priests and the sacred ark behind them,
and he commands the priests, to make the people bolder,
to blow the terrifying blasts of seven trumpets.
Then, as ordered, the army silently circles the city,
so that, closely packed, it may then raise the battle cry
when the watchword gives the officers the terrifying signal.
And now the seventh day had opened on a joyful world
when Joshua orders the bronze-clad ranks to advance to battle
with confident step, and to send a vast roar
from their chests, and their weapons quickly follow it.
No ram shakes the masonry and batters down the towers
or attacks the walls and proud gates;
instead the roar and the mighty voices, sounding together,
act as a deadly siege engine, and at it the walls sink down
and everything lay open, stripped of its bars.
At once they eagerly burst into the overthrown city,
destroying everything with sword and devouring flame.
One woman alone was granted the safety she had earned;
she was spared the slaughter of her fellow citizens and kept hidden in the camp
along with her kinsfolk, so that no soldier, not knowing her,
might kill her as he roamed from door to door.
The rich goods are set aside for the Lord of hosts,
from all the things that could delight the eye.
When this was done, the leader made the people swear
that no one would try to rebuild the fallen walls,
on pain of losing his firstborn for laying the foundations
and then his last-born if he should attempt to raise the gates.
Meanwhile wickedness spoils their happy successes.
The people go after idols and bow down to worship
stones set up by hand, believing rocks to be gods.
Their ringleader is Achar, son of Carmi, the son of Ambri;
following him, the band abandoned the Lord and the law.
But they did not long rejoice in forbidden things: for after three thousand
men were sent, as usual—the shame of it!—across the enemy's
fields, believing that the young men of Ai would easily be frightened and conquered,
they fearfully turn their backs and flee across the fields
and in headlong flight make for their camp and their leader again.
When this disgrace reached the leader's ears,
he tears his clothes and beats his foreseeing breast.
At once a crowd of mourning elders joins him
in supplication, while Hoshea pleads with innocent words:
"O Lord, why did you bring your people
out of their home in Egypt? Why hold up the waves
of the sea, and then everything that you know you gave
from your mighty and generous hand, than which nothing is richer?
Was it so that the arrogant Amorite might lay your afflicted people low?
Then it would have been safer to live beyond the great river
that opened for us, dried up on its thirsty sand.
What will your wounded people do, or what will it say in its confusion,
unless you would rather thrust your chosen ones into slavery?
And yet true salvation and the gifts of sure healing
lie with you, and all that gentle mercy grants.
The nations you had given us to conquer will gather together;
the Jebusite and the Amorite, in a combined phalanx,
will stir up fierce wars against you, highest Creator.
Will you then let the proud laugh at your name,
and will nations that do not know you have the upper hand?"
The Lord is moved by these words and told the prophet to rise,
gradually revealing the crimes of a shameful guilt
that must be punished by death for whoever had prompted such deeds.
Then, when the first light of day had driven off the dark night,
he rouses himself from sleep, sets his companions to work,
and goes through the related tribes name by name;
finding the guilty man, he gives the wicked to death,
while their cattle too are cast into the fire.
Achar first confessed the crime he had committed,
wretched man, inflamed with greed for plunder and spoils,
which he kept buried in the ground of his own house.
Men are sent at once to search for them; they were quickly found
and laid out before the leader and the thronging people.
When he saw that the plunder sought was all there,
the ruler speaks thus and terrifies the frightened man:
"Come, tell everyone now what madness seized you,
or what good your ignorant handling of these things did you,
that you forgot the law and followed the ways of the guilty?
Had not the glory on high saved the people,
the victorious Amorite would have bowed our free necks beneath the yoke.
Come now, pay on behalf of all the penalty for your misdeeds,
so that our God and Lord may return to the camp he has saved."
When he had said this, a shower of stones is raised
and crushes the condemned man and strikes down his offspring;
and his cattle and whatever goods he had kept
the white-hot flame seizes and reduces to gray ash.
When this was done, their troubles were removed: God looks kindly
on everything and restores to all alike their customary
strength, with which they could drive back every army.
Then the ruler receives the Lord's remarkable commands
on how to draw up the allied cohorts for any war:
he is to choose a thousand young men outstanding in strength and age,
so that, as they prepare a stratagem of war, they may take cover in the thickets;
he hides them silently not far from the walls of Gergesa,
so that when he begins to turn his back in pretended fear
and lures the men shut inside out onto the plain,
they may swiftly leave their wooded hiding places
and strive to get through the gates left empty of men.
Without delay, everything turns out as the prophet planned.
After the squadrons have fought in slanting columns,
the leader ordered his men to turn their backs at once,
and the hostile crowd rushes upon them in a dense mass,
presses on with much shouting, and brandishes the sword.
Seeing this, the cohort that lay hidden in the hollow valley
flies out and breaks into the city through the empty gates,
setting swift fires to the lofty roofs.
Then, when a confused noise and a sound of weeping
forced the Gergesites to turn their heads and look,
they see black ash flying up to the sky,
balls of flame spewing from the captured rooftops,
and an enemy force threatening them from behind and in front:
trapped, they shudder and drop their nerveless weapons.
Before the eyes and faces of their weeping parents, run through,
some are driven into steep ditches as the victor rushes on,
or dash themselves against the gates of the captured city.
Twelve thousand young men are laid low by the sword.
The king himself, too, exultant and daring to burst out onto the plain,
is captured in the first assault and held in chains
and nailed to a cross; stones give him a wretched tomb.
Everything was consumed; the fire swallowed all
but what eager hands snatched; and only the beasts of burden
that carry loads on their backs were spared from death.
Meanwhile word of the victory flies back to the kings; all of them
hear it: the Amorite who lives by the pleasant Jordan,
those who set their halls in the thorny mountains
or live in fertile fields and sloping valleys,
and those who dwell on the shore of the blue sea.
The Hittite and the Canaanite whisper together,
the Hivite trembles and the Perizzite wavers,
and the Jebusite band and the Girgashite alike turn pale.
Yet they are not wholly broken; though utterly cast down,
they raise their spirits and steel themselves for battle:
all share one desire, to drive Joshua from their realms.
They gather at Gabana and halt their columns there.
Joshua, amid the cares of war, builds an altar
to God after the custom of Moses; no iron
binds it, while the stones hold together, fitted
level with one another; and he brings out offerings
pleasing to God, from which a sweet fragrance rises on high.
He also writes out the statutes of the teaching law:
its name is Deuteronomy, since it goes over again what has passed;
and it is right that the whole world should know it too.
The gracious ark is carried on the priests' shoulders,
so that everyone may see the gifts of the highest Lord.
And the prophet, accustomed to bless the people,
runs through what was first commanded and what was then forbidden,
with a full account of events and in proper order.
But when the people of Gibeon see that by their great successes
the Jews had grown strong and slain the tyrants,
overthrown cities, and that no one could resist them,
they cunningly hatch a crafty scheme,
and though their territory adjoined Israel's lands,
they pretend they have come from a far-distant country,
admiring the hero's trophies and fresh victories,
hoping that by their prayers they might join hands with the victor,
unite their homes with his, and attach their whole nation to him,
to live on agreed terms, unless hostile hearts
should scorn the humble and reject necks bowed in submission.
And to keep up the appearance of good faith,
they drive mules weighed down with heavy loads,
carrying moldy grain with great haste and effort,
held in old sacks that were worn out;
and wineskins, patched where they had been torn many times,
scarcely hold the wine, for the splits will not keep in the liquid.
Their clothing left their bodies bare with tattered rags;
their shoes gave wretched covering to their worn-out feet.
The leader of the people gives way before them; won over
by their suppliant hands, he believes their hearts match their words.
He receives them as they beg for pardon and admits them to the camp.
But, as often happens, falsehoods are not hidden for long,
and the evidence of the truth exposes the contrived deceit.
At once the prophet rebukes them to their faces, though kindly;
and because he had sworn by the name of the eternal Lord,
his pledge of friendship stood; but equal rights were denied them:
they were ordered, as menial servants around the sanctuary,
to carry water from clear springs, with no share in the land.
When it was reported to Adonibezek that these people had defected—
he then ruled the Jebusite kingdom from his court—
he stirs up five kings, loyal to the war he had undertaken,
more fiercely hostile to his former allies for breaking the treaty
than to the people who had routed vast armies in battle.
But Gibeon, terrified by the gathering of so many kings,
sends envoys and begs the prophet, its friend,
to come at once with his whole army to help them in their distress.
Without delay he takes up the standards and leaves Gilgal,
making for the enemy camp, while the Lord gives him strength
with these words: "Do not fear the names of the kings,
so many together, nor think their cohorts strong;
however much their troops trust in their vast cloud of numbers,
their infantry will achieve nothing, nor will their weapons avail;
scorn their four-horse chariots armed with curved scythes.
For I will shake the nations with pale fear;
nowhere will the enemy meet you hand to hand on equal terms,
scattered by your strong army in overwhelming slaughter."
When he heard this, he marches against the numerous enemy;
for the tyrants held Apaphum [?] as their base for the war,
and at once they abandon their soldiers and take to flight.
The rest of the crowd of men fell in a heap of confused slaughter
and lay strewn across the open plains.
Nor did the victors' sword strike down as many dead
as did the hail pouring thick from an icy cloud;
and though swords flash on one side and bright lightning on the other,
a single day is not long enough for such triumphs.
So, seeing the swords grow blunt and the slaughter slow,
the leader begs the Lord for help, as he was accustomed to do:
"However long its hours stretch, this daylight is not enough
unless you command the hours of night to be added to the day.
Let the flame of the wandering sun now stand poised and still,
and let the moon's circle not move its trembling fires,
so that the heavenly bodies, as if not knowing how to run to their goals,
may prolong the time while the massed enemy falls."
He is heard at once: the sun stands still, and the wandering moon
checked its easy course from either pole.
He also ordered the kings who were hiding in hollow caves
to stand in the open with their necks in chains.
Then the Jews run up from all sides, laying down their weapons,
and pressing down with their knees they trample the necks of the groaning kings.
At once the lifeless kings are fixed on high crosses,
hanging there until dark night returned.
Then he takes the men's hanging bodies down from the wood,
and they are weighed down with heaps of piled-up stones.
When this was done, the warrior hurries to subdue Libnah,
and he kills the old; nor were the children spared the sword;
no one at all in the whole nation was allowed to live.
Next Lachish is attacked, and burns with its walls laid low;
the king of its people too is captured and put to the sword.
Debir also, buried in similar ruin,
perishes, its army wiped out along with its allied tyrant.
And the people who held strongholds on the thorny hills
or dwelt in the winding valleys and low-lying plains
fell, their companies destroyed along with their king.
And while everything flowed happily with success upon success,
Jabin, seeing the brave deeds of the victorious nation—
he ruled the rich kingdom of Hazor and its peoples—
hurrying to put out the flame of a war on his doorstep,
gathers outstanding kings and fierce peoples.
Roboam quickly comes to him from the court of Madon,
and Somorus, and Axinus, who became his comrade in arms,
and the chieftain who reigned in the citadel of Sidon.
Ceneritus and Arabus, whose kingdoms bordered his,
strengthened their resolve out of loyalty to an allied throne.
Ernadurus joins them, and Chanannus, who farms lands
that border the sea, and those who see the sun's red
beginnings when the rosy sky first opens.
Besides these, the Amorite, neighbor to the Jebusite, hurries up;
the Hittite, the Hivite, and the Perizzite follow,
who dwell in the remote wilds of barren Thitsa [?].
All are minded to attack in one dense crowd.
Then each hurls his darts after his own fashion:
here the infantry advances, and in a dense cloud
the four-horse chariots charge with iron-clad soldiers,
so that the very din might rout the enemy pressing them at close quarters.
But on the other side Joshua presses on, not at all afraid,
coming by the waters known by the name of Merom;
and when he had climbed a hill with picked soldiers,
he charges down from above and crushes the unsuspecting enemy.
Everything is drenched in slaughter, and the earth is stained with blood.
Soon fire set beneath them devours the swift chariots,
and the horses' legs are hamstrung with the sharp sword.
Asurus himself, chief of the kings, gives his breast to the sword;
his city too falls, undermined, with all its walls.
Here all the plunder is given in common to the victors.
In this war he slew twenty-nine leaders,
he alone, who had received his signal from the starry court.
Forthwith the prophet assigns and divides among the people, man by man,
the cities taken from the many nations that perished,
cities spread across the breadth and the quarters of the earth:
from where the flame of coming day glows saffron-red
beyond the river called by its ancient name, the Jordan,
as far as the low-lying valley called Hebron,
to Mount Hermon, which rises with its vast summit,
and to the sea of Amar [?], to Chinnereth and its gray-blue waters,
and to remote Pisgah and the place long called Ashdoth.
When the wars were over, only one prize remained:
the ruler of Bashan (the ancients called him Og),
fierce with the strength of the giants whom he ruled and led,
whose home was Ashtaroth and his seat Edrei.
His land is given to two tribes to plow
and to a half-tribe, since the fertile, grassy valley pleases them:
to Reuben and Gad together and to their ally Manasseh.
The rest the leader shares out fairly among all his allies.
To this is added the region where Lebanon rises into the sky,
and the sea of Misrephoth and the fertile fields of Sidon.
The Lord withholds from the Levites any title to estates.
Balaam, who used to foretell the future, is slain.
But Caleb, his companion, whose heart was ever bound
to the leader, speaks, steadied by a calm spirit:
"You know my mind, leader,
from that time when we were sent together to view
the enemy's lands, and while everyone trembled, I alone,
with you as my partner, declared that nothing could withstand us;
that however huge the giants who might start new wars,
God stands against them and takes our side.
You surely remember how the old man kindly promised
us the greatest things, and by a separate lot
gave this hill to me and to all my family.
And now, since a war with the race of Anak remains,
I will wage it with the young men of my clan, not weakened by age,
though my fortieth year has now come round twice.
Remember the arrangement, and assign me the place I ask for,
for my sons and my sons' children to hold as their own."
At his request Joshua settled him on the hill of Hebron.
Ardoc too is added, a city not inferior to great ones.
When this was done, he hurries to destroy the people of Debir,
whose customary work was writing learned words
and having grave teachers dictate the alphabet to boys.
Caleb calls forth a man to win the hand of his promised daughter,
one with ready courage and a resolute spirit in his breast.
Meanwhile, though all the other peoples were forced into servitude,
the Jebusite band does not leave its ancestral fields,
and the Canaanite stays on at home in the houses of his fathers.
The rest of the land is measured out and handed over to nine tribes.
For the Levites he rightly sets apart six cities
and made them a refuge for anyone who feared punishment for a harmful deed,
so that punishment might not fall on wrongs committed by accident.
He charges the elders to weigh these cases in a balanced scale,
so that, if the deed was more serious, a fitting death might condemn the guilty.
He himself dedicates forty cities to the Levites,
who have no share in the land's yield. Then, by the people's unanimous voice,
he receives the hill of Ephraim for all time to come,
with a city attached to it on the heights, whose name remained Timnath.
Here he buried the knives made of hard stone,
and with them he had cut away the parts that decency forbids us to name.
When all this was done, he addressed his comrades, who wished to go back
and live beyond the waters of the Jordan, with these words:
"Band dear to us and chosen by the holy Thunderer,
by your brave deeds you have earned the same honours
that the Almighty gave to all who have built
their homes on these hills. And now go back rejoicing.
Above all, one thing I will repeat and often urge on you:
be mindful of the everlasting care
with which the Almighty loves you, and the rewards he has given you;
and know that what he has commanded us to do in his holy words
must be kept, because eternal life
is gained by these things, if the grace of God's law
remains unoffended and dwells always in the heart.
Therefore let our God and Lord be both feared and loved
with all our inmost being and with all our heart:
so it will come about that nations are pressed beneath your yoke."
When he had said this and prayed for blessings on them all,
they finish the journey they had begun, draw near the river,
and set up a conspicuous structure with a towering top.
When this monument they had built came to the notice of the nine tribes,
the tribes, as though their kinsmen had forgotten the Lord, were eager to clash with them in war;
yet first men were sent who could learn the truth:
Phinehas was chosen, Aaron's shining heir,
and ten leaders of the tribes, foremost in merit and in rank,
who, mindful of their charge, set out the commands
of the chief and the elders alike, though the dismayed tribes were guilty of no crime:
"Tell us, what was your purpose in building a shrine?
Has God slipped from your minds? The oracles of the holy law?
Have you then forsaken the Thunderer and gone seeking
pagan rites? Do you, the living, build altars to the dead?
Was it so slight a lesson that Peor gave us all,
condemned to a hideous end for its wretched daring?"
This message the people and the elders sent in anger against the tribes,
while they prepared for war among allies and took up arms again.
"Were the acres of land given to you too few,
though they pleased you? Or if you wish to extend
and push out your borders, take from our fields:
only let the mother synagogue remain forever consecrated
to the starry Thunderer, and not stand apart from us in discord.
Let the deed of mad Achan warn your minds,
when he fashioned lifeless idols out of hard stone.
Did not the headlong evil of the crime he committed
rouse the avenger who struck the whole people for the guilt of one?"
They humbly replied with gentle words like these:
"We worship the one who created all things by his holy word
and who sees the crimes that lurk in the silent depths of the heart;
nor is there any need for us to call witnesses to public deeds:
God himself knows the reason that raised this altar.
Our concern was to build beside the river an enduring structure,
so that a testimony might remain to the land we have taken,
lest at some time the oracles of the holy temple, divided
among the believers, should become a reproach to the generations to come.
We know nothing of offerings made to empty gods.
No indeed, may no such madness ever change the devout,
that anything should please them which displeases the Lord on high!
For us it is right to slay and lay out only those victims
which the synagogue has been accustomed to offer to the everlasting God."
At these words their faith was plain, and the tribunes, now at peace,
left them rejoicing and honoured with well-deserved praise.
Meanwhile the prophet, now grown old with long years,
summoned the people and filled them with faithful counsel:
"You see, my fellow citizens, how long old age
weighs upon me and my limbs grow slow with their last movements;
and now I warn you, or, if you do not mind, I beg you,
let God be your life, and the law be always on your lips,
and let a mindful heart recount in speech what he has bestowed
on us and on all the fathers of our ancestors.
For the fierce nations whose kingdoms you now hold
were not tamed by our sword, nor struck down by our bow,
but by the Lord, who in his kindness went before our standards and our column,
marching ahead of us whenever the enemy came to close quarters;
who sent an icy terror and so subdued such great peoples,
and willed that kings should give way before us;
and who, preparing fields emptied for our farmers,
after war and arms bade wild creatures burst forth,
so that with their gathered stings they might devour the rest.
Come, then, and learn how the sea was dried up for you,
and how the river, halting its course in an unheard-of way,
stood solid, as though its thin surface water,
though not yet bound into ice, had hardened in the summer heat:
so that through the vast ages God may receive the praise
due for that immense deed, while the tongue, in harmonious applause,
sings that nothing is higher than the one God.
Go on where the teaching of the law leads you,
lest your course, driven through winding turns, should go astray.
Let no idols of the conquered peoples survive among you.
Let the Lord be your God, God most high and God most great.
But if empty and lifeless deities are dear to your hearts,
say so. I will depart, so that those who worship vanities may not harm me.
Choose, all of you, whatever suits you.
The Almighty abandons deserters and drives them far away,
he who once, in the face of the schemes of baleful Balak,
promised only the more joyful things through the prophet who became his friend.
Look at what you hold, what mighty enemies you have routed,
and what great gifts God adds to all the faithful.
Worship him, and bind your strong minds to the law."
The people answered the prophet with one voice:
"Hear, greatest of leaders, where our trust lies:
him who deigned to lead us out of the lands of the Nile
we worship, and we all acknowledge that he alone
is God of heaven and earth and the deep sea;
at whose command the waters of the Red Sea opened,
and who gave signs that fully answered our prayers,
who subjected all nations beneath our feet."
When the people had spoken these faithful words,
a praiseworthy page was drawn up in holy words.
The old man himself recorded in a book the stone by the terebinth,
so that it might be known as a witness to everlasting faith.
So, when the deeds of his life were complete, that most excellent leader,
whose life had stretched across a hundred
and ten years, died and was given, as he deserved, to a tomb
on the hill of Ephraim, which had been the place fitted for his dwelling.
Because of the merit of his righteousness, no friend wept for him.
They laid beside the chieftain's ashes only the knives
with which the youth of Judea had been circumcised;
and the bones of Joseph rest, laid in Shechem,
where the body of Jacob also had been buried.
After him Eleazar left this earthly life.
So when such great men had died after their glorious deeds,
the people took up pagan worship and idols,
fleeing from the Lord of the earth and Lord of the heavens.
For these deeds they were made subject to the tyranny of Eglon,
and lived as captives for forty years.
JUDGES.
After Joshua had departed from his illustrious career
and God had given his servant rest after the wars,
at once Judea, swelling with pride, sought a leader for itself;
and first it asks the Lord what his will may be,
so that the band of Canaan, not yet subdued in war,
which stirred its rival hearts with warlike tumult,
might learn to submit to rule once its sword was struck away.
Judah is set over them, and he, with his brother Simeon,
at once joins battle and destroys the Canaanites.
Along with them the Perizzites are laid low in the common slaughter:
nearly ten thousand fell, their blood poured out.
The very head of the war, the cause of great evils,
its leader and chief, was Adoni-bezek: as he strayed in flight
he is seized and pays the penalty his crime deserved.
For with hands and feet alike cut off in an unheard-of way,
he mourns with flowing tears the limbs he no longer has,
the very limbs he once used when, wicked, he raged in a like deed:
before this he had maimed the bodies of seventy kings.
So he suffered the penalty he had inflicted, and, paying evils
fitting his deeds, he died at Jerusalem and left his kingdom.
Jeru itself is also taken, and, burned through with flames,
it falls, swiftly torn down in vast ruin;
after that Hebron falls, and the Canaanite youth
who hold the lofty ridges of land rising to the sky.
Then Debir is taken in an anxious struggle, a city rich
and skilled from of old in unfolding the measures of learned speech.
And so that its walls might fall the more swiftly,
Caleb, her father, offered to join his daughter Achsah in marriage
to the man who, towering in mighty arms,
should utterly overturn its sloping citadels.
At once, fired with desire to win the promised bride,
Othniel, the praised offspring of Kenaz, takes up the task;
and when he had fulfilled his joy and his vows were accomplished,
he receives her as his earned prize, with a great dowry from her father.
For he gave him high acres, lofty on curving hills,
and granted the use of the waters she longed for.
Sent off, they hasten, and leaving the familiar walls of the City of Palms
they search out the lonely sands of the desert.
Swiftly they come to where the rushing south wind spreads its wings
and veils the stars with shadowy clouds.
A home is made for both, which they call by the name of Arad.
And Amalek, taken in, is joined to these pleasant fields.
Then Judah attacks Zephath, tilled by the Canaanite,
and calls the subdued land by a grim name,
that it should be banished and forever set apart.
Gaza alone he could not bring under his scepter,
nor Ashkelon and Ekron, nor subdue the territory of Ashdod.
He himself, trusting in God and joined to the eternal Lord,
won easy success in every war.
He took possession of the hill country, because he was not able to subdue
the winding valley, which had been vowed to brave Caleb.
After these deeds the band of Joseph, with Judah as avenger,
hastens to destroy Bethel with the warlike sword.
It had once been Luz; in time it changed its name.
When they had hemmed in its walls here with a terrifying host,
they seize a man who chanced to come out, and ask him
to show them the ways into the city, by which, entering in dense column,
they might break down the iron-bound gates.
The first reward the young man asked for was his life,
which he earned by gladly tearing down his ancestral rampart,
a traitor, letting them into his own walls by hidden stealth:
to ransom himself, he sold his kindred city,
and after the destruction of his fellow citizens he flees
to the acres of the Hittites and builds a hall named after his homeland.
But on the other side Manasseh did not hold the estates of Beth-shean,
which had been seized by Scythian settlers,
nor Taanach and its daughter towns, nor the heights of Dor,
nor Ibleam, nor the fields of Megiddo joined to these;
for the Canaanite had long been settled in these lands.
He alone, when all were captured by avenging Judea,
earned the right, there in their midst, not to lose his ancestral seats,
since he was accustomed to render the benefit of perpetual tribute.
Only he whom Midsa [?] nurtures, and whom the farmland of Beth-shean,
remained exempt and paid no tax to the foe.
No less fearless, the Amorite, scorning war,
drives out the offspring of Dan and hems them in with the sword,
since, having forced them to live on a swelling hill,
he had not allowed them an easy way back down to the plains below;
they dwelt on a mountain where a great throng of wild beasts
teems and terrifies the glades with varied roaring.
Then the routed band conceives a returning wrath
and, inflamed by its own wounds, comes forth more warlike.
And it strips the victor of just now of the honor he had won,
and orders the Amorite to pay the tribute imposed on him,
and keeps him in check, fined of a great part of his lands.
For where Idumea lies, a plain of fertile soil,
and where the rugged rocks of overhanging Akrabbim swell,
the victor holds it all; servitude presses on the subject.
Amid these things the Lord shakes forth his gathered wrath,
and bids his servant descend from the heavenly realms
to deliver faithfully the eternal words of the Lord.
He flashes forth in flight, visiting the Place of Weeping from Gilgal,
coming to Bethel, where the youth of Judea,
with wars laid to rest, had taken up sweet leisure,
had worshiped the gods of the Gentiles, and long since had offered
profane and harmful incense to carved stones.
So he approaches them with these words and terrifies them in their fear:
"Unmindful of my command and forgetful of your own history,
where are you rushing, Judea? What deities are you now fashioning?
What superstition is this, to set earth above heaven
and to wait upon clay gods with insane worship?
Where has God gone, profane one, who, when you groaned under harsh burdens
among the nations of the Nile under the tyrant Pharaoh,
brought you out through the divided sea, over the scorching rocks of the desert,
and made such great nations yield before you,
only that, victorious and done with all your wars at once,
you should fall away and dedicate other rites and sacred things
than those the rule of the heavenly law had given you?
See, you hold the land that was sworn to the holy prophets
and is given through the ages to a chosen people.
The covenants of my word are no longer known,
since, mingled with Gentile peoples and evil counselors,
you pray to mute gods, the offspring of craftsmen.
Rather, it would have befitted your way of life
to crush all these things and turn away from false worship.
But since no faith has been given to my commands,
I will give kingdoms to the conquered; I will send you back under the yoke,
so that you may be like the gods you believe exist."
When Judea had received these commands of God,
it turns to groaning and, beating its sorrowful breast,
begs pardon with flowing tears; nor was there any delay
in answer to their prayers: as they made petition through God's holy temple,
mercy attends them, which opens gladness to the grieving.
So the scattered people returns gladly to its familiar
homes, and gave the place a tearful name. [?]
Again their hearts waver; they return to their accustomed crimes
and worship the Baals; and since the Lord is offended by such things,
they suffer the punishments they deserved for their false gods.
They are made subject to masters they had conquered (alas, bitter grief!),
nor does their once-proven valor come to the help of the wretched anywhere.
Soon God's anger is softened and leaders are raised up,
who snatched the people from headlong danger.
When these too are despised, the accustomed madness rises again,
and they do not merely share the rites: they join in marriage,
and dedicate unshorn groves and restore the altars.
Yet their deeds do not go unpunished: they are crushed
by servitude and tremble before the king Cushan-rishathaim,
who then gave laws where the island that divides the twin rivers
separates the Persians from the Assyrian border,
keeping them subject for eight returning years.
At last Judea groaned over its deserved guilt
and, prostrate, implores the Lord; and he, softened, with friendly
power restored the comforts of life to the fearful:
for a savior is sent and is at hand, and brings salvation to the people
and wipes sad cares from their hearts:
a warrior, sprung from Kenaz, the hero Othniel,
vigorous like his brother Caleb, but younger in age.
The Spirit of the Lord raised him up, renowned for the gift of valor,
and set him on high in a lofty seat.
Strong and faithful to God, he took away the perils of the conquered
and forced the frightened king to serve.
In such circumstances Judea for many years
prospered and was exposed to no treachery.
But after the leader, having run the course of his life,
lay down in death, the people gladly restored their old rites;
times change, and war and servitude press upon them;
the peoples whom King Eglon led gather together,
Ammonites and Moabites alike, and the brave Amalekites,
and rout the Hebrew battle line with a hail of iron,
and as victors wrench away the very scepter of the City of Palms.
The nobles surrender, seeking to escape death,
and they endured masters for ten and eight harvests.
Bent by these evils, the nation shudders at what it had done
and calls upon God, who alone forgives sins.
At once Ehud is chosen to take up the scepter:
striving with either hand with the strength of the right,
he never felt his left to be weaker under any burden.
When he was bringing his people's tribute to the victor,
secretly girded beneath his garment with a two-edged sword,
he was admitted, and then, bowing low, he does homage to the king,
who was infirm; for his limbs, bereft of muscle, tottered
so much that he could fall down at the slightest push [?].
He declares that he still has something he wishes to say,
and asks the crowded throng of attendants to withdraw.
It is granted, and the barbarian leader, seated in the middle of the hall,
rises and, coming near, presses close to him with his whole body;
and once the band of trusted men had gone far off,
Ehud snatches from his thigh the sword he had hidden under his garment
and buried it wholly in the king's belly, up to the hilt.
Then he rushes out, leaving the blade in the wound,
shutting the doors and proud doorposts on the great man.
But the servants, wondering that their lord, who usually came out to his duties,
remains alone in the silent chamber,
suppose that perhaps he is relieving his bowels
in private, avoiding the eyes of his attendants.
And now Ehud, mindful of his deed, rouses his comrades to war
and stirs up the terrible blare of the trumpet:
swiftly moving his standards, he seals off the banks of the Jordan,
so that no one could cross its shallow streams.
And when he had cut down ten thousand with the hard sword,
he restored to his people their lost name and glory.
Then wars fall silent, battles stir no unrest,
and weapons rested for twice four times ten years.
After this Shamgar, proud in equal valor,
ruled the Jewish peoples and left them glorious.
But while their joys feed on carefree times,
the grim race grows weary of God, and with vain prayer
consecrates altars to the wretched deities of those it had conquered.
So they are afflicted with punishments and pay penalties
worthy of their crime. Jabin, a royal hero,
gathering a Canaanite force from the youth of Hazor,
makes war with Sisera as commander and chief of the army,
and fills his iron battle lines with nine hundred chariots.
And although he leads vast squadrons in a loyal column,
the terror he sought achieves still more: for with flying axle
the hoof shakes the crumbling plain with four-footed thunder.
The people of Jerusalem are everywhere defeated as the Canaanite rampages,
and they pass twenty Decembers through every kind of sorrow.
At this very time the prophetess Deborah rules,
whose husband was Lapidoth, her home Metibile [?],
giving laws to the peoples, leaning against the trunk of a palm.
She summons the chieftain Barak from the city of Kedesh,
and, instructed by God's admonitions, commands ten thousand
to take their stand against Sisera's wedges of troops.
He is afraid and asks the prophetess to be his ally in war,
not knowing that the palm of the great undertaking would be denied him
if he called to the camp as his equal the one to whom the first glory belongs:
but the woman, a woman only in her sex, takes up new duties
and moves the chosen cohorts through the barbarian farmlands
to the river Kishon, which, coming down in a headlong flood,
rolls rocks along and, swelling, delights to overrun its banks.
And now the battle lines had come within a spear's throw,
when the Lord, in whom is the power by which he changes the stars,
by which the lands tremble, by which lightning blazes in the clouds,
by which he warns the restless sea with its receding surge,
sends terror upon Sisera and puts him to flight; he, rashly headlong,
abandons his chariots and, taking every byway,
left his army to fall in the midst of the fight.
Driven by thirst (for he had fled the enemy on foot),
he asks Jael for a drink; soon, covered with a skin,
he hurries to save his life by a woman's gift;
but Jael, eager for glory, scorns the helpless man
and swiftly drives a stake through his hollow temples.
Seized by icy death, his brain flowing out,
he breathes out his thin life through his pierced head.
Then the leaders sing to the Thunderer in words like these:
"Whoever is renowned for royal power, you who govern great cities,
who are a satrap or bear a scepter second to the king,
bow low and worship God. Give worthy songs
to the Everlasting; for the Lord wishes to compel you to nothing else,
he who shakes the lands, who shakes the rocks, who with his blast
stirs up the sea and furrows the black clouds with thunder,
who raises the lofty from the lowly, who overturns the great.
Sing, sweet-voiced choirs, and let hills and woods
answer back, and let the sky renew the praises with its ringing,
and let the echoes at once join in harmony with your voice.
The Lord has looked again on those he had abandoned, and to the sorely broken
he has restored dominion and taken them back from the midst of the enemy."
So for forty years there was wondrous rest.
And while they enjoy good things, their guilt returning once more,
what had been condemned pleases them; for they gladly
set up idols and abandon the name and power of God.
The offended Lord ravaged them for seven years
and made them, in their fear, serve the king of Midian.
They do not venture onto the open field, nor present
their breasts to the foe, but are content to hide behind walls alone:
now in fear they strengthen camps and lofty fortifications,
and, hidden in hollow caves, even so they grow pale.
Then all their cattle begin to be seized, all their estates
to be burned, and nothing but punishment is left in their enclosures.
So, destitute, and fearing famine and the sword together,
they returned to the Lord God, who is moved
by the suppliant throng and sends a prophet bearing his holy commands,
that at last, mindful of past events and the recent war,
they should look back and worship the Lord, who with favoring power
called back his beloved people from the city of Pharaoh,
lest again, while they kindle altars with forbidden flames,
they incur the wrath of heaven, which is not always easily appeased.
Then a messenger of God sat beneath a pleasant oak
and urges Gideon with these words as he threshes the wheat:
"Come now, no more delay! The Lord has bidden you to take up
the scepter, by which you may rescue the people from harm."
He tells the Lord's messenger, in biting words on every side,
that the Lord is hostile and deals out grievous ruin all too heavily;
moreover, that the people is exhausted, with no soldiers left,
and that he himself is too weak to be able to press on in war.
He is urged to serve God, who with lofty strength
terrifies armies of every kind by his invincible might.
He assents to the commands and invites the holy one to a meal;
a kid is chosen, which, fed on milk alone
and more tender than all the rest, wandered not yet knowing grass;
soon unleavened cakes made of snow-white flour are set out:
having bidden the young man pour these out on a nearby rock,
he himself, stretching out his hand, touched them with the very tip
of his staff, and left the man in the middle of their conversation.
So when Gideon saw clearly, and pondered with devout mind
that the Lord's minister had flown before his eyes,
he at once raises an altar consecrated to the Lord
and gave the place a name, and called it Peace.
Warned by visions in the night, he overthrows the temples of the Gentiles
and tears up the groves by their deep roots.
And so that his profane father might not raise
quarrels against him, he silently by night overturned what had been wickedly built,
setting a young bullock at the overturned temple.
When these things were discovered and made plain, and the sudden ruin
inflamed their minds, the author of the deed is sought throughout the town,
and they learn that Gideon had laid the groves low.
Joash is asked to hand over his son for the crime.
Refusing, he reminds them that the gods are their own avengers
and ought to protect what is theirs, if they exist and are alive.
At this the Spirit of the Lord strengthens Gideon for battle;
already the war trumpets sound; the horn gives the signal.
The Lord is asked that on a fleece of white wool
the dews of heaven might flow in the nighttime:
without delay it was soaked through, and when wrung out it filled a basin;
then he set another test in turn: the ground was wet,
and the wool stayed dry and felt none of the frosty moisture.
To these was added another: that he should order twenty-two thousand
of the fearful common people to go back again,
and that the total of the fighting force be set at ten thousand.
At God's warning he reduced this number too, lest the assembled throng,
trusting in its own strength, should fail to see the arms of the Lord.
When the leader of the young men brings the troops down to the river,
he orders them to lap the flowing waters as dogs do,
so that he might have comrades of eager valor.
Three hundred men were approved; for the rest of the throng,
listless, did not take the drink in the way shown with the palm of the hand,
and were to return to their homes as men who knew nothing of battle.
Relying on this band, he makes war on so many thousands
that they cannot be counted even by men whose custom it is,
taught by skill, to reckon totals on outstretched fingers:
on this side, ranks of horsemen with companies of foot mixed in,
on that, countless camels of grim bulk.
But Gideon, hastening, with his servant Purah following,
makes for the enemy camp and, covered by dark night,
goes down, and surveying the site and the minds and spirits of the men,
he heard someone telling a comrade a dream
which, sleeping fitfully, he had noted with wakeful senses.
For he seemed to see a loaf rolling toward him,
the kind made of barley whenever wheat is lacking,
and wheeling this way and that through the camp, through the ranks,
until it came through the middle of the rampart's defenses
and with its weight burst deep into the king's quarters.
These portents, the men declared, were an omen
of bloodshed, and they say the end of Midian had come.
When the young man, having worshiped the Lord, had gone away from there,
with heightened spirit he begins to unfold to his men the dream he had learned,
and soon leads his band out in three columns.
He puts trumpets of horn in their hands as weapons, and torches too,
and bids them take him as their example in the task,
and, giving thanks to God, to make the opening of the battle,
so that the Lord, under whose leadership they would conquer, might not fail them.
The first hour of the night had already changed the watch,
when they rush swiftly at the gates and tear away the closed
bars, and fill their trumpets with windy blasts;
then they whirl the jars, which, struck with great force,
burst apart; they rouse the glades, and with ringing bronze
they make a din and raise their broken cries to the stars.
The rows of flames held out in their left hands flash
and, shining, overcome the night with abundant light.
At this uproar their spirits are shaken, every mind is terrified:
wherever a gate is open, they rush out and abandon the terrified camp.
Soon all Judea gathers and pursues the scattered fugitives;
some seize the watering springs and roaring rivers,
so that the enemy throng, scattered by fear, their veins parched with thirst,
might rush headlong into the weapons of the guards.
Nor did so great a stratagem fail; for in headlong column
the chiefs of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb, come on,
fierce, and meet steel instead of water.
And although envy of his valor tormented those
who had been far off and had no share in the common praise,
yet Gideon, with eloquence and humble speech,
soothed them, since they held the twin trophies of the leaders.
When after the battle he kindly asks Succoth for provisions,
he is spurned because part of the struggle was still unfinished,
and they say the enemy kings are still alive;
yet he puts off the punishment they deserved and withdraws with threats.
Then he finishes the task begun and clings to the fugitives.
He finds the Sabaeans pitching camp at Karkor;
for they were packing their column with forty thousand men
after the slaughter in which a hundred thousand had fallen by the sword,
and twenty thousand besides: this number was renewing the war.
But the whole race, entangled in its own deserts, fell.
Zebah the commander, after so many deaths of his men,
and Zalmunna flee; but their minds, overcome by danger,
faltered, as they came to the mockery of their final lot.
For Gideon leads the two captives together through each place
and shows them to the men who earlier, with harsh muttering,
had laughed with stupid guffaws when he asked them for food.
Without delay their guilty limbs are dragged through thorns,
and the unshorn briars are spattered with the men's blood.
Moreover, so that no trace of so great a crime might remain,
the city falls, overthrown by the sword, and its menacing towers,
torn up from their foundations, collapsed in long ruin.
Then he orders the kings brought into the open, and a crowd
of wondering people surrounds them on all sides; then he ordered them to tell
what men, and with what slaughter, they in their pride had laid low
in the place where Judea perished. They said the men had been such
that the splendor of their looks revealed them as sons of kings.
He turns his brothers over in his brotherly heart,
picturing the bearing of the slain as though they were there in the flesh.
Then, deeply moved, he speaks thus: "I call you to witness, holy one, God
almighty, and the sublime deeds of your right hand,
that you grant a memorable reward to a woman's praise."
Tola follows him, who for twenty
and three years was troubled by no plague of war.
Then Jair the Gileadite flourishes, and in peace
equally mighty in many things [holds the scepter for twenty years] . . .
very rich, a father rejoicing in thirty children,
noble, he holds the kingdom for twice eleven years.
After his death new idols swiftly spring up;
for besides the accustomed altars of the demon Astarte
and the gods of Assyria, or of Sidon and Moab,
Judea took up for itself rites unknown before.
Because of these, oppressed by the Ammonites in harsh wars,
it dragged out twice nine winters, worn down by dangers.
At last it reflects deeply, and at last it ponders
that God must rather be appeased, who by his supreme power
could put an end even to the long guilt of the people.
And they renew the holy laws of God: for at once they throw down
the altars, and break all the gods and the stone
idols, mindful of the Thunderer who abides through the ages.
Meanwhile the order of events turns in its separate courses,
and the people chooses a leader who, with a steadfast army,
might govern the cities in war or in peace.
A certain Jephthah found favor, born a Gileadite,
whose noble birth drew a stain from his mother,
who lived in a brothel, prostituted to men everywhere.
His brothers drove him from home, because as a tainted heir,
lacking a known father, he shared his mother's lot.
Fearing them, he fled, and among dark hills
found companions in crime and lived on plunder.
But on the other side the Ammonite was waging war,
pressing hard on the Jebusites of Jerusalem; for Judea
lacked a leader and, weakened, offered easy triumphs.
Young men are sent to meet Jephthah, famed in war,
and call him to battle with flattering persuasion.
At first he refused his help; soon he joins the ranks
and, holding command, drives back the Ammonite enemy.
But first, ready to put out the war by negotiation,
he gave instructions to envoys, who then, returning,
report that nothing was achieved and say the enemy is pressing on.
So when the hope of the longed-for peace was set aside,
Jephthah rushes to the sword, and praying to the Lord
he vows great vows, which the father would bitterly regret:
namely, that whoever should first meet him on his return
would become a fitting victim for the eternal Thunderer.
This done, he advances exultant, and with chosen soldiers
moves his standards and routs the enemy, and destroying them
with bloody slaughter he swiftly overthrows twenty cities:
but as he returns, while he himself is the herald of his own glory
and victory follows, coming on in a long procession,
his daughter, who alone looked after her father's household,
runs to meet him and sings sweetly with a band of companions,
and lightly rises on tiptoe to kiss him:
when her father saw her, he tears his girded garments
and moves to weeping the eyes that behold his misfortune.
"Alas, victory deadly to my fate! This vow
has proved more my enemy than the foe! Where are you running, daughter,
where are you rushing? This is the last time I shall speak to you.
For while, moving my standards, I asked the Lord for protection,
you, made a victim to God, are brought to the holy altars."
But the maiden, untroubled for herself and her blessed death,
rejoices all the more sweetly and plays amid the danger.
She even entreats him to hold firm to his decision,
and not to doubt or waver as her father; and she asks for a short
time in which she may mourn her youth with tears.
It is granted, and two months are given her, rejoicing.
So the appointed day was at hand, and her father, acting as priest,
was sending her maiden soul up to the Lord in heaven.
Meanwhile the people rushed madly to arms,
and fury drove kindred ranks against each other. Devouring envy,
while it carped at the man's godly deeds, destroyed itself:
for thirty-two thousand fell by the sword
from your peoples, Ephraim; and, victor in the war,
Jephthah earned triumphs even over his own countrymen.
Judea, bereft of its former leader, took a new one.
Ibzan, at first a plain Israelite, was afterwards named leader.
Chosen, he took up the reins as ruler of his country.
He was the father of many: for forty
sons were born to him from lawful marriage; such was his hope of grandchildren
that he kept thirty brides at one and the same time.
When seven years were completed while he ruled and judged,
he died, and, covered by a tomb, left the things of this world.
Elon the Zebulunite followed and held the sceptre;
after ruling for twice five years he left the government.
Soon after him came Abdon, son of Hillel, as chief,
the father of thirty daughters; for his male offspring
were forty, while he was a far richer
parent through a concubine and in his number of bastards.
He held the judgeship of the people for twice four years.
And as long as the worship of God alone flourished, lasting
peace was kept for the happy people; but idols, once more
worshipped by the men, stirred up bloody war;
for the Lord subjected them all to the arms of warring foes
and made them pay the penalty for eight times five years.
In those days Manoah was in the vigour of youth
and not yet a father; for, joined to a barren wife,
he prayed that he might rejoice in the distinction of children.
To his wife the Lord, gliding down from above the heavens,
appeared, promising the gift of an unaccustomed birth,
and commanding that her son should not taste wine or strong drink,
nor allow unclean things to be bitten off with open mouth,
because she would be happier than all
mothers and would make up in one child for the lack of many.
"For he will be of noble strength, and no one will be allowed
to violate his unconquered head or harm it with a blade;
he is chosen by the Lord from the fruitful womb of his mother,
so that he may save the people and, beating back war,
fiercely turn its losses upon the enemy companies."
She came and told her husband; for she said
the man's face was aflame, and that she had seen the glory of a shining God,
and that when she asked God's name the Thunderer had kept silent.
"He who is born of you will be a Nazirite," she said.
Manoah supports his wife, joining his prayers to hers,
that the holy one who had been sent might repeat his godly words
and kindle a new light, by which he might learn
what befits the boy, who is loved though not yet born.
At once he is sent down from heaven, and, bringing new tidings,
he hastens, and seeing the wife lying on the grass,
her husband being away, he immediately stands close beside her.
She rises and, running to her husband, tells what she had seen.
He follows, trembling yet glad to look upon the holy one,
and sees a face shining with extraordinary light.
He approaches and asks the man whether he speaks the truth,
and to set out what he wishes done. To them, with serene countenance,
the angel declares that the same rules must be kept
in all things, and that the child to be born must not put his lips to unclean things,
nor drink wine or strong drink, nor take any cups
that could drive the mind from its senses.
Exulting, the young man offers the holy one a kid to eat;
soon he is bidden instead to offer to the Thunderer the customary
gifts, which He might wish to accept in return for the gift of life.
Moreover, they seek to learn the Lord's name,
which no one can search out: for it is wonderful.
Then the young man brings out the offerings commanded him,
setting the goat-born young at the holy altar.
Soon, rising in flames toward the bright stars,
the crest of fire struck the upper air and reached the sky,
and through it the holy one, plainly seen, climbed the clouds.
Without delay, her womb swells with the promised child,
and the longed-for offspring is given. By a fixed name
his parents called him Samson: on this both agreed.
And while the boy, tottering, planted his first steps,
he walked with God as his companion; for the Spirit
was his guide, at whom the earth trembles and whom the stars obey.
Relying on him, he dwelt in the camps of Dan and Eshtaol.
From there, his body now growing to manhood, he came to Timnah,
where he was captivated by the fairness of a striking girl.
He speaks to his parents and asks for her as his wife:
they put him off and say it is not lawful, since the woman
was not born of their tribes. At this he presses the harder,
insisting and swearing to the parents he had
that she had pleased him: the girl he sought is joined to him who desired her.
And as he walks among vines green with flourishing shoots
and silently turns his gaze to each thing in turn,
behold, a lion, as though lord of the wilds of Lehi,
spurring himself on with dreadful roaring and the lash of his tail
and shaking his brawny shoulders, comes against him with gaping jaws.
Catching it, without any effort, with the force of his right hand
he tears it apart and scatters it, rent limb from limb.
Endowed with the gift of a hidden strength, he conceals
the deed and rejoices, content with his own mind as witness.
Some days later he returns and looks for his prey:
and here—a fearful portent, and wondrous to tell—
he sees honey in the very jaws of the lion,
mingled with golden comb. He at once takes it away,
and, having tried it by tasting, the young man more confidently offers it
to his excellent brothers. And now he had begun
to be a terror to many through the great fame of his strength.
So he goes out with thirty men accompanying him together,
men of outstanding strength; then a riddle is put
to them all, and, jesting, he imposes a heavy penalty on them if they cannot solve it:
that they must at once produce garments woven
of snow-white thread, if they cannot speak out the truth.
Beginning, he wrapped his words in an intricate figure:
"Out of the eater came forth food common to men,
and sweeter than the honeycomb it flowed from the body of the strong."
When no one could bring this out with truthful lips,
and the penalty was coming back on his friends after seven days,
confounded, they contrived a trick, and, hating their comrade,
they came to their countrywoman, who, as we said before,
had pleased the man for marriage. And they ask her threateningly
to tell them the secret by deceiving Samson; and if
she does not do it, they swear that flames will be their avengers.
Terrified, with a woman's tears she softens the hard
heart of her husband; for he keeps it locked up, reminding her: what he had not told
his father and his own mother—why does she chatter and demand it?
But what will a woman's tears not strive to compel?
He is overcome and lays bare the secrets of his silent mind.
And she tells the men. On the seventh day
the setting world was growing pale in uncertain light:
the companions answer: "What is sweeter than honey, or what
can be stronger than a lion shaking his mane?"
The hero at once recognizes that it is his wife's deceit,
and at once says: "O young men, this answer is not your own:
for if a woman had not cajoled me with coaxing persuasion,
the riddle with its tangled terms would never have been known."
Then the Spirit of God sends the young man against the enemy;
exulting, he cuts down thirty, and as victor takes all the spoils
of the fallen, and offers his men the garments he had named.
And little by little the seeds of mighty deeds grow in the man;
for his father-in-law, led by the desire of a wavering mind,
refuses the young man his wife, and gives her whom he has refused
to a stranger, lest afterwards, inflamed and fierce,
he might demand that she be restored; and he promises his younger daughter,
if perhaps he wishes. "Ah, a mighty avenger I shall be!"
he cries, and with grim eyes threatens fearful
and immediate destruction, intending to take long and heavy vengeance
for such daring. He finds a means by which to vent his rage:
eagerly he catches three hundred foxes, and, tying their tails
to one another and joining them two by two in order,
he drives them out far and wide through the olive groves and vineyards of the pleasant hill,
and fastens blazing torches to their tails.
Scarcely released, they made for the fertile fields;
wherever they hasten, they drag widespread fires behind them.
At once the devouring fire, swollen by the blasts of the winds,
rolls on: the flames overflow and, drawn along, follow.
Nor did the trick go unnoticed. The thronging crowd of farmers,
struck down by such heavy losses, gathers together, and
the young men throw into the flames the woman who had once been his wife
and her father too, and burned the roofs of their houses.
Thus their punishment became their grave-mound, the flame their tomb.
Grim vengeance spurs him on, for he threatens much,
and brings ruin with vast slaughter on the enemy and their people.
Meanwhile three thousand young men of the tribe of Judah
burn with hatred, to kill Samson with so great a force
and to attack one man with the swords of so many thousands.
But the young man soon takes up arms and entreats his countrymen
as they press upon him to let him take up the war for glory.
As he wished, a pledge was given: then they bring out bonds
of hemp, which bind his arms with ninefold knots;
he is driven from the rock. He comes to the border of Lehi,
and the gathered crowd rejoiced to see him captured.
And while they eagerly stretch out their hands and threaten with dreadful
roaring, he draws his hands apart and breaks the linen
bonds; then—for what weapon will anger not supply?—
he grips, straining, the curved jawbone of a sluggish ass:
with this (a wondrous thing) he strikes and slays a thousand men.
And when thirst, with his lungs parched, warned the young man
to hope for the help of God, who without any seed
creates all things, for whom, when he wills, a parched thing becomes a spring,
who at his command either waters dry ground or dries up rivers,
who among vast crags and in the burning desert
released watering streams from hard rocks—
without delay, a crack opening in the smooth bone of the jaw
pours forth, and a stream quivers in its escaping course.
The young man is filled with drink from a heavenly flood.
He does wonders and sees great things, and earns praise;
under his rule Judea, strong for twice ten
years, shone forth, trusting in him as leader and soldier.
From there he went away and came to Gaza, where a base woman,
wounded by love, sold her nights to hot-blooded young men.
He went in to her, and she was soon the first cause of his danger.
Behold, the band of Gaza flies to the spot, and with a bar
secures the hard gates and sets iron bolts beneath them,
keeping him shut in, eager to make sport of him as a captive.
About midnight sleep leaves Samson;
roused, he rages terribly: then, beating on the threshold,
he tears both gateposts from their creaking hinges,
and, getting under the load, carries it at a run up the heights
to the ridges of a mountain facing it at a distance. And
stronger than all dangers, the warrior is next captured by love of Delilah.
All the men came to her, whom envy drove
to overcome the unconquered man, so that, joined with him in bed,
she might soften and soothe him with sweet allurements, and soon learn
what nourishments renew his strength, what seeds feed
such might: whether he is so strong by nature or by art?
If she tells them what he says, they affirm that she will be rewarded with a gift.
Entreated, the young man said cunningly: "If I am bound
with seven sinews that the moisture has not yet left,
I shall lose all my strength and be weaker than anyone."
She instructs her people, a deceiving woman deceiving the deceiver.
The young man is bound with the hard strength of sinews,
which with a slight pull he broke as if they were soft fleeces.
And, consulted next, he says he fears ropes
never used, which cannot be loosened by any twisting.
She binds the man when, worn out by toil,
his weary breast was breathing out light sleep.
As soon as he felt the knots, he lashes the air
and laughed at them, as though they were the webs a spider spins.
Twice cheated in different ways, she nonetheless dared to plead
and again tries Samson with a veiled request.
He answered her quite otherwise, and not truthfully, as she asked:
"Undo my hair, and, twisting it back again,
weave it carefully, plaiting no more than one ell;
so it will come about that my strength perishes, stripped of its vigour."
She does what had been told her, and anxiously unwinding it,
she ties it with her hand held up, and, bending it around pegs,
binds it, and Delilah reveals the captive to her companions:
leaping up, he throws off the pegs and unknots his hair.
So often forsworn, so often rebuffed, she fears nothing;
once more, half-mad, she swears with tears made ready
and summoned every art to make it easier.
His softened mind no longer endures her feigned griefs
and fraud, but to his beloved he revealed what was dire for himself:
"I am the Lord's Nazirite, believe me, forever,
and my strength is in my hair, nor does any blade
with iron edge cut my locks: if anyone, applying it,
should leave my neck bare with my head shaved,
that will be the sure end of my unbought strength."
At these words she was convinced: soon, having taken the bribe,
the woman cradles Samson in her lap; a barber hired for a fee
takes away all his strength and his hair.
Samson is shaken from the couch; changed, and yet the same,
he is seized, and God departs along with his strength.
At once he is robbed of both his eyes; for
his eyeballs gouged out left empty hollows,
and he mourns, his legs bound in a hard fetter;
and yet he does not know the darkness that the blind possess.
Shut in prison, he turns the mill with the force of his hand:
thus under a double weight the strength of his flanks served him.
Before long, with the glory of his returning hair,
his locks came back to life, and at the same time
they restored with them both his strength and his comeliness.
Behold, one day the lords gathered in great numbers
to offer solemn sacrifice to the god whom, worshipping vain things,
they hold as a deity. They call him Dagon, and by the name of sea-monster.
While they rejoice there over the downfall of Samson, brought low,
standing far off in the middle of the temple's vault,
they ordered the man to be summoned, who was now ready to conquer.
And he, condemned to die, is dragged in, and to those loosened in laughter
his blinded eyes give occasion for wicked mockery.
It happened that the whole house rested on two columns
beneath it: moving between them, he grips both
and holds them in his whole embrace and leans back,
so that it might fall with greater force; and, having prayed to the Lord,
he brought down an avenging ruin together with his own death.
Bereft of him, his father and brothers and all his kin
gather, mourn the dead man, and honour him with a tomb.
[Shamgar follows him as leader, who with brave daring
slays six hundred and brings back happy times.]
Meanwhile Micah asks his mother for a very large talent
of silver, which the woman, in her faith, teaches him is holy
and vowed to God, but to be returned at a fixed time;
soon he makes lofty offerings to the holy one,
and teraphim and a temple for God; and, with his hands filled,
his younger son brings gifts to the Lord as priest.
Afterwards Micah chose Judah [?], who was seeking a home,
and binds him to himself with a heaped-up store of gifts,
and, taken on, he gained by his vows the shrine of God.
Behold, the tribe of Dan, suddenly seeking new realms,

to search out and test everything: which portion of land

Laish is attacked in war, and, its houses burned,
it loses its dwellings and is denied its citadels to its grieving people.
The victors' band eagerly settles there

There was a certain man, a Levite, who, having no wife,
sought a concubine from among the slave women. She, though given to him, left,
breaking the shared yoke, and, in anger, far away
she flies and flees the partnership of the spurned bed.
When her husband anxiously wished to call her back,
he took with him their common servant and beasts of burden,
and, coming to his father-in-law, he asks for the daughter by right of their bond;
the father promises, and treats him kindly, and, by gradually detaining him,
entices him to stay with him. Soon he, settling down,
eats and rests, carefree, in a peaceful abode.
